Hong Kong Tax Study Hub

Consolidated internal reference for HK profits, property and salaries tax, stamp duty, and depreciation allowances — built for (1) tax computation and taxable/deductible analysis on Hong Kong incorporated companies' financial statements, and (2) team study with worked illustrations drawn from IRD's Departmental Interpretation & Practice Notes (DIPNs).

雙語參考資料，涵蓋香港利得稅、物業稅、薪俸稅、印花稅及折舊免稅額，供稅務計算分析及團隊溫習之用。本平台僅供學習參考，不能取代《稅務條例》（第112章）及稅務局現行指引。

Study material — not professional advice · 學習材料，非專業意見 Nothing here is tax advice, and reading it creates no adviser–client relationship. This is written to one finance team's internal working standard and published openly because the underlying material is public — not because it has been reviewed for anyone else's use. It contains mistakes and goes out of date as the law changes. Verify against the Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112), the Stamp Duty Ordinance (Cap. 117) and current IRD guidance before relying on any figure for a filing position.
本平台所載內容並非稅務意見，閱讀不構成顧問關係。內容按某財務團隊的內部工作標準撰寫，因所依據的資料屬公開而公開發布，並未經審核供他人使用；內容或有錯誤，亦會隨法例變動而過時。在依賴任何數字作報稅立場前，請核對《稅務條例》（第112章）、《印花稅條例》（第117章）及稅務局現行指引。

1. How to use this page

The Study Hub's tax pages state the law as it stands. This page is the audit trail behind them: what IRD announced, whether it is enacted or still proposed, and which page was edited as a result.

MarkerMeaning
EnactedIn force, or an ordinance already gazetted. Safe to apply, subject to its own commencement date.
Gazetted / billPublished or before LegCo but not yet law. Know it is coming; do not apply it.
ProposedPolicy announcement only, needs an amendment ordinance. Do not apply it to a live filing or transaction.
The trap this page exists to stop A Policy Address measure is not law on the day it is announced. Both 2026 Policy Address measures below are drafted into this Hub as proposed, alongside the enacted figure. Quote the enacted figure in any computation until the amendment ordinance is gazetted.

3. Salaries tax & individuals

2026 Policy Address — child allowance 16 September 2026 · proposed

Child allowance rises from HKD 140,000 to HKD 160,000 for a taxpayer's second and subsequent children born on or after 16 September 2026, claimable until age 25 on the usual conditions. The additional child allowance for the year of birth and the following year rises to HKD 160,000 on the same basis — so HKD 320,000 per qualifying child in each of those two years.

ChildBorn before 16 Sep 2026Born on/after 16 Sep 2026
First child140,000140,000 (unchanged)
Second and subsequent140,000160,000 (proposed)

Intended effect from YA 2026/27, but it requires an amendment ordinance. Two traps: the increase does not reach first-born children, and it is keyed to the child's date of birth, not the year of assessment — an existing second child born in 2024 stays at HKD 140,000 indefinitely. IRD source.

4. Stamp duty

2026 Policy Address — newborn-family concession 16 September 2026 · proposed

A family with a child born in Hong Kong on or after 16 September 2026, at least one parent being a Hong Kong permanent resident, would receive a stamp duty waiver capped at HKD 20,000 on a residential property bought in the window from one year before to two years after the birth. Effective on enactment of the amendment ordinance. It is a capped waiver, not a rate change — on any purchase where AVD exceeds HKD 20,000 the benefit is a flat HKD 20,000. IRD source.

Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 3) Bill 2026 — intra-group relief Announced 29 Sep 2026, gazetted 2 Oct 2026 · bill

Relaxes the s.45 associated bodies corporate relief on intra-group transfers in three ways: the association test drops from 90% to 75%; "association" may be established through direct or indirect beneficial interests or voting rights, not only issued share capital; and relief is extended to entities with no share capital to measure, such as limited liability partnerships and companies limited by guarantee. First reading is set for 14 October 2026, and the Bill proposes to apply retrospectively to instruments executed on or after 25 February 2026.

Not law yet. The Stamp Duty page continues to state the enacted 90% test as its primary figure, with the proposed 75% carried as a marked note. The retrospective date matters: if the Bill passes as drafted, instruments already executed since 25 February 2026 that failed the 90% test but meet 75% would become relievable — worth flagging on any live transaction, but not a basis for stamping today. Press release.

Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 2) Ordinance 2026 Passed 8 Jul 2026, gazetted 17 Jul 2026 · enacted

Stamp duty on a transfer of dual-counter stock traded at the RMB counter may be calculated and paid in Renminbi, letting an investor settle trade and duty in one currency at one counter. The 0.2% rate is unchanged. Commencement is on a day to be appointed by the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury, pending HKEX system readiness — so it is gazetted but not yet operative. Press release.

8. Fraud alerts

IRD issued fraudulent-email alerts on 6 July (fake legal prosecution notices), 22 July (phishing for email passwords), 4 September (fake tax audit notices) and 15 September 2026 (fake compliance notices and suspicious links), and warned on 25 August 2026 against downloading the eTAX Mobile Application from any unofficial channel.

Rule of thumb for clients IRD does not ask for passwords, does not send payment links by email, and does not distribute eTAX Mobile outside the official app stores. Any "compliance notice" arriving by email with a link should be verified by phoning IRD directly, not by clicking.

9. Noted — no content change

Read and deliberately not acted on, so a later reviewer need not re-read them: the five "Full text of The Chief Executive's 2026 Policy Address" transcripts (16 Sep 2026, the underlying speech text for the two measures above); LCQ19 on regulating charitable organisations (8 Jul 2026); LCQ21 on e-commerce tax policy and LCQ16 on fertility measures (17 Jun 2026); and the 15 Jun 2026 notice that LegCo would consider the AEOI Bill. These are position statements and procedural notices, not changes to the charging provisions.

Refresh discipline Re-read IRD What's New monthly, and always before finalising a filing position. When you do, update the "read on" date in the banner at the top of this page and add a row to §2 — an undated freshness claim is worse than none.

Exam preparation — TX-HKG (Taxation, Hong Kong)

ACCA TX-HKG

Syllabus coverage against this Hub, what the examining team actually reports as weak, and original practice questions in the exam's own format — worked on the current basis with the exam-year figure alongside.

ACCA TX-HKG 考試考試大綱對應本平台頁面、考官報告所指的弱項，以及依考試格式原創的練習題（15 條 MCQ 及三條 Section B），以現行年度計算並並列考試年度數字。附已驗證的 ACCA 官方連結。
A complete 100-mark mock paper §5 to §11 together make up a full TX-HKG paper at the real weighting: 15 MCQs × 2 marks (30) plus four 10-mark and two 15-mark questions (70). Sit it in three hours against the clock, or take the questions individually. Answers follow each question — cover them first.
Everything here is original or linked No ACCA question, model answer or examiner's report is reproduced on this page. Their material is linked to ACCA's own site, where it is free to download. The practice questions below were written for this Hub. See §10.

1. Exam format

SectionStructureMarks
A15 multiple-choice questions, 2 marks each, across the whole syllabus30
B4 questions of 10 marks + 2 questions of 15 marks. All compulsory.70
TotalThree-hour computer-based exam, predominantly computational100
Section A is 30% of the paper and the cheapest marks in it The examining team note that a good Section A performance "greatly facilitates the task of obtaining an overall pass". Fifteen two-mark questions with no working required is the highest marks-per-minute rate in the paper — and unlike Section B, a wrong figure costs you the whole 2 marks rather than one mark in a chain.

2. Which year of assessment applies

This matters more than it looks, and it is the first thing to settle before working any question.

The June and December 2025 exams were set on YA 2024/25 — not 2025/26 The TX-HKG J25–D25 syllabus and study guide states that candidates should use the latest 2024/25 editions for the June and December 2025 exams. The June 2026 paper was set on YA 2025/26 — its questions state that year explicitly — so December 2026 is examined on YA 2025/26 too, sharing the same syllabus period. Conveniently, IRD publishes 2024/25 and 2025/26 as a single column: the allowances are identical across both, so one set of exam-year figures covers J25 through D26. A past paper worked on any other year's allowances will not reconcile to the published answer.

Everywhere on this Hub the current basis is YA 2026/27. The practice questions below are worked on that basis, with the exam-year figure shown alongside wherever it differs — so you can see both what the rule is now and what the 2025 papers wanted.

ItemYA 2026/27 — current, used hereYA 2024/25 & 2025/26 — J25 to D26
Basic allowance145,000132,000
Married person's allowance290,000264,000
Child allowance, 1st–9th child140,000130,000
Single parent allowance145,000132,000
Dependent parent, 60 or over55,00050,000
Dependent parent, 55–5927,50025,000
Salaries tax progressive bands2% / 6% / 10% / 14% on four $50,000 bands, then 17% — same both years
Salaries tax standard rate15% on the first $5,000,000 of net income, 16% above — two-tiered from 2024/25, same both years
Profits tax, corporations8.25% on the first $2,000,000, 16.5% above — same both years
Property tax15% on net assessable value — same both years

Only the allowances moved. Every rate is the same on both bases, which is why the computations below are identical in structure and differ only at the allowance lines.

Two things on this Hub that are beyond TX-HKG Stamp duty is not in the TX-HKG syllabus — it sits in ATX-HKG. Our Stamp Duty pages are useful for work and for ATX, but do not spend TX revision time on them.
Also excluded by the syllabus: general anti-avoidance under s.61 and s.61A, all specific anti-avoidance provisions, and service company rules including DIPN 24 and 25. Our profits tax pages mention some of these — they are not examinable in TX.

4. What the examining team reports as weak

Summarised in our own words from ACCA's published examiner's reports for June 2026 (the most recent), June 2025 and December 2018. Read the originals — these are the single most useful free resource ACCA publishes.

What two consecutive years tell you
June 2026June 2025
WeakestTax administration · profits tax expense treatment · personal assessment computationTax administration · depreciation allowances · partnerships
BestProperty tax · profits tax computationProperty tax · salaries tax · profits tax
Tax administration is weakest in both years, and in both the report blames the same thing: candidates find written questions harder than computational ones and under-prepare a topic that is "examined regularly". It is the most reliable source of cheap marks in the paper.

Two things moved. Personal assessment became a weak area in 2026 having not featured in 2025, and salaries tax fell from best-performing to "far from satisfactory". Do not assume last year's strong topics are safe.
The one piece of advice the examiners repeat most In a computation, list every item the question mentions — and put a zero (0) against anything that is not taxable, not deductible, or needs no adjustment. The June 2026 report repeats this with the word "again", and every computational question that session carried the instruction in its own rubric. Marks are available for those items, and they are only awarded if the zero appears in the computation. A separate list of non-adjusting items underneath does not get them.

This refines the advice on our Tax Reconciliation page: say "no adjustment" in your working, but in the computation itself, write 0.
TopicReported performance and the errors named
Tax administration
weakest		 Poor, "despite the topic being examined regularly". Candidates were unprepared for written rather than computational questions. Specifically missed: the duty to notify an employee's departure from Hong Kong and to retain money due to the employee. Those who knew the obligation often could not state the time limit and due date. Some answered on record-keeping when asked about notifying chargeability.
Depreciation allowances
weak		 "Far from satisfactory", though not a difficult topic. Those who laid out a proper schedule scored well; those who did not scored very low. Named errors: disposal proceeds deducted from the wrong pool, or not deducted at all; a hire-purchase asset put into the pool; initial allowance on a hire-purchase asset computed on full cost instead of the capital portion of instalments paid; a balancing allowance claimed while the pool still had a positive balance; commercial building allowance brought-forward figure wrong; balancing adjustment on the building omitted.
Partnerships
weak		 Unsatisfactory, and less frequently examined so less well prepared. Candidates allocated on the loss per the accounts instead of first computing the adjusted loss. Non-deductible MPF and loan interest were not allocated to the partners. Few knew that where the partnership has an adjusted loss, profit allocated to one partner must be reallocated to the loss-making partners. Loss relief for corporate partners was not understood. Salaries and MPF for a partner's spouse, and loan interest to a partner, wrongly treated as deductible; MPF for a partner wrongly treated as non-deductible.
Property tax
satisfactory		 Errors named: lease premium spread wrongly; irrecoverable rent miscalculated; a forfeited rental deposit not set off against irrecoverable rent; rates and management fees payable by the tenant treated as deductible or as income; a rent-free period included in assessable rental income; the 20% statutory allowance omitted; irrecoverable rent deducted after the 20%, corrupting the 20% itself; and "assessable value" / "net assessable value" mixed up with "assessable income" / "net assessable income".

June 2026 adds: the rental deposit itself included in assessable income; and a reminder that property tax is computed for each property separately, not on an aggregated basis. On a follow-up part, candidates could say repairs were not deductible but could not explain that they are deemed covered by the 20% allowance and that no depreciation allowance exists under property tax. Covered here →
Salaries tax
best		 Best performing. Remaining errors were in the newer concessionary deductions: qualifying annuity premiums not restricted, and the unused portion not transferred to the spouse; failing to see that the wife's donations should be claimed by the husband to reduce the couple's total liability. Also: employer-reimbursed medical expenses not assessed; relocation shipping and air fares, and interest saved on a staff loan, wrongly taxed; reimbursed medical expenses wrongly included in the base for the 10% rental value; 8% applied to a two-room hotel serviced apartment where 10% was right; hotel service charges treated as "rent suffered".

June 2026 — fell to "far from satisfactory". A share award valued at the market value on the grant date instead of the vesting date; income taxed on a time basis rather than applying the s.8(1A)(c) exemption; reimbursed deductible self-education expenses wrongly taxed while reimbursed medical expenses wrongly untaxed; rental value at 8% where 10% applied; child allowance omitted; dependent parent allowance claimed for a parent holding a Hong Kong identity card but not ordinarily resident here; the standard rate applied to net chargeable income; and foreign tax paid deducted from either the income or the tax.
Personal assessment
weak — new in 2026		 Unsatisfactory on a question the report calls straightforward. Some candidates computed the tax payable when only reduced total income was asked for. Named errors: the 20% statutory allowance not deducted; the loss brought forward not set against the proprietorship profit; approved donations not deducted from that profit after the loss set-off; mortgage interest on the couple's own home not claimed as home loan interest; the share of a partnership loss not taken off total income after the interest and concessionary deductions. And two transfers between spouses missed — that a husband's unabsorbed approved donations and his excess loss can both pass to the wife.
Profits tax — expense treatment
weak — new in 2026		 A "state deductible / partially deductible / non-deductible and explain why" table, and performance was not satisfactory — with many candidates leaving the reasons column blank, which is where half the marks are. Rules not known: the initial one-off MPF contribution is deductible over five years, and an electrically powered car is 100% deductible. Wrong both ways: an employee's salaries tax paid by the employer and the wages of a driver employed by a director are deductible staff costs; compensation for a restrictive covenant is capital and is not; a staff loan written off and its legal fees are not; and a family car bought for a director's use is.
Profits tax computation
good		 Good overall. Errors on less-common items: foreign exchange gains and insurance compensation wrongly deducted as non-taxable; cash paid for a table at a charity banquet claimed as a donation; MPF special contributions — only one fifth is allowed in the year, so 80% must be added back; a staff loan written off allowed when s.16(1)(d)(i) does not permit it; legal fees for dealing with IRD enquiries wrongly disallowed; only 80% of rental income assessed; and the two-tier rate not applied.

June 2026 adds: the finance charge on a hire purchase not disallowed; no tax charged on interest from a HKD fixed deposit used to secure an offshore loan; a capital loss on disposal of a computer not added back; interest to a parent company and to a director not chargeable on it, not added back; commission to a non-disclosed agent not added back; the 100% deduction claimed for an electric vehicle bought on hire purchase instead of depreciation allowances; and disposal proceeds of a hire-purchase computer not taken out of the 30% pool.
How to read that table The three weak topics — administration, depreciation allowances, partnerships — are where marks are cheapest to gain, because most candidates drop them. The three practice questions below target the first two directly.

5. Practice — Section A

Fifteen questions, two marks each, on the current YA 2026/27 basis. Where a 2024/25 figure differs it is shown so you can see both. Answers and reasoning follow each question — cover them first.

Q1 · Salaries tax — source

Ivan is employed by Crestway Ltd, a company centrally managed and controlled in Hong Kong. He manages Crestway's branch in a country with no double taxation arrangement with Hong Kong, and spent nine months of the year working there and three months in Hong Kong. His salary is $100,000 a month. The salary for the nine months abroad was charged to income tax there; the tax of $180,000 was paid and borne by Crestway.

What is Ivan's assessable income for the year?

  1. $180,000
  2. $300,000
  3. $480,000
  4. $1,380,000
C — $480,000. Crestway is managed and controlled in Hong Kong, so Ivan has a Hong Kong employment and is chargeable on all his income. But s.8(1A)(c) excludes income for services rendered in a non-DTA territory where tax of substantially the same nature has been paid there — so the nine months' salary drops out. The foreign tax borne by the employer is itself a taxable perquisite. ($100,000 × 3) + $180,000 = $480,000. The trap is answering $300,000: excluding the foreign salary correctly but forgetting the tax the employer paid.
Q2 · Administration — penalty

Nora let out a flat and did not notify the Commissioner of her chargeability to property tax. She has no reasonable excuse. The property tax that would have been undercharged is $15,000.

What is the maximum penalty she faces under s.80(2)?

  1. $10,000
  2. $45,000
  3. $55,000
  4. $10,000 and imprisonment for six months
C — $55,000. Failure to notify chargeability under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse is an offence under s.80(2): a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged. ($15,000 × 3) + $10,000 = $55,000. Answering $10,000 — remembering the fine but not the treble-tax element — is the common error.
Q3 · Property tax

Raymond let a flat for the whole year at $25,000 a month. He paid rates of $9,000. The tenant paid management fees direct to the building's manager.

What is the property tax payable?

  1. $34,920
  2. $36,000
  3. $43,650
  4. $45,000
A — $34,920. Assessable value $300,000; less rates paid by the owner $9,000 = $291,000; less the 20% statutory allowance $58,200 = net assessable value $232,800; × 15% = $34,920. Management fees paid by the tenant to a third party never enter the computation at all — they are neither income nor a deduction.
Q4 · Property tax — premium

A premium of $240,000 is received on the grant of a four-year lease.

How much is included in assessable value each year?

  1. $60,000
  2. $80,000
  3. $240,000
  4. Nil — a premium is capital
B — $80,000. A premium is spread over the lease term but capped at 36 months (s.5B(4)). $240,000 × 12⁄36 = $80,000 a year for three years, not $60,000 over four.
Q5 · Profits tax — two-tiered rates

Meridian Ltd, a Hong Kong corporation, has assessable profits of $3,000,000. It is the only Hong Kong entity in its group.

What is the profits tax payable?

  1. $247,500
  2. $330,000
  3. $495,000
  4. $225,000
B — $330,000. ($2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($1,000,000 × 16.5%) = $165,000 + $165,000. Answering $247,500 applies 8.25% to everything; $495,000 applies 16.5% to everything. The examiners specifically name "not applying the two-tier profits tax rate" as a recurring error.
Q6 · Depreciation allowances — hire purchase

A van with a cash price of $400,000 is acquired under hire purchase. In the year, a deposit of $100,000 and three monthly instalments of $10,000 were paid; the capital element of each instalment is $8,000.

What initial allowance is available?

  1. $240,000
  2. $78,000
  3. $74,400
  4. $60,000
C — $74,400. For a hire-purchase asset the initial allowance is 60% of the capital sums actually paid in the year, not of the cash price: 60% × ($100,000 + 3 × $8,000) = 60% × $124,000. Computing 60% × $400,000 = $240,000 is the error the examiners name explicitly. $78,000 wrongly uses the full instalments of $10,000 rather than the capital element.
Q7 · Profits tax — donations

Harbourline Ltd's profit after depreciation allowances is $800,000. It paid $320,000 to approved charitable institutions.

What deduction is allowed?

  1. $320,000
  2. $280,000
  3. $112,000
  4. Nil
B — $280,000. Capped at 35% of the profit after depreciation allowances: 35% × $800,000. The $40,000 excess lapses — it cannot be carried forward. Applying 35% to the donation itself gives $112,000, which is the wrong base.
Q8 · Salaries tax — rental value

Priya's income after allowable outgoings is $600,000. Her employer provides her with two rooms in a hotel.

What rental value is assessable?

  1. $24,000
  2. $48,000
  3. $60,000
  4. Nil
B — $48,000. 8% for two rooms in a hotel, hostel or boarding house; 4% for one room; 10% for a flat or other self-contained accommodation. 8% × $600,000. The examiners flag candidates going the other way — applying 8% to a two-room serviced apartment where 10% was correct — so read what the accommodation actually is.
Q9 · Personal assessment — eligibility

Which of the following individuals may elect for personal assessment for YA 2026/27?

  1. A 17-year-old whose parents are both alive
  2. A person who spent 170 days in Hong Kong in the year and 140 the year before, and is not ordinarily resident
  3. A person not ordinarily resident who spent 200 days in Hong Kong during the year
  4. A person not ordinarily resident whose spouse is ordinarily resident
C. A temporary resident is someone in Hong Kong for more than 180 days in the year, or more than 300 days across two consecutive years including the year of election. B fails both (170, and 310 across two years — but only if one of them is the election year and the total exceeds 300; here 170 + 140 = 310, so B is arguable on the two-year limb, which is precisely why you check both limbs; on the facts given B is not ordinarily resident and 170 ≤ 180, and the two-year test would need the 300 to be exceeded — it is, so B would also qualify. C is the unambiguous answer: 200 > 180 on the single-year test). D was the rule up to 2017/18 only — from 2018/19 the elector must satisfy the residence test personally. A fails the age test, which is only relaxed if both parents are dead.
Q10 · Personal assessment — time limit

By when must an election for personal assessment for YA 2026/27 be made?

  1. 31 March 2028
  2. 31 March 2029, or two months after a notice of assessment is issued, whichever is later
  3. Within six months of the assessment
  4. 31 March 2027
B. The later of two years after the end of the year of assessment (2026/27 ends 31 March 2027, so 31 March 2029) and two months after a notice of assessment or additional assessment. Six months is the withdrawal window, not the election window.
Q11 · Depreciation — commercial buildings

What is the annual allowance for a commercial building?

  1. 4% of the cost of construction
  2. 4% of the purchase price including land
  3. 20% of the residue of expenditure
  4. 10% of the cost of construction
A. 4% of the cost of construction, not of the whole purchase price — land does not qualify. No initial allowance is available for a commercial building, unlike an industrial building.
Q12 · Profits tax — bad debts

Which is deductible under s.16(1)(d)?

  1. An increase in the general provision for doubtful debts
  2. A specific trade debt written off as bad
  3. A loan to a member of staff written off
  4. All of the above
B. Only a specific debt, proved to the Assessor's satisfaction to be bad, and only where it was included in assessable profits or was money lent in the ordinary course of a money-lending business. A general provision is not deductible. A staff loan written off fails s.16(1)(d)(i) — the examiners name this exact item as a common error.
Q13 · Administration — objection

Within what period must a notice of objection be lodged?

  1. One month after the date of the notice of assessment
  2. Two months after the date of the notice of assessment
  3. One month after the end of the year of assessment
  4. Six years after the year of assessment
A. One month from the date of the notice of assessment, under s.64. The objection must state the precise grounds — an unparticularised objection can be rejected as invalid. Tax in dispute is not automatically suspended; a separate holdover application is needed.
Q14 · Profits tax — R&D enhanced deduction

Delta Ltd incurred the following on qualifying research and development in the year: plant and machinery $0.6m, a consultancy fee to an independent expert $0.4m, staffing costs of the research team $1.5m, and consumable items $0.9m.

What deduction may Delta Ltd claim under s.16B?

  1. $3.4m
  2. $7.2m
  3. $7.8m
  4. $8.2m
C — $7.8m. Split the spend first. Type B is staffing and consumables, $2.4m: the first $2m at 300% = $6.0m, the remaining $0.4m at 200% = $0.8m. Type A is plant and machinery plus the consultancy fee, $1.0m at 100%. Total $7.8m on $3.4m actually spent. The distractors are the three standard errors: $8.2m applies 300% to all of Type B, ignoring the $2m limit; $7.2m leaves the plant and machinery out as capital when s.16B allows it at 100%; $3.4m takes no enhancement at all. This was the question fewest candidates answered correctly in June 2026. Full treatment →
Q14b · Profits tax — MPF special contribution

Stanhope Ltd made a special contribution of $250,000 to its MPF scheme, charged in full in the accounts.

What adjustment is required in the profits tax computation?

  1. No adjustment
  2. Add back $250,000
  3. Add back $200,000
  4. Add back $50,000
C — add back $200,000. A special contribution is allowed over five years, so one fifth ($50,000) is deductible this year and the other 80% is added back. The examiners list this among the items candidates get wrong.
Q15 · Salaries tax — standard rate

Vivienne's net income, before personal allowances, is $6,000,000.

What is the standard-rate computation?

  1. $900,000
  2. $910,000
  3. $960,000
  4. $1,020,000
B — $910,000. The standard rate has been two-tiered since YA 2024/25: 15% on the first $5,000,000 and 16% above. ($5,000,000 × 15%) + ($1,000,000 × 16%). A flat 15% gives $900,000 and is the pre-2024/25 answer. Remember this figure is only the comparison — the tax payable is the lower of this and the progressive computation on net chargeable income.

6. Practice — Section B: tax administration 10 marks

The topic the examining team called the weakest in June 2025. It is written rather than computational, which is exactly why it is under-prepared — and therefore where marks are cheapest.

Question

Lantau Marine Limited prepares accounts to 31 March. The following events occurred during the year ended 31 March 2027:

  1. The company commenced a new business on 1 June 2026. It has not yet received a profits tax return for the year.
  2. It employed a new engineer, Mr Sandhu, on 1 September 2026.
  3. Mr Sandhu will leave Hong Kong permanently on 31 May 2027 at the end of his contract, and has told the company so.
  4. The company changed its registered office address on 1 January 2027.

REQUIRED: For each event, state the company's reporting obligation, the statutory provision, and the time limit or due date. (10 marks)

EventObligation and provisionTime limit / due date
1 Notify chargeability to profits tax — s.51(2). A person chargeable to tax who has not received a return must notify the Commissioner in writing. Separately, the company must apply for business registration within one month of commencing business. Notify within 4 months after the end of the basis period in which the profits arose — the basis period ends 31 March 2027, so by 31 July 2027.
Business registration: within 1 month of commencement, so by 30 June 2026.
2 Notify commencement of employment — s.52(4), Form IR56E. Required for any employee likely to be chargeable to salaries tax. Within 3 months of commencement, so by 30 November 2026.
3 Two separate obligations, and this is the one candidates miss.
(a) Notify the impending departure — s.52(6), Form IR56G.
(b) Withhold all money due to the employee — s.52(7) — until the Commissioner gives written consent or one month has passed from receipt of the IR56G, whichever is earlier.		 (a) Not later than 1 month before the expected date of departure, so by 30 April 2027.
(b) Retention runs from filing the IR56G for 1 month, or until consent is given.
4 Notify change of address — s.51(8). Any person chargeable who changes address must inform the Commissioner in writing. Within 1 month of the change, so by 31 January 2027.
Where the marks actually are Event 3 carries the most marks and is the one the examining team singled out: candidates knew neither the duty to notify a departure nor the duty to retain money. Two marks are lost by giving only the notification. And throughout, a stated obligation with no time limit attached scores roughly half — the report notes that those who could explain the obligation often could not state the deadline. Give a date, not just a period: "within one month" is worth less than "by 31 January 2027".

7. Practice — Section B: depreciation allowances 10 marks

"Far from satisfactory" in June 2025. Every trap the examiners named is planted below.

Question

Reddane Engineering Limited prepares accounts to 31 March. Written down values brought forward at 1 April 2026 were: 20% pool $180,000; 30% pool $240,000.

During the year ended 31 March 2027:

  1. A lathe (20% pool) was bought for cash, $250,000.
  2. A delivery van (30% pool) was acquired under hire purchase, cash price $360,000. A deposit of $120,000 was paid, followed by six monthly instalments of $22,000 each, all paid in the year. The capital element of each instalment is $20,000.
  3. A computer from the 30% pool, originally costing $60,000, was sold for $18,000.

REQUIRED: Prepare the depreciation allowance schedule for YA 2026/27. (10 marks)

Reddane Engineering Limited — Depreciation Allowance Schedule · YA 2026/27
20%30%Allowances
Written down value b/f180,000240,000
Additions — lathe, cash250,000—
Additions — van, capital sums paid
$120,000 deposit + (6 × $20,000) = $240,000, not the $360,000 cash price		—240,000
Less: initial allowance, 60%(150,000)(144,000)294,000
280,000336,000
Less: disposal proceeds — computer, 30% pool
limited to original cost; $18,000 < $60,000 so the full proceeds come out		—(18,000)
Reduced value280,000318,000
Less: annual allowance(56,000)(95,400)151,400
Written down value c/f224,000222,600
Total depreciation allowances445,400
The trapWhy the wrong answer is wrong
IA on the van's full cash price60% × $360,000 = $216,000 instead of $144,000. On hire purchase the allowance follows the capital sums actually paid in the year. Named by the examiners as a specific error.
Van put in the pool at full costOnly the capital paid enters. The remaining $120,000 of cash price attracts allowances in later years as it is paid.
Disposal taken out of the 20% poolThe computer was in the 30% pool. Also named as a specific error.
Balancing allowance on the disposalBoth pools still hold a positive balance, so there is no balancing adjustment — the annual allowance simply runs on the reduced value. The examiners name claiming a balancing allowance on a positive pool.
AA before IAThe 20% pool's annual allowance is $56,000 on $280,000, not $86,000 on $430,000. Order is: additions → initial allowance → disposals → annual allowance.

Carry the $445,400 forward — it is the depreciation allowance figure in Question 8 below, exactly as a real paper would chain them.

8. Practice — Section B: profits tax computation 15 marks

Question

Reddane Engineering Limited (as above) reported a profit per the audited accounts of $4,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. The following were charged or credited in arriving at it:

  1. Depreciation, $600,000. Depreciation allowances are as computed in Question 7.
  2. Cash donations to approved charitable institutions, $180,000.
  3. $50,000 paid for a table at a charity fundraising banquet.
  4. Interest of $90,000 on a loan from a director. The director is not chargeable to profits tax on it.
  5. A loan to a member of staff, $40,000, written off as irrecoverable.
  6. A special contribution to the company's MPF scheme, $250,000.
  7. Legal fees of $35,000 for answering IRD enquiries on the company's tax return.
  8. An exchange gain of $70,000 on trade receivables.
  9. Insurance compensation of $110,000 for trading stock destroyed by fire.
  10. Dividend income of $120,000 from a Hong Kong company, and service income of $400,000 accepted by the Assessor as offshore.

The company is the only Hong Kong entity in its group. REQUIRED: Compute the profits tax payable for YA 2026/27. (15 marks)

Note the three zeros Items 7, 8 and 9 need no adjustment — and each is written into the computation as 0. That is the examining team's most-repeated piece of advice, and those three lines are worth marks. Leaving them out entirely earns nothing and is indistinguishable from not having considered them.

All three are items the examiners named as commonly mishandled: candidates wrongly deducted exchange gains and insurance compensation as non-taxable, and wrongly disallowed the legal fees for IRD enquiries.

9. Practice — Section B: partnership assessment 10 marks

Unsatisfactory in June 2025, and less frequently examined — so less well prepared, which makes it cheap marks. Every error the examining team named is planted here.

Question

Harbour Spice is a partnership carrying on a restaurant business in Hong Kong. Amy and Ben share profits and losses 60 : 40. The partnership accounts for the year ended 31 March 2027 show a loss of $200,000, after charging:

  1. Salary to Amy, a partner — $360,000
  2. Salary to Amy's husband, employed as a chef — $240,000
  3. MPF contributions for Amy's husband — $12,000
  4. Amy's own mandatory MPF contributions as a self-employed person — $18,000
  5. Interest on a loan from Ben, a partner — $50,000
  6. Depreciation — $80,000
  7. Purchase of new kitchen utensils — $30,000
  8. Replacement of existing kitchen utensils — $25,000

Depreciation allowances for the year are $95,000.

REQUIRED: Compute the partnership's assessable profits, show the allocation between the partners, and state the profits tax payable. (10 marks)

Harbour Spice — Profits Tax Computation · YA 2026/27
Loss per the accounts(200,000)
Add: salary to Amy, a partner — s.17(2)360,000
Add: salary to a partner's spouse — s.17(2)240,000
Add: MPF for a partner's spouse — s.17(2)12,000
Add: interest on a loan from a partner — s.17(2)50,000
Add: depreciation80,000
Add: purchase of new utensils — capital30,000
Amy's own mandatory MPF — deductible, s.16AA0
Replacement of utensils — deductible, s.16(1)(f)0
572,000
Less: depreciation allowances(95,000)
Assessable profits477,000
Allocation between the partners
TotalAmyBen
Salary — Amy360,000360,000—
Salary and MPF — Amy's husband
disallowed under s.17(2), so attributed to Amy as the related partner		252,000252,000—
Interest — Ben50,000—50,000
Prior allocations662,000612,00050,000
Balance, shared 60 : 40(185,000)(111,000)(74,000)
Sub-total477,000501,000(24,000)
Reallocation of Ben's loss share
the partnership has assessable profits, so a partner cannot be left with a loss		—(24,000)24,000
Allocated assessable profits477,000477,000nil
Profits tax — unincorporated business, two-tiered: $477,000 × 7.5% (all within the first $2,000,000)35,775
The trapWhy
Allocating the loss per the accountsAllocation is of the adjusted figure. The accounts show a $200,000 loss; the adjusted position is a $477,000 profit. Named by the examiners as a specific error.
Not allocating the disallowed itemsThe spouse's salary and MPF are disallowed, but the benefit went to Amy's household — they are attributed to Amy in the allocation, not shared 60:40.
Leaving Ben with a lossWhere the partnership has assessable profits, a partner's negative share is reallocated to the profit-making partners. Ben pays nothing; Amy bears the whole $477,000. The mirror rule applies to a partnership loss.
Amy's own MPF added backA partner's mandatory MPF as a self-employed person is deductible under s.16AA. Treating it as non-deductible is named as an error — it is the spouse's MPF that is disallowed, not the partner's own.
Utensils treated alikeNew utensils are capital and added back; replacement of existing utensils is deductible under s.16(1)(f). The question gives both precisely to see whether you separate them.
Corporate rates usedA partnership is unincorporated: 7.5% / 15%, not 8.25% / 16.5%.

10. Practice — Section B: property tax, original and revised 10 marks

June 2025 asked for both the original and the revised computation, and the report notes candidates who produced only the revised one lost marks. This is the same reconciliation shape as our Tax Reconciliation page, at property tax scale.

Net assessable value per the original computation496,000
Rent for the pre-lease and rent-free months, wrongly included (5 × $40,000, net of 20%)(160,000)
Premium not spread over 36 months ($180,000 − $45,000, net of 20%)(108,000)
Irrecoverable rent, net of the forfeited deposit, not deducted ($40,000 net of 20%)(32,000)
Management fees paid by the tenant, wrongly deducted ($24,000 net of 20%)19,200
Revised net assessable value215,200
Four errors, and the tax is more than double $74,400 against $32,280. Each error the examining team named for June 2025 is here: the rent-free period included, the premium not spread, the forfeited deposit not set off against irrecoverable rent, and management fees payable by the tenant treated as a deduction.

Note also the order: irrecoverable rent comes out before the 20%, not after. Deducting it afterwards would compute the 20% on $325,000 rather than $285,000 — the examiners name that too. And every reconciling item above is shown net of 20%, because that is how each error actually flows through to the net assessable value.

11. Practice — Section B: salaries tax, husband and wife 15 marks

Question

Mr and Mrs Kwok are both employed in Hong Kong. For the year ended 31 March 2027:

Mr Kwok received a salary of $1,200,000 and a bonus of $150,000. His employer reimbursed medical expenses of $30,000, and paid $50,000 of shipping and air fares to relocate him and his family to Hong Kong. He is provided with a rent-free self-contained flat. He paid a professional subscription of $3,000, mandatory MPF of $18,000, and made approved charitable donations of $100,000.

Mrs Kwok received a salary of $280,000 and paid mandatory MPF of $14,000. She made no donations.

They have no children or dependants.

REQUIRED: (a) Compute each spouse's salaries tax liability under separate assessment. (b) State, with figures, whether an election for joint assessment would be beneficial. (c) Advise which spouse should claim the donations, and why. (15 marks)

(a) Mr Kwok — Salaries Tax Computation · YA 2026/27
Salary1,200,000
Bonus150,000
Medical expenses reimbursed by the employer — assessable30,000
Relocation shipping and air fares — not assessable0
1,380,000
Less: professional subscription — s.12(1)(a)(3,000)
Income after allowable outgoings1,377,000
Add: rental value, 10% (self-contained flat)137,700
Net assessable income before concessionary deductions1,514,700
Less: approved charitable donations
cap is 35% × $1,514,700 = $530,145, so the full $100,000 is allowed		(100,000)
Less: mandatory MPF contributions(18,000)
Net income1,396,700
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000(145,000)
Net chargeable income1,251,700
Progressive: 1,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 + 7,000 + ($1,051,700 × 17%)194,789
Standard rate: $1,396,700 × 15% (below the $5,000,000 threshold)209,505
Tax payable — the lower194,789
Mrs Kwok — Salaries Tax Computation · YA 2026/27
Salary280,000
Less: mandatory MPF contributions(14,000)
Net income266,000
Less: basic allowance(145,000)
Net chargeable income121,000
Progressive: 1,000 + 3,000 + ($21,000 × 10%)6,100
Standard rate: $266,000 × 15%39,900
Tax payable — the lower6,100
(b) Joint assessment comparison
Combined net income ($1,396,700 + $266,000)1,662,700
Less: married person's allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $264,000(290,000)
Net chargeable income1,372,700
Progressive: 16,000 + ($1,172,700 × 17%)215,359
Standard rate: $1,662,700 × 15%249,405
Tax under joint assessment215,359
Total under separate assessment ($194,789 + $6,100)200,889
Joint assessment is worse by14,470

(b) conclusion. Joint assessment should not be elected. The married person's allowance of $290,000 is exactly twice the basic allowance, so the couple gain nothing on allowances — and Mrs Kwok already absorbs her own allowance in full. Aggregating merely pushes her income, currently taxed at 2%–10%, up into Mr Kwok's 17% band.

The rule to take away from part (b) Joint assessment helps only where one spouse cannot absorb their own allowances — typically where they have little or no income. Where both spouses have income comfortably above their allowances, it is neutral at best and, as here, actively harmful. Never assume it is beneficial: compute both.

(c) Who should claim the donations. Mr Kwok — as computed above. Two reasons, and the second is the one candidates miss:

  • The cap. Mrs Kwok's ceiling would be 35% × $280,000 = $98,000, so $2,000 of the $100,000 would be lost outright.
  • The marginal rate. Mr Kwok's top slice is taxed at 17%, Mrs Kwok's at 10%. The same deduction is worth $17,000 to him and would be worth far less to her — and in fact the deduction would take her net chargeable income to just $23,000, wasting most of its value.

Donations may be claimed by either spouse regardless of who paid them, so the couple should always allocate them to the spouse with the higher marginal rate and sufficient cap. The examining team specifically noted that candidates failed to advise this.

13. Why nothing is reproduced here

Not affiliated with ACCA This Hub is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to ACCA in any way. “ACCA” and “TX-HKG” are used here only to identify the qualification this page helps you prepare for. Nothing here is an official ACCA study resource, and where this page and ACCA’s own materials disagree, ACCA is right and this page is wrong.

ACCA publishes past papers, model answers and examiner's reports free for students to download. That is a licence to use them for study — it is not a licence to republish them. Their PDFs carry "© ACCA — All rights reserved", and this Hub is a public website.

So the division on this page is deliberate:

What this page doesWhat it does not do
Links to ACCA's own PDFs on their own siteHost or mirror any of them
Maps the published syllabus areas to our pagesReproduce the study guide
Summarises, in our own words and with attribution, the weaknesses the examining team reportedReproduce the examiner's reports
Sets original questions in the exam's format, with our own facts and figuresReproduce any ACCA question or model answer
On the practice questions Every question in §5–§8 was written for this Hub. The topics and the errors they test are drawn from what the examining team reported — that is the point of them — but the scenarios, names and figures are ours, and every figure was computed and checked. They are modelled on the exam; they are not taken from it.

Section A Section B Section C

What this is

A large, filterable bank of original Section A-style MCQs, built to mirror the ACCA TX-HKG syllabus weighting and the errors the examining team has actually reported — not a copy of any past paper or examiner's report question.

How the computational questions were built Every computational question's correct answer and its wrong-option distractors come from the same small Python tax-computation module (scripts/qbank_tax.py) that this Hub's other worked illustrations use. The distractors are not arbitrary wrong numbers — each one reproduces a specific error pattern the examining team has reported (forgetting the treble-tax element of a s.80(2) penalty, applying the standard rate to net chargeable income instead of net income before allowances, spreading a lease premium over the full term instead of the 36-month cap, and so on).

Spread over 110 distinct topics; 68 of the 282 questions are computational (the rest test a rule, a deadline or a distinction conceptually).

How to use it

  • Filter by syllabus area or difficulty, or type a keyword or section reference (e.g. s.16B, "premium", "two-tier") into the search box — the filters combine.
  • Random 15 pulls a fresh, shuffled set of 15 questions from whatever the current filters allow — close to a real Section A sitting's length and a reasonable practice pace of under two minutes each. It also resets the score and clears every answer, so each draw is a clean attempt.
  • Select an option, then click Show answer — it marks your choice Correct or Incorrect, then reveals the full explanation and section reference. 1 correct answer = 1 mark; the Score counter at the top right of the toolbar counts marks scored out of questions checked so far.
  • Show all clears the Random 15 selection and returns to the ordinary filtered view — it does not affect the score.

A · Tax system and administration Statutory time limits Easy

Q001. Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify chargeability to profits tax where no return has been issued?

Correct: A — 4 months after the end of the basis period.

A person chargeable to tax who has not received a return must notify the Commissioner in writing within 4 months after the end of the basis period for the year of assessment concerned.

s.51(2)
A · Tax system and administration Statutory time limits Easy

Q002. Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify the commencement of an employee's employment?

Correct: B — 3 months after the date of commencement.

An employer must file Form IR56E within 3 months of employing anyone likely to be chargeable to salaries tax.

s.52(4), Form IR56E
A · Tax system and administration Statutory time limits Easy

Q003. Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify the cessation of an employee's employment?

Correct: C — 1 month before the date of cessation.

Form IR56F is due not later than 1 month before the employee ceases to be employed.

s.52(5), Form IR56F
A · Tax system and administration Statutory time limits Easy

Q004. Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify that an employee is about to leave Hong Kong permanently?

Correct: D — 1 month before the expected date of departure.

Form IR56G must be filed not later than 1 month before the expected date of departure. This is the obligation the June 2026 examining team reported candidates most often missed.

s.52(6), Form IR56G
A · Tax system and administration Statutory time limits Easy

Q005. Within what period must a taxpayer or employer notify a change of the taxpayer's postal address?

Correct: A — 1 month after the change.

Any person chargeable who changes address must inform the Commissioner in writing within 1 month.

s.51(8)
A · Tax system and administration Statutory time limits Easy

Q006. Within what period must a taxpayer or employer apply for business registration after commencing business?

Correct: B — 1 month after commencement.

Business registration must be applied for within 1 month of commencing business, separately from the s.51(2) notification of chargeability.

Business Registration Ordinance
A · Tax system and administration Statutory time limits Easy

Q007. Within what period must a taxpayer or employer lodge a valid notice of objection against an assessment?

Correct: C — 1 month after the date of the notice of assessment.

An objection must be lodged in writing within 1 month of the date of the notice of assessment, and must state the precise grounds.

s.64
A · Tax system and administration Statutory time limits Easy

Q008. Within what period must a taxpayer or employer appeal to the Board of Review against the Commissioner's determination?

Correct: D — 1 month after the determination is transmitted.

An appeal to the Board of Review must be lodged within 1 month of the Commissioner's written determination.

s.66
A · Tax system and administration Records Easy

Q009. For how long must a person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong retain sufficient business records?

Correct: A — 7 years.

Section 51C requires records sufficient to enable assessable profits to be readily ascertained to be kept for at least 7 years after the transaction. Failure carries a fine at level 6.

s.51C
A · Tax system and administration Records Medium

Q010. From what point does the statutory retention period for business records run?

Correct: B — 7 years after the transaction to which they relate.

The period runs for 7 years from the completion of the transaction, not from the year end or the date of assessment.

s.51C
A · Tax system and administration Records Medium

Q011. A landlord letting a Hong Kong property is obliged to keep rental records. What must those records cover?

Correct: C — Rent records, and records of rates and any irrecoverable rent.

Records must be sufficient to establish the assessable value: rent receivable, any premium, rates paid by the owner, and any rent treated as irrecoverable. June 2026 candidates could state the 7-year period but not what had to be kept.

s.51D
A · Tax system and administration Additional assessment Medium

Q012. Within what period may the Assessor normally raise an additional assessment where income has been under-assessed?

Correct: D — 6 years from the end of the year of assessment.

Six years from the end of the relevant year of assessment, extended to 10 years in a case of fraud or wilful evasion.

s.60
A · Tax system and administration Additional assessment Medium

Q013. Where a taxpayer has been guilty of fraud or wilful evasion, within what period may an additional assessment be raised?

Correct: A — 10 years.

The ordinary 6-year limit is extended to 10 years.

s.60
A · Tax system and administration Penalties Medium

Q014. A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $11,250. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?

Correct: B — $43,750.

Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $11,250) = $43,750. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

s.80(2)
A · Tax system and administration Penalties Medium

Q015. A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $24,000. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?

Correct: C — $82,000.

Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $24,000) = $82,000. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

s.80(2)
A · Tax system and administration Penalties Easy

Q016. A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $8,400. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?

Correct: D — $35,200.

Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $8,400) = $35,200. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

s.80(2)
A · Tax system and administration Penalties Hard

Q017. A taxpayer failed to notify chargeability to tax under s.51(2) without reasonable excuse. The tax that would have been undercharged is $46,500. What is the maximum penalty on summary conviction?

Correct: A — $149,500.

Section 80(2) imposes a fine at level 3 ($10,000) plus treble the tax undercharged: $10,000 + (3 × $46,500) = $149,500. Answering $10,000 alone - the fine without the treble-tax element - is the error the examining team reports most often on this question type.

s.80(2)
A · Tax system and administration Penalties Medium

Q018. What is the maximum additional tax the Commissioner may assess under s.82A for an incorrect return made without reasonable excuse?

Correct: B — Additional tax not exceeding treble the amount undercharged.

Section 82A is an administrative penalty - no criminal intent need be proved - of up to treble the tax undercharged. It is assessed by the Commissioner, in place of prosecution.

s.82A
A · Tax system and administration Penalties Hard

Q019. What is the maximum penalty for wilfully and with intent evading tax, on conviction on indictment?

Correct: C — A fine of treble the tax undercharged and imprisonment for 3 years.

Section 82 is the criminal provision: a fine of treble the tax undercharged plus imprisonment for up to 3 years. Distinguish it from s.82A, which is administrative and carries no imprisonment.

s.82
A · Tax system and administration Late payment surcharge Hard

Q020. Tax of $100,000 remained unpaid more than six months after the due date. What is the total amount now payable, including surcharges?

Correct: D — $115,500.

A 5% surcharge arises on the due date ($5,000), and a further 10% is then charged on the tax plus that surcharge ($10,500), giving $115,500. The total surcharge is 15.5% of the original tax, not 15% - the second surcharge compounds on the first.

s.71(5), s.71(5A)
A · Tax system and administration Late payment surcharge Hard

Q021. Tax of $48,000 remained unpaid more than six months after the due date. What is the total amount now payable, including surcharges?

Correct: A — $55,440.

A 5% surcharge arises on the due date ($2,400), and a further 10% is then charged on the tax plus that surcharge ($5,040), giving $55,440. The total surcharge is 15.5% of the original tax, not 15% - the second surcharge compounds on the first.

s.71(5), s.71(5A)
A · Tax system and administration Late payment surcharge Hard

Q022. Tax of $250,000 remained unpaid more than six months after the due date. What is the total amount now payable, including surcharges?

Correct: B — $288,750.

A 5% surcharge arises on the due date ($12,500), and a further 10% is then charged on the tax plus that surcharge ($26,250), giving $288,750. The total surcharge is 15.5% of the original tax, not 15% - the second surcharge compounds on the first.

s.71(5), s.71(5A)
A · Tax system and administration Late payment surcharge Hard

Q023. A demand note is payable in two instalments and the taxpayer misses the first. What is the consequence?

Correct: C — The second instalment becomes immediately due and the 5% surcharge applies to the whole outstanding balance.

Missing the first instalment accelerates the second, and the 5% surcharge is imposed on the entire outstanding balance - not merely on the instalment that was missed.

s.71(5)
A · Tax system and administration Late payment surcharge Medium

Q024. A taxpayer in financial difficulty applies successfully to pay tax by instalments. What is the effect on surcharges?

Correct: D — Surcharges are still imposed on tax unpaid after the due date.

IRD is explicit that an approved instalment arrangement does not stop the surcharge. It buys time and heads off recovery action; it is not a waiver.

s.71
A · Tax system and administration Recovery of tax Medium

Q025. Under which provision may the Commissioner issue a recovery notice to a third party who owes money to the defaulter?

Correct: A — s.76.

A recovery notice under s.76 may be served on an employer, bank, tenant, debtor or customer, requiring them to pay the money to IRD instead.

s.76
A · Tax system and administration Recovery of tax Medium

Q026. Under which provision may the Commissioner apply to a District Judge to stop a defaulter leaving Hong Kong?

Correct: B — s.77.

A departure prevention direction under s.77 lasts until the tax is paid or security is given.

s.77
A · Tax system and administration Recovery of tax Medium

Q027. Under which provision may the Commissioner sue for tax in default as a civil debt in the District Court?

Correct: C — s.75.

Tax in default is recoverable as a civil debt, with the usual consequences of judgment including costs.

s.75
A · Tax system and administration Recovery of tax Medium

Q028. Four people own a let property as co-owners in equal shares. How are they liable for the property tax?

Correct: D — Jointly and severally - any one owner may be pursued for the whole.

Liability is joint and several: IRD may pursue any one co-owner for the whole amount, not merely their quarter share. Once one pays in full, recovery against the others stops and tax is never collected twice.

s.56A
A · Tax system and administration Provisional tax Hard

Q029. By when must an application to hold over payment of provisional tax be made?

Correct: A — Not later than 28 days before the due date, or 14 days after the notice is issued, whichever is later.

The later of 28 days before the due date and 14 days after the notice. The grounds are prescribed - for instance a fall in income of more than 10%, cessation, or an election for personal assessment.

s.63E
A · Tax system and administration Provisional tax Medium

Q030. Which of the following is a valid statutory ground for holding over provisional salaries tax?

Correct: B — Assessable income for the year is likely to be less than 90% of that of the preceding year.

A fall to below 90% of the preceding year's assessable income is one of the prescribed grounds. Mere disagreement with the amount is not.

s.63E(2)
A · Tax system and administration Assessment Medium

Q031. What may the Assessor issue where a taxpayer fails to file a return?

Correct: C — An estimated assessment based on the best information available.

An estimated assessment under s.59(3). It protects the statutory time limit and is superseded once the actual figures are agreed, usually through an objection.

s.59(3)
A · Tax system and administration Objections Medium

Q032. What happens to the tax in dispute while an objection is under consideration?

Correct: D — It is not automatically suspended; a separate holdover application is needed.

Lodging an objection does not suspend the tax. The taxpayer must separately apply to hold over the disputed portion, and the Commissioner may require security or purchase of a Tax Reserve Certificate.

s.71(2)
A · Tax system and administration Objections Medium

Q033. A notice of objection is lodged in time but states no grounds. What is the consequence?

Correct: A — It may be rejected as invalid.

An objection must state the precise grounds. A bare, unparticularised objection can be rejected as invalid even though it was lodged within the month.

s.64(1)
A · Tax system and administration Sources of tax law Easy

Q034. What is the status of a DIPN?

Correct: B — Departmental Interpretation and Practice Notes are not binding on taxpayers or the courts.

DIPNs explain how IRD interprets and administers the law. They bind nobody - a taxpayer may object to a treatment set out in one. In the hierarchy of authority they sit below statute, case law and Board of Review decisions.

DIPN practice
A · Tax system and administration Sources of tax law Medium

Q035. Which sequence correctly ranks the authority of Hong Kong tax sources, highest first?

Correct: C — Statute, then case law, then Board of Review decisions, then DIPNs, then advance rulings.

Statute is supreme, followed by subsidiary legislation and case law, then Board of Review decisions, then DIPNs, with advance rulings least persuasive because they turn on their own facts.

A · Tax system and administration Avoidance and evasion Easy

Q036. What distinguishes tax avoidance from tax evasion?

Correct: D — Tax avoidance uses lawful means; tax evasion is illegal.

Avoidance arranges affairs lawfully to reduce tax; evasion involves deceit, concealment or false statements and is criminal. Note that general and specific anti-avoidance provisions are excluded from the TX-HKG syllabus.

A · Tax system and administration Advance rulings Medium

Q037. What is the effect of a specific advance ruling issued by the Commissioner?

Correct: A — A ruling applies only to the applicant and the arrangement described.

A specific ruling may be relied on only by the applicant, and only for the arrangement and period described. Published versions are anonymised and are persuasive at best.

Sch. 10
A · Tax system and administration Administration Easy

Q038. Who is empowered to assess and collect tax under the Inland Revenue Ordinance?

Correct: B — The Commissioner.

The Commissioner of Inland Revenue, who is also Collector of Stamp Revenue and Commissioner of Estate Duty.

s.3
A · Tax system and administration Board of Review Easy

Q039. What is the Board of Review?

Correct: C — An independent statutory body that hears tax appeals.

An independent statutory body constituted under s.65, with a chairman, deputy chairmen with legal training, and up to 150 members appointed by the Chief Executive. It hears appeals against the Commissioner's determinations.

s.65
A · Tax system and administration Appeals Medium

Q040. On what basis may a Board of Review decision be appealed to the Court of First Instance by way of case stated?

Correct: D — A point of law only.

The Board is the final arbiter of fact. An appeal by case stated under s.69 lies on a question of law only.

s.69
A · Tax system and administration Block Extension Scheme Hard

Q041. For 2025/26 profits tax returns with Accounting Date Code 'D', what were the extended lodgement dates announced by the Commissioner on 14 July 2026?

Correct: A — 31 August 2026 for paper filing and 2 October 2026 for electronic.

Code 'D' covers accounting dates from 1 to 31 December. The paper deadline moved from 17 August to 31 August 2026, and the electronic deadline from 17 September to 2 October 2026. Codes 'N' and 'M' were unchanged.

Circular to Tax Representatives, 14 Jul 2026
A · Tax system and administration Returns and filing Medium

Q042. When is a newly incorporated Hong Kong company normally issued with its first profits tax return?

Correct: B — Around 18 months after incorporation or commencement of business.

Usually about 18 months after incorporation or commencement. The company must still notify chargeability under s.51(2) within 4 months of the basis period end if no return has arrived by then.

s.51(1)
A · Tax system and administration Compliance Medium

Q043. Besides simply processing what a return states, what compliance activity does the Inland Revenue Department carry out?

Correct: C — Field assessments/audits, and desk audits and field investigations into offshore claims and transfer pricing risk.

IRD runs a risk-based programme of field audits and investigations - including into offshore profits claims and transfer pricing - as well as desk-based reviews, quite separately from the routine processing of assessments.

A · Tax system and administration Filing Easy

Q044. What must generally accompany the first return filed by a newly registered taxpayer, in addition to the return itself?

Correct: D — A Hong Kong identity card, or - for a company - its certificate of incorporation and business registration certificate, plus supporting documents as requested.

Basic identification and registration documents - an HKID for an individual, or the certificate of incorporation and business registration certificate for a company - together with any supporting schedules IRD specifically requests.

B · Salaries tax Source of employment Easy

Q045. Under the totality of facts test in Goepfert, which three factors principally determine whether an employment is a Hong Kong employment?

Correct: A — Where the contract was negotiated and is enforceable, the residence of the employer, and where remuneration is paid.

The three Goepfert factors. They are indicative, not conclusive - the test is the totality of the facts (DIPN 10).

DIPN 10
B · Salaries tax 60-day rule Easy

Q046. Income from services rendered wholly outside Hong Kong by a non-Government employee is excluded from salaries tax unless the person visited Hong Kong for what period during the basis period?

Correct: B — More than 60 days.

Section 8(1B) brings the visit days back into charge where the person was in Hong Kong for more than 60 days. It is a cliff edge: 61 days loses the whole exemption, and both the arrival and departure day count in full, even for a same-day transit.

s.8(1A)(b), s.8(1B)
B · Salaries tax 60-day rule Hard

Q047. An employee's ordinary visits to Hong Kong total 59 days. On two occasions he also departed very early in the morning on a connecting flight. How many days does he count as present?

Correct: C — 61.

Both the day of arrival and the day of departure count as a full day each, even for a same-day transit. 59 + 2 = 61, which exceeds 60, so the s.8(1B) exemption fails entirely.

s.8(1B)
B · Salaries tax s.8(1A)(c) exclusion Hard

Q048. An employee has a Hong Kong employment with a company managed and controlled in Hong Kong. He spent 9 months working in a territory with no double taxation arrangement with Hong Kong, and that salary bore local income tax of $180,000, which the employer paid on his behalf. His salary is $100,000 a month. What is his assessable income?

Correct: D — $480,000.

Section 8(1A)(c) excludes income for services rendered in a non-DTA territory where tax of substantially the same nature has been paid there, so the 9 months' salary drops out. But foreign tax borne by the employer is itself a taxable perquisite: ($100,000 × 3) + $180,000 = $480,000. Omitting the employer-paid tax is the commonest error.

Q117. Who is chargeable to profits tax and on what?

Correct: A — A person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong, on profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong from that trade, profession or business.

Section 14(1) charges every person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong, on profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong from that trade, profession or business. Hong Kong operates a strict territorial, source-based system - residence and place of incorporation are irrelevant, and offshore profits are outside the charge however the money is received.

s.14(1)
C · Profits tax Source Medium

Q118. How is the source of profits determined, following HK-TVB v CIR and later cases?

Correct: B — A question of fact, decided by looking at what the taxpayer did to earn the profit and where they did it.

The 'operations test': look at what the taxpayer actually did to earn the profit in question, and where. It is a practical, fact-specific enquiry, not a single mechanical rule - contract location and place of incorporation are each relevant but never decisive on their own.

DIPN 21
C · Profits tax Source - trading profits Medium

Q119. For a business of trading in goods, what is the primary factor in determining the source of the trading profit?

Correct: C — Where the contracts of purchase and sale are effected.

For trading profits the place where the contracts of purchase and sale are effected is the key factor - not necessarily where they are signed, but where the effective negotiation happens. A contract effected outside Hong Kong points to an offshore claim.

DIPN 21
C · Profits tax Source - contract processing Hard

Q120. A Hong Kong company has goods manufactured under a contract-processing arrangement in the Mainland, and sells the goods from Hong Kong. How is the profit sourced?

Correct: D — Manufacturing profits are apportioned between the processing and the trading/selling functions.

DIPN 21 apportions the profit 50:50 between the Mainland processing operation and the Hong Kong trading operation, reflecting that both contribute to earning it. An import-processing arrangement, by contrast, is not apportioned in the same way because the Mainland entity's own factory does the work.

DIPN 21
C · Profits tax Source - service income Medium

Q121. What is the basic rule for sourcing profits from the provision of services?

Correct: A — Fees for services are sourced where the services are rendered.

Profits from services are sourced where the services are rendered - a different test from trading profits, which look at where contracts are effected.

DIPN 21

Q122. Which of the 'badges of trade' does the following describe?
A short period of ownership before resale

Correct: B — It is a badge of trade indicating a trading, not a capital, transaction.

The badges of trade (subject matter, length of ownership, frequency, supplementary work, circumstances of realisation, motive) are drawn from case law and none is conclusive alone - the question is always the overall impression from all the facts.

The taxpayer's stated intention at the time of acquisition, taken with the surrounding circumstances

Correct: C — It is one badge of trade among several, not conclusive on its own.

The badges of trade (subject matter, length of ownership, frequency, supplementary work, circumstances of realisation, motive) are drawn from case law and none is conclusive alone - the question is always the overall impression from all the facts.

The number and frequency of similar transactions

Correct: D — Repeated, systematic transactions point towards trading.

The badges of trade (subject matter, length of ownership, frequency, supplementary work, circumstances of realisation, motive) are drawn from case law and none is conclusive alone - the question is always the overall impression from all the facts.

Q125. Which of the 'badges of trade' does the following describe?
An asset acquired to be modified or improved before resale

Correct: A — Work done to make an asset more saleable is a badge of trade.

The badges of trade (subject matter, length of ownership, frequency, supplementary work, circumstances of realisation, motive) are drawn from case law and none is conclusive alone - the question is always the overall impression from all the facts.

C · Profits tax Capital vs revenue Hard

Q126. A company receives a lump sum as compensation for the permanent loss of an agency it held, the agency being a capital asset of the business. How is the receipt treated?

Correct: B — A capital receipt, outside the scope of profits tax.

Compensation for the loss or sterilisation of a capital asset is itself capital, following Van den Berghs v Clark. Contrast compensation for loss of trading stock or lost profits, which is a revenue receipt.

C · Profits tax Capital vs revenue Medium

Q127. An insurer pays out for trading stock destroyed by fire. How is the payment treated?

Correct: C — A revenue receipt, taxable in the year it accrues.

Compensation that replaces a revenue item - here, stock that would have been sold in the ordinary course - is itself revenue in nature and taxable.

C · Profits tax General deduction Medium

Q128. What is the statutory test for deducting an expense under profits tax?

Correct: D — Outgoings and expenses to the extent incurred in the production of assessable profits.

Section 16(1) is deliberately looser than the salaries tax test: expenses to the extent incurred in the production of profits. There is no 'wholly, exclusively and necessarily' requirement, so an expense with a dual purpose can still be apportioned and partly deducted.

s.16(1)
C · Profits tax Non-deductible expenditure Easy

Q129. Which of the following IS normally deductible under s.17?

Correct: A — Capital expenditure.

Section 17(1) specifically prohibits deducting capital expenditure, domestic or private expenditure, and expenses not incurred in the production of chargeable profits. Ordinary business rent is none of these and is deductible under s.16(1).

s.17(1)
C · Profits tax Non-deductible expenditure Medium

Q130. A trader incurs legal costs in acquiring a new shop lease for the business. How is the expenditure treated?

Correct: B — Not deductible - it is capital expenditure.

Costs of acquiring a capital asset - including the legal costs of acquiring it - are themselves capital and non-deductible, even though the asset itself (the lease) will be used to earn trading profits.

s.17(1)(c)
C · Profits tax Deductions Medium

Q131. A company incurs legal costs defending a claim brought by a customer over defective goods sold in the ordinary course of business. How are the costs treated?

Correct: C — Deductible - it is incurred in defending the taxpayer's trading position.

Legal costs take their character from what they protect. Costs incurred in the ordinary course of trade - defending a trading claim, recovering a trading debt - are revenue and deductible. Costs of acquiring or defending title to a capital asset are not.

s.16(1)
C · Profits tax Donations Medium

Q132. A company's assessable profits before deducting donations are $500,000, and it made approved charitable donations of $30,000 in the year. What deduction is allowed?

Correct: D — $30,000.

Section 16D caps the deduction at 35% of assessable profits before the donation itself is deducted: 35% × $500,000 = $175,000. Here the allowable amount is $30,000. The donation must also be at least $100 and not merely a payment for goods, advertising space or a dinner ticket at an inflated price.

s.16D

Q133. A company's assessable profits before deducting donations are $280,000, and it made approved charitable donations of $15,000 in the year. What deduction is allowed?

Correct: A — $15,000.

Section 16D caps the deduction at 35% of assessable profits before the donation itself is deducted: 35% × $280,000 = $98,000. Here the allowable amount is $15,000. The donation must also be at least $100 and not merely a payment for goods, advertising space or a dinner ticket at an inflated price.

Correct: B — $60,000.

Section 16D caps the deduction at 35% of assessable profits before the donation itself is deducted: 35% × $900,000 = $315,000. Here the allowable amount is $60,000. The donation must also be at least $100 and not merely a payment for goods, advertising space or a dinner ticket at an inflated price.

Q135. A company replaces a factory's flat roof with a completely new and improved roof structure of superior design, rather than patching the original. How is the cost treated?

Correct: C — Not deductible - it is capital in nature.

A repair restores an asset; an improvement makes it better than before and is capital. Replacing with something of a materially superior specification tips this into capital expenditure, non-deductible under s.17(1)(c), though it may qualify for a depreciation allowance instead.
