Q136. A trader makes a specific provision against a named customer's debt, having reasonable grounds to believe it will not be paid. Is the provision deductible?

Correct: D — Deductible - a specific provision for a debt reasonably estimated to be irrecoverable.

Section 16(1)(d) allows a deduction for bad debts and doubtful debts specifically identified as estimated to be bad. A general, unspecific provision (e.g. 2% of all debtors) is never deductible.

s.16(1)(d)
C · Profits tax Bad and doubtful debts Medium

Q137. A bad debt previously allowed as a deduction is unexpectedly recovered in a later year. How is the recovery treated?

Correct: A — Assessable as a trading receipt in the year recovered.

The recovery is a trading receipt of the year it is received, taxable in full, mirroring the property tax treatment of recovered irrecoverable rent.

s.15(1)(g)
C · Profits tax Interest deduction Hard

Q138. Under what condition is interest expense generally deductible against profits tax?

Correct: B — Deductible - interest on money borrowed for the purposes of producing chargeable profits, subject to the anti-avoidance conditions in s.16(2).

Section 16(1)(a) allows interest on borrowings used to produce chargeable profits, but s.16(2) imposes several conditions aimed at related-party and circular back-to-back arrangements - interest paid to an overseas associate not itself subject to Hong Kong profits tax on the interest, for instance, can be restricted.

ss.16(1)(a), 16(2)
C · Profits tax Depreciation allowances Medium

Q139. What initial allowance is available on qualifying capital expenditure on plant or machinery?

Correct: C — 60% of the cost, in the year of purchase, regardless of how long the asset is used in the year.

Section 39B(1A) gives a flat 60% initial allowance in the year of purchase, with no time-apportionment for part of a year and no reduction for private use by a company - private use apportionment applies to sole traders and partnerships, not companies.

s.39B(1A)
C · Profits tax Depreciation allowances Easy

Q140. At what rates is the annual allowance on plant and machinery computed?

Correct: D — 10%, 20% or 30% a year on the reducing balance of each pool.

Assets are grouped into pools taxed at 10%, 20% or 30% depending on their prescribed class, each on the reducing balance of that pool's written-down value.

s.39B; Sch. 3
C · Profits tax Depreciation allowances Hard

Q141. A 30%-pool has a written-down value brought forward of $800,000. During the year the business bought qualifying plant for $200,000 and sold plant for $50,000. What is the total depreciation allowance for the year?

Correct: A — $369,000.

Additions $200,000 less the 60% initial allowance $120,000 leaves $880,000; less disposal proceeds of $50,000 = $830,000; the annual allowance is 30% of that = $249,000. Total allowance = IA $120,000 + AA $249,000 = $369,000. Deducting disposal proceeds before the initial allowance, or omitting the IA entirely, are the two errors most often made.

s.39B; Sch. 3

Additions $100,000 less the 60% initial allowance $60,000 leaves $1,540,000; less disposal proceeds of $300,000 = $1,240,000; the annual allowance is 20% of that = $248,000. Total allowance = IA $60,000 + AA $248,000 = $308,000. Deducting disposal proceeds before the initial allowance, or omitting the IA entirely, are the two errors most often made.

Q145. Disposal proceeds from selling the only asset in a pool exceed its written-down value brought forward, after also deducting the year's additions. What is the tax result?

Correct: A — A balancing charge, added back to assessable profits.

Where proceeds exceed the pool's residue, the excess is a balancing charge - effectively clawing back allowances given in earlier years - and is added back as if it were extra profit, capped at the total allowances actually given. Where proceeds are less than the residue and the pool ceases to have any asset in it, the shortfall is a balancing allowance instead.

s.39B(4)
C · Profits tax Depreciation allowances - hire purchase Hard

Q146. Plant is acquired on hire purchase with a deposit of $60,000, and 6 monthly instalments are paid in the year, each with a capital element of $8,000. What initial allowance is available for the year?

Correct: B — $64,800.

For hire purchase, the initial allowance runs only on the capital sums actually paid in the year - the deposit plus the capital element of instalments paid - not on the full cash price of the asset: ($60,000 + 6 × $8,000) × 60% = $64,800. Using the full cash price overstates the allowance.

For hire purchase, the initial allowance runs only on the capital sums actually paid in the year - the deposit plus the capital element of instalments paid - not on the full cash price of the asset: ($100,000 + 4 × $12,000) × 60% = $88,800. Using the full cash price overstates the allowance.

Correct: D — $51,000.

For hire purchase, the initial allowance runs only on the capital sums actually paid in the year - the deposit plus the capital element of instalments paid - not on the full cash price of the asset: ($40,000 + 9 × $5,000) × 60% = $51,000. Using the full cash price overstates the allowance.

Q149. What allowance is available on capital expenditure on constructing a commercial building or structure used in the business?

Correct: A — Straight-line: 20% initial allowance plus 4% annual allowance on cost.

A 20% initial allowance in the year the expenditure is incurred, plus a 4% annual allowance on a straight-line basis (i.e. on cost, not written-down value) for 25 years, given to whoever owns the relevant interest at the end of the basis period. Industrial buildings attract the same rates under a parallel code.

ss.34, 36A

Q150. A company buys a completed commercial building for use in its business. On what amount is the buildings allowance computed?

Correct: B — The cost of the land itself is excluded.

Only the cost of construction qualifies - the value attributable to the land must be stripped out first, whether the building was constructed by the taxpayer or bought already built.

s.40

Q151. What allowance is available for capital expenditure on a prescribed fixed asset such as computer hardware and software, or manufacturing machinery specified by the Commissioner?

Correct: C — 100% deduction in the year of purchase.

Section 16G gives a 100% deduction in the year of purchase for prescribed fixed assets, in place of the normal pooled initial-plus-annual allowance system - though a specific exclusion applies to office furniture and fixtures, motor vehicles, and structures.

C · Profits tax R&D expenditure Hard

Q152. A company incurred Type A R&D expenditure of $400,000 and Type B (qualifying) R&D expenditure of $2,500,000 in the year. What total deduction is available under s.16B?

Correct: D — $7,400,000.

Type A gets a plain 100% deduction: $400,000. Type B is enhanced - 300% on the first $2,000,000 and 200% on the excess: (min($2,500,000, 2,000,000) × 3) + (max(0, $2,500,000 - 2,000,000) × 2). Total deduction = $7,400,000. Forgetting the enhancement tiers and simply deducting 100% of the Type B spend is the commonest error - this is the exact scenario the examining team published a worked example on.

s.16B

Total deduction = $8,000,000. Q155. What distinguishes 'Type B' qualifying R&D expenditure from 'Type A'?

Correct: C — Type B must relate to one of the specified fields and either seek to extend general knowledge or have an industrial, agricultural or scientific purpose.

Type B research must fall within a field specified in Schedule 45 and meet the purpose test in s.2. Type A is a residual category - R&D expenditure that does not qualify as Type B still gets a plain 100% deduction rather than none, provided it otherwise relates to the trade.

s.16B; Sch. 45
C · Profits tax Trading losses Easy

Q156. How is an unrelieved trading loss of a Hong Kong business normally treated?

Correct: D — Carried forward indefinitely and set off against future assessable profits of the same trade.

Losses are carried forward with no time limit and set off against future assessable profits, but there is no carry-back and (unlike personal assessment) no automatic set-off against the owner's other income.

s.19C
C · Profits tax Trading losses Medium

Q157. A sole proprietor's business makes a loss for the year, and they also have rental income from a separate let property. How can the business loss be set against the rental income in the same year?

Correct: A — Only through electing personal assessment.

Only by electing personal assessment, which aggregates all the individual's chargeable income and lets a current-year business loss shelter it. Within the profits tax computation alone, the loss is simply carried forward.

s.42(1)
C · Profits tax Trading losses - partnerships Hard

Q158. How is a partnership's trading loss for a year treated?

Correct: B — They are shared among the partners in the profit-sharing ratio and each partner deals with their own share.

The loss is allocated to the partners in the agreed profit-sharing ratio, just like a profit would be. Each partner then carries forward, or otherwise relieves, their own share - an individual partner might elect personal assessment to set it against salary; a corporate partner simply carries its share forward against future profits.

s.19C(4)
C · Profits tax Two-tier profits tax Easy

Q159. A Hong Kong company has assessable profits of exactly $2,000,000 for the year, with no connected entities. What profits tax is payable?

Correct: C — $2,000,000 &times; 8.25% = $165,000 - the two-tier system only changes the rate on profits above $2,000,000.

At or below the $2,000,000 threshold the two-tier system makes no difference at all - the whole profit is simply taxed at 8.25%, the lower tier rate. The higher 16.5% rate only ever applies to the slice above $2,000,000.

s.14AA
C · Profits tax Two-tier profits tax - corporation Medium

Q160. A Hong Kong company (not connected with any other entity electing the two-tier regime) has assessable profits of $2,500,000 for the year. What profits tax is payable?

Correct: D — $247,500.

The first $2,000,000 is taxed at 8.25%, and the excess at 16.5%: (2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($500,000 × 16.5%) = $247,500. Applying 16.5% to the whole profit, as if there were no two-tier relief, gives $412,500 and overstates the tax by $165,000.

The first $2,000,000 is taxed at 8.25%, and the excess at 16.5%: (2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($10,000,000 × 16.5%) = $1,815,000. Applying 16.5% to the whole profit, as if there were no two-tier relief, gives $1,980,000 and overstates the tax by $165,000.

Q164. How does the two-tier regime apply where several companies are 'connected entities' of one another?

Correct: D — Only one entity in a group of connected entities may benefit from the two-tier rates; the others pay flat 16.5%/15%.

Connected entities must nominate only one of themselves to enjoy the two-tier rates for a year of assessment; the rest pay the flat rate (16.5% corporate, 15% unincorporated) on all their profits. This stops a group multiplying the $2,000,000 band by splitting into subsidiaries.

Correct: A — $210,000.

For an unincorporated business the two-tier rates are 7.5% on the first $2,000,000 and 15% above: (2,000,000 × 7.5%) + ($400,000 × 15%) = $210,000. Using the corporate rates of 8.25%/16.5% instead of 7.5%/15% is a common slip when candidates confuse the two sets of rates.

For an unincorporated business the two-tier rates are 7.5% on the first $2,000,000 and 15% above: (2,000,000 × 7.5%) + ($1,600,000 × 15%) = $390,000. Using the corporate rates of 8.25%/16.5% instead of 7.5%/15% is a common slip when candidates confuse the two sets of rates.

For an unincorporated business the two-tier rates are 7.5% on the first $2,000,000 and 15% above: (2,000,000 × 7.5%) + ($3,000,000 × 15%) = $600,000. Using the corporate rates of 8.25%/16.5% instead of 7.5%/15% is a common slip when candidates confuse the two sets of rates.

Q168. How is a sole proprietor's business profit assessed to profits tax?

Correct: D — As if the business and the owner's personal affairs were entirely separate - only business income is assessed to profits tax.

The business is assessed on its own trading results at the unincorporated two-tier rates (7.5%/15%), entirely separately from any salaries tax on the owner's employment income - the two are only brought together if the owner elects personal assessment.

C · Profits tax Sole trader Medium

Q169. A sole trader draws a monthly 'salary' from the business and records it as an expense. How is this treated in the profits tax computation?

Correct: A — Drawings and a notional salary to the proprietor are not deductible - the whole profit, before any such appropriation, is assessable.

A proprietor cannot be their own employee. Any salary, bonus or drawings taken by a sole proprietor (or by their spouse, under s.16(2)(e)) must be added back - the entire profit before that appropriation is what is assessable.

s.17(2)
C · Profits tax Sole trader Hard

Q170. A sole trader pays a salary to their spouse, who works full-time managing the shop. Is the salary deductible?

Correct: B — Deductible, if the spouse genuinely works in the business and the amount is not excessive - subject to the same restriction as the proprietor's own salary.

Section 17(2) treats salaries paid to the proprietor's spouse the same way as a payment to the proprietor - it is not deductible and must be added back, regardless of how genuinely the spouse works, because husband and wife are not treated as being at arm's length for this purpose.

s.17(2)
C · Profits tax Partnership Medium

Q171. How is a Hong Kong partnership assessed to profits tax?

Correct: C — The partnership itself is not a separate chargeable person - it files one profits tax return, but the assessable profit is allocated to and assessed on each partner individually.

A partnership is not itself a person chargeable to tax, but it files one return covering the whole business (s.22), and the resulting assessable profit or loss is then divided among the partners according to their profit-sharing ratio, each partner being assessed on their own share.

s.22
C · Profits tax Partnership Hard

Q172. Partners are paid a salary and interest on capital under the partnership agreement, both charged as expenses in the partnership accounts. How are these treated for profits tax?

Correct: D — Added back in the partnership computation, then reallocated to each partner as part of their share of profit.

Section 16(2)(e)/(2A) treats any salary, interest on capital, or interest on loans from a partner as a mere appropriation of profit, not a real expense - it is added back in arriving at the partnership's total assessable profit, and then each partner's own salary/interest is added to their share when the profit is divided, so nothing is actually lost.

s.16(2A)
C · Profits tax Two-tier profits tax - mixed partnership Hard

Q173. A partnership with 3 partners has assessable profits of $3,000,000 for the year, shared 50% : 30% : 20%. One partner is a company and the rest are individuals. What is the total profits tax payable, applying the two-tier rates separately to each partner's share?

Correct: A — $306,000.

The $2,000,000 first-tier band is apportioned between the partners in the profit-sharing ratio, and each partner's slice of profit is then taxed at their own rates (7.5%/15% for an individual partner, 8.25%/16.5% for a corporate partner): total tax = $306,000. Applying one flat set of rates to the whole partnership profit, as if it had a single $2,000,000 band, ignores that a mixed partnership has more than one type of partner and is the error most often seen in this question.

s.14AA; DIPN 28
C · Profits tax Two-tier profits tax - mixed partnership Hard

Q174. A partnership with 2 partners has assessable profits of $5,000,000 for the year, shared 60% : 40%. One partner is a company and the rest are individuals. What is the total profits tax payable, applying the two-tier rates separately to each partner's share?

Correct: B — $624,000.

The $2,000,000 first-tier band is apportioned between the partners in the profit-sharing ratio, and each partner's slice of profit is then taxed at their own rates (7.5%/15% for an individual partner, 8.25%/16.5% for a corporate partner): total tax = $624,000. Applying one flat set of rates to the whole partnership profit, as if it had a single $2,000,000 band, ignores that a mixed partnership has more than one type of partner and is the error most often seen in this question.

s.14AA; DIPN 28
C · Profits tax Two-tier profits tax - mixed partnership Hard

Q175. A partnership with 3 partners has assessable profits of $4,000,000 for the year, shared 30% : 30% : 40%. One partner is a company and the rest are individuals. What is the total profits tax payable, applying the two-tier rates separately to each partner's share?

Correct: C — $468,000.

The $2,000,000 first-tier band is apportioned between the partners in the profit-sharing ratio, and each partner's slice of profit is then taxed at their own rates (7.5%/15% for an individual partner, 8.25%/16.5% for a corporate partner): total tax = $468,000. Applying one flat set of rates to the whole partnership profit, as if it had a single $2,000,000 band, ignores that a mixed partnership has more than one type of partner and is the error most often seen in this question.

C · Profits tax Partnership - personal assessment Hard

Q176. A partnership has one individual partner and one corporate partner. How does each partner's share of the partnership profit interact with personal assessment?

Correct: D — The individual partner's share is included in their personal assessment total income; the corporate partner's share never is.

Personal assessment is available only to individuals. The individual partner's share of assessable profit (or loss) is aggregated into their own personal assessment total income, alongside salary and property income; the corporate partner's share simply stays in the corporate profits tax computation and is assessed at corporate rates with no personal assessment route available to it.

ss.41, 42
C · Profits tax Partnership - personal assessment Hard

Q177. An individual partner elects personal assessment. How is interest paid by them personally to fund their share of the partnership's borrowings restricted?

Correct: A — Restricted to that partner's own share of the partnership's net assessable value or profit, mirroring the individual property/business rule.

The same restriction that applies to a sole proprietor's or property owner's interest applies partner by partner: it cannot exceed that partner's own share of the relevant assessable profit or net assessable value, and cannot create or increase a loss.

s.42(1)
C · Profits tax Common corporation Easy

Q178. At what rates is an ordinary Hong Kong company (not a qualifying professional reinsurer, corporate treasury centre or similar concessionary case) taxed on its assessable profits?

Correct: B — Only the two-tier corporate rates of 8.25%/16.5% - the unincorporated rates never apply to a company.

A company is always taxed at the corporate two-tier rates - 8.25% on the first $2,000,000 and 16.5% above - never at the unincorporated rates, which are reserved for sole proprietorships and partnerships (other than any corporate partner within one, who is still taxed at the corporate rates on their own share).

s.14AA
C · Profits tax Common corporation Medium

Q179. How does a company's payment of remuneration to its director, who is also its sole shareholder, differ in tax treatment from a sole trader's own drawings?

Correct: C — A director's remuneration is a deductible expense of the company - the director/shareholder is separately assessed to salaries tax on it.

A company is a separate legal person from its shareholders, so a director can validly be an employee of their own company: the remuneration is a normal deductible expense in the profits tax computation (subject to being reasonable in amount) and is separately taxed on the director as salaries tax. A sole proprietor has no such separate legal identity, so their own drawings are never deductible.

C · Profits tax Common corporation Medium

Q180. How are dividends paid by a Hong Kong company treated for profits tax purposes?

Correct: D — Dividends paid by a Hong Kong company are not deductible in computing its own profits, and are not further taxed in the hands of the shareholder.

Dividends are a distribution of after-tax profit, not an expense, so they are never deductible to the paying company - and Hong Kong does not tax dividend income at all, so the recipient (individual or corporate) is not taxed on them either. There is no dividend withholding tax and no need for any relief against double taxation of the same profit.

s.26(a)
C · Profits tax Trading stock Easy

Q181. On what basis is trading stock normally valued at the end of an accounting period, for both accounting and tax purposes?

Correct: A — The lower of cost and net realisable value.

The lower of cost and net realisable value - a conservative basis that recognises a fall in value before the stock is sold, but never revalues stock upward above cost.

s.15C; HKAS 2
C · Profits tax Trading stock Medium

Q182. Which cost formulas are acceptable for valuing trading stock under Hong Kong tax and accounting practice?

Correct: B — FIFO or a weighted average cost formula.

FIFO and weighted average are both accepted. LIFO is not permitted under HKAS 2 and is not accepted for Hong Kong tax purposes either.

HKAS 2
C · Profits tax Trading stock Hard

Q183. A trader takes stock out of the business for personal use, or gives it away, without any question of trade to trade sale. How is this treated for profits tax?

Correct: C — At its open market value on the date of the gift or appropriation.

Section 15C deems trading stock disposed of otherwise than in the ordinary course of business - including a gift or appropriation for personal use - to be sold at open market value on that date, bringing the notional profit into the computation.

s.15C
C · Profits tax Basis period Easy

Q184. For an established business preparing annual accounts, what is the basis period for a year of assessment?

Correct: D — The accounting year ending within that year of assessment.

The basis period is normally the accounting year ending within the year of assessment - a company with a 31 December year end is assessed for YA 2025/26 on the year ended 31 December 2025, not on the year of assessment itself.

s.18C
C · Profits tax Basis period - new business Hard

Q185. A business commences on 1 October 2025 and its first accounts are made up to 31 December 2026, a period of 15 months. What is the effect on the basis periods for the first two years of assessment?

Correct: A — The whole period from commencement to the end of its first accounting period may be taxed twice, in the first two years of assessment, unless the taxpayer applies for relief.

Because the first accounts straddle more than one year of assessment, part of the profit is included in the basis period for both YA 2025/26 (the whole first period, being the only accounts available) and YA 2026/27 (the 12 months to 31 December 2026) - the overlapping months are taxed twice unless the taxpayer successfully applies under s.18E for the assessments to be revised on a fair and just apportionment.

ss.18B, 18E
C · Profits tax Basis period - cessation Medium

Q186. A business permanently ceases on 30 June 2026, having last made up accounts to 31 December 2025. What is the basis period for the year of assessment in which it ceases?

Correct: B — The basis period runs from the end of the previous basis period to the date of cessation.

On cessation the basis period is simply whatever period is left: from the end of the last basis period to the actual date of cessation, however short or long that turns out to be - here, 1 January to 30 June 2026.

s.18D
C · Profits tax Basis period - change of accounting date Medium

Q187. What must a business do if it wants to change its accounting year end?

Correct: C — It must apply to the Commissioner, who may accept the change and issue directions on how the transitional basis periods are computed.

Section 18C(3) requires the Commissioner to be satisfied of the change and to give directions on the resulting basis periods, to ensure no period of profit is missed and none is taxed twice as a result of the change.

s.18C(3)
C · Profits tax Provisional profits tax Medium

Q188. A company's final assessable profits for the preceding year were $2,400,000, on which the two-tier rates were applied. In the absence of any estimate supplied by the company, on what figure will provisional profits tax for the current year normally be raised?

Correct: D — $231,000.

Provisional profits tax is normally based on the preceding year's assessable profits, taxed at the current year's rates: $231,000, applying the two-tier rates exactly as they would to a final assessment. The company may instead apply to have it based on a lower estimate of the current year's actual profits, and must do so in writing before the return is due if it wants that lower figure used.

s.63

Q189. A company's final assessable profits for the preceding year were $3,200,000, on which the two-tier rates were applied. In the absence of any estimate supplied by the company, on what figure will provisional profits tax for the current year normally be raised?

Correct: A — $363,000.

Provisional profits tax is normally based on the preceding year's assessable profits, taxed at the current year's rates: $363,000, applying the two-tier rates exactly as they would to a final assessment. The company may instead apply to have it based on a lower estimate of the current year's actual profits, and must do so in writing before the return is due if it wants that lower figure used.

Q190. A company's final assessable profits for the preceding year were $6,000,000, on which the two-tier rates were applied. In the absence of any estimate supplied by the company, on what figure will provisional profits tax for the current year normally be raised?

Correct: B — $825,000.

Provisional profits tax is normally based on the preceding year's assessable profits, taxed at the current year's rates: $825,000, applying the two-tier rates exactly as they would to a final assessment. The company may instead apply to have it based on a lower estimate of the current year's actual profits, and must do so in writing before the return is due if it wants that lower figure used.

s.63
C · Profits tax Provisional profits tax Medium

Q191. A company's actual assessable profits turn out to be much lower than the figure on which provisional profits tax was charged. How is the provisional tax reconciled once the final assessment is made?

Correct: C — A note is served requiring immediate application within a set time; if refused, the excess already paid is refunded once the actual assessment is made.

Provisional tax already paid is set off against the final tax liability for that year, and any excess is refunded (or set against the following year's provisional tax). Before the final figures are known, the company can also apply under s.63E to hold over part of the provisional tax on prescribed grounds, such as profits being likely to be substantially lower.

s.63
C · Profits tax Group relief Medium

Q192. Can a loss-making Hong Kong subsidiary surrender its trading loss to a profitable fellow group company, to reduce the group's overall tax?

Correct: D — No - each company in a group is separately assessed and a loss in one company cannot be set against profits of another.

Hong Kong has no group loss relief at all. Each company is a separate person chargeable to profits tax in its own right; a loss simply carries forward within the loss-making company itself, however profitable the rest of the group may be. This is a frequently tested contrast with jurisdictions that do have group relief.

C · Profits tax Group relief Medium

Q193. What is the profits tax consequence of one group company charging another a management fee?

Correct: A — Nil - inter-company management fees, royalties and interest are all assessed and deducted on normal profits tax principles, company by company.

There being no group relief or consolidated filing, each company remains separately assessed: the fee is ordinary assessable income to the recipient and an ordinary deductible expense to the payer (subject to the general deduction rules), exactly as if the companies were unconnected.

s.16(1)
C · Profits tax Offshore claims Medium

Q194. Where a taxpayer claims that profits included in its Hong Kong accounts are in fact offshore and not chargeable, where does the burden of proof lie?

Correct: B — The burden is on the taxpayer to prove the profit was not derived from Hong Kong.

Section 68(4) places the burden squarely on the taxpayer to satisfy the Commissioner (and, on appeal, the Board of Review) that the assessment is excessive or wrong - which in an offshore claim means proving what operations actually generated the profit and where they took place.

s.68(4)
C · Profits tax Offshore claims Medium

Q195. What kind of evidence does the Inland Revenue Department expect to support an offshore profits claim?

Correct: C — Contemporaneous documentary evidence of what was actually done and where - correspondence, contracts, travel records, minutes.

IRD wants to see the operations that actually earned the profit - where negotiations happened, who visited whom, where contracts were concluded - not bare assertions. A customer's location and the absence of local staff are each a factor but neither is decisive on its own; DIPN 21 stresses that the totality of the facts is what matters.

DIPN 21
C · Profits tax Exchange differences Hard

Q196. How is a foreign exchange gain or loss on a trade debtor denominated in a foreign currency treated for profits tax?

Correct: D — A revenue receipt or loss, if it arises on a revenue account (e.g. trade debtors or creditors in foreign currency).

An exchange difference takes the character of the underlying item: a difference on a revenue item (trading debtors, trading creditors, floating loan capital used as working capital) is itself revenue and is taxable or deductible; a difference on a capital item (a fixed loan for acquiring a capital asset) is capital and outside the charge.

DIPN 42
C · Profits tax Exchange differences Hard

Q197. A company borrows in US dollars to fund the purchase of a new factory building. An exchange loss arises when the loan is partly repaid. How is the loss treated?

Correct: A — Capital - the borrowing itself is a fixed capital loan used to acquire a capital asset.

Because the loan itself is fixed capital raised to buy a capital asset, an exchange difference on repaying it is capital and non-deductible, unlike a difference on a revenue-account trade debt.

DIPN 42
C · Profits tax Pre-trading expenditure Hard

Q198. A company incurs marketing and staff recruitment costs while setting up a new business, several months before it actually starts trading. Are these costs deductible against the profits once trading begins?

Correct: B — Not deductible, because the trade had not yet commenced when the expenditure was incurred.

Section 16(1) only allows a deduction for expenses incurred in the production of chargeable profits - which requires the trade to already exist. Genuine pre-trading expenditure is outside the charge altogether and is never deductible, however necessary it was to get the business started.

s.16(1)
C · Profits tax Post-cessation expenditure Hard

Q199. A business pays a trade debt it still owed after it permanently ceased trading. Can this expense still be deducted?

Correct: C — Still deductible, provided they relate to debts or liabilities of the trade that was carried on.

An expense does not lose its deductible character merely because the trade has since ceased, provided it genuinely relates to a liability of that trade - it is deducted in computing the profit or loss of the final basis period.

s.18F
C · Profits tax Capital vs revenue Medium

Q200. A private investment holding company buys a block of shares intending to hold them long term for dividend income, and sells them years later at a large profit after an unsolicited takeover offer. How is the gain treated?

Correct: D — A capital asset realised without any further trading intention - the gain is not taxable.

Realising a genuine long-term investment - even profitably, and even where the sale was prompted by someone else's offer rather than the taxpayer's own initiative - remains a capital transaction. The stated investment intention, the long holding period, and the absence of any dealing pattern all point away from trading.

C · Profits tax Capital vs revenue Medium

Q201. A property developer, in a transaction unrelated to its normal projects, buys a plot of land, obtains planning permission to increase its value, and resells it within the year at a profit, having taken out short-term finance for the purchase. How is the profit treated?

Correct: A — A trading transaction - an isolated adventure in the nature of trade, taxable on the whole profit.

Even a single, isolated transaction can amount to trading - an 'adventure in the nature of trade' - where the badges point that way: short ownership, supplementary work to enhance saleability (the planning permission), and short-term finance consistent with an intention to resell rather than hold.

C · Profits tax Deeming provisions Hard

Q202. A foreign company, with no other presence in Hong Kong, licenses a patent to a Hong Kong manufacturer for use in Hong Kong and receives royalties for it. How is the royalty income treated?

Correct: B — Deemed to be a trading receipt of a trade carried on in Hong Kong, even though the recipient carries on no other business here.

Section 15(1) deems specified sums - royalties for the use of intellectual property in Hong Kong being one - to be a trading receipt arising in Hong Kong, so as to bring a non-resident owner into charge even without any physical presence here. Special reduced deemed-profit percentages then apply under s.21A depending on whether the payer is an associate.

s.15(1)
C · Profits tax Deeming provisions Hard

Q203. Under s.21A, what proportion of a royalty paid to a non-resident (who is not an associate of the payer) for the use of intellectual property in Hong Kong is deemed to be the assessable profit?

Correct: C — 30% of the gross royalty, taxed at the standard corporate rate - an effective rate of about 4.95% - or the full amount where paid to an associate that has claimed a Hong Kong deduction for it.

Only 30% of the gross sum is deemed assessable, taxed at the ordinary corporate rate, giving an effective rate of roughly 4.95% on the gross royalty. Where the recipient is an associate of the Hong Kong payer and the IP was previously owned by a person carrying on business in Hong Kong, the full 100% can instead be deemed assessable, closing off a straightforward profit-extraction route.

s.21A

Q204. A non-resident person carries on a trade in Hong Kong through a local agent, and profits arise here. How does IRD collect the tax if the non-resident itself has no assets or presence in Hong Kong?

Correct: D — The non-resident's agent, manager or representative in Hong Kong may be assessed and required to pay the tax on the non-resident's behalf.

Section 20B lets the Commissioner assess and collect the tax from the non-resident's agent, manager, or anyone else who transacts business with or on behalf of them in Hong Kong, in the name of the non-resident.

s.20B
C · Profits tax Double taxation relief Hard

Q205. A Hong Kong resident's profits, already taxed in a country with which Hong Kong has no comprehensive double taxation agreement, are also taxed in Hong Kong because they are (unusually) treated as Hong Kong sourced. What relief is available under s.50?

Correct: A — Unilateral tax credit relief for the foreign tax paid, capped at the Hong Kong tax attributable to that income.

Unilateral tax credit relief allows the foreign tax paid to be credited against the Hong Kong tax on the same income, but the credit can never exceed the Hong Kong tax that would otherwise be payable on that income - it cannot be used to shelter unrelated Hong Kong profits.

C · Profits tax Double taxation relief Hard

Q206. What is the practical effect of Hong Kong's comprehensive double taxation agreements on profits that are genuinely offshore under Hong Kong's own source rules?

Correct: B — It has no effect - profits genuinely sourced outside Hong Kong are outside the charge regardless of any treaty.

Hong Kong's territorial system already excludes genuinely offshore profits without needing a treaty. The DTA network mainly matters where profits would otherwise be taxed in both jurisdictions under each one's own rules, or to reduce foreign withholding tax on Hong Kong residents' cross-border income - it does not change what counts as Hong Kong-sourced in the first place.

C · Profits tax Interest income Medium

Q207. A Hong Kong company deposits its surplus cash with a licensed Hong Kong bank and earns interest. Is the interest chargeable to profits tax?

Correct: C — Taxable - the exemption for interest on a deposit was withdrawn for any person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong.

Since April 1998 the blanket exemption for Hong Kong-source deposit interest was withdrawn for any person carrying on business in Hong Kong: the interest is a trading receipt of the business and taxable, and, if the money deposited represents funds of the trade, it may even be considered sourced in Hong Kong on ordinary principles regardless of the deposit exemption question.

Q208. A company insures its trading stock and premises against fire. Are the premiums deductible?

Correct: D — Deductible - insurance premiums covering the trade's own risks are a normal revenue expense.

Ordinary business insurance premiums, covering the risks of the trade itself, are incurred in the production of profits and deductible under s.16(1) like any other overhead.

C · Profits tax Non-deductible expenditure Medium

Q209. A company is fined for breaching pollution control regulations while operating its factory. Is the fine deductible against its profits?

Correct: A — Not deductible - a fine or penalty for breaking the law is never an allowable expense, however closely connected with the trade.

A fine or penalty imposed for breaking the law is against public policy to allow as a deduction, and case law is consistent that it is never deductible, regardless of how directly it arose out of the trade.

Q210. A company contributes to a retirement scheme for the benefit of its staff. What is the deduction limit for an ordinary (non-mandatory) employer contribution?

Correct: B — Deductible - a contribution to a recognised occupational retirement scheme or MPF scheme for employees, up to 15% of the employee's total emoluments for the year.

Section 16A caps the deduction for an employer's ordinary annual contribution at 15% of the total emoluments of the employees concerned for the period - a special, more generous rule applies to the special contribution made when a scheme is first set up.

Correct: C — $332,000.

Additions $400,000 less the 60% initial allowance $240,000 leaves a reduced pool of $460,000; the 20% annual allowance on that gives $92,000. Total allowance = IA $240,000 + AA $92,000 = $332,000.

Q212. A 20%-pool has a written-down value brought forward of $900,000. During the year the business bought qualifying plant for $150,000 and sold plant for $200,000. What is the total depreciation allowance for the year?

Correct: D — $242,000.

Additions $150,000 less the 60% initial allowance $90,000 leaves a reduced pool of $760,000; the 20% annual allowance on that gives $152,000. Total allowance = IA $90,000 + AA $152,000 = $242,000.

Q213. Who determines which of the 10%, 20% or 30% pool an item of plant or machinery falls into?

Correct: A — A trader has no general right to choose the pool rate for an asset - the rate is prescribed by the Board of Inland Revenue according to the asset's type.

The rate for each type of asset is prescribed in the Inland Revenue Rules; a taxpayer cannot simply choose a more favourable rate for an asset that does not qualify for it.

Q214. A company takes out fidelity guarantee insurance against loss caused by employee dishonesty. Is the premium deductible?

This protects the trade's own assets against a trading risk and is treated the same way as fire or other business insurance - a normal deductible overhead.

Property tax is charged at the standard rate of 15% on the net assessable value of land or buildings in Hong Kong, on the owner.

s.5(1A)
D · Property tax Deductions Medium

Q232. In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
The actual cost of repairing the roof

Correct: D — Not deductible.

Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

s.5(1A)
D · Property tax Deductions Medium

Q233. In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
The cost of replacing air-conditioners

Correct: A — Not deductible.

Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

s.5(1A)
D · Property tax Deductions Medium

Q234. In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
Rates paid by the owner

Correct: B — Deductible.

Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

s.5(1A)
D · Property tax Deductions Medium

Q235. In computing net assessable value, how is the following treated?
Rates paid by the tenant direct to the Government

Correct: C — Not deductible.

Only rates paid by the owner are deducted. Everything else - Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, replacements - is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much was really spent. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax.

s.5(1A)
D · Property tax Depreciation Hard

Q236. What depreciation allowance is available for plant installed in a property let by an individual and charged to property tax?

Correct: D — No depreciation allowance is available under property tax.

None. Part 6 does not apply to the property tax charge - the 20% statutory allowance is the only relief. If the owner is a company carrying on business the income falls within profits tax instead, where allowances are available.

Part 6
D · Property tax Multiple properties Medium

Q237. A taxpayer owns three let properties. How is property tax computed?

Correct: A — Separately, property by property.

Property by property: each gets its own assessable value, its own rates deduction and its own 20% allowance. Aggregating them is named in the June 2026 report.

s.5
D · Property tax Corporate owners Hard

Q238. A Hong Kong company carrying on business lets a property it owns. What relief is available from property tax?

Correct: B — It may apply for exemption, the income being chargeable to profits tax instead.

Section 5(2)(a) allows a corporation carrying on a trade or business in Hong Kong to apply for exemption from property tax where the income is included in its profits tax computation. Without an application, property tax is charged and set off under s.25.

s.5(2)(a)
D · Property tax Set-off Hard

Q239. A company pays property tax on a let property and the rental income is also assessed to profits tax. How is the property tax relieved?

Correct: C — Set off against the profits tax payable.

Section 25 sets the property tax paid off against the profits tax payable. Separately, the property tax charged in the accounts must be added back in the computation - it is two adjustments in two places from one fact.

s.25
D · Property tax Chargeable person Easy

Q240. On whom is property tax charged?

Correct: D — The owner.

On the owner of the land or buildings, which includes a beneficial owner, a life tenant, a mortgagor in possession and a person holding under a Government lease.

ss.2, 5
D · Property tax Rent-free period Medium

Q241. A lease grants two rent-free months at the start. How are those months treated?

Correct: A — Nothing is assessable for the rent-free months.

No consideration is payable for those months, so nothing enters the assessable value. Including the rent-free period is named in the June 2026 report.

s.5B(2)
D · Property tax Corporate owners Hard

Q242. A company lets a property and does not apply for the s.5(2)(a) property tax exemption. It reports the rental income in its profits tax computation as well. How does the tax actually payable work out?

Correct: B — Corporation profits tax at 8.25%/16.5%, with a full credit for the property tax already paid, so the tax on the rental profit is not duplicated.

Property tax is charged in the ordinary way, and the rental profit is also brought into the profits tax computation (with the property tax itself added back as a disallowable expense), but s.25 then sets the property tax paid off against the profits tax payable, so the company is not really taxed twice on the same rent - it is simply an awkward two-step mechanism instead of a straightforward exemption.

ss.5(2)(a), 25
D · Property tax Losses Medium

Q243. A let property's outgoings (rates paid by the owner, for example) exceed the rent receivable for the year. Can the resulting 'loss' be used anywhere in the property tax system itself?

Correct: C — No - property tax has no concept of a loss; each property stands on its own and a negative net assessable value is simply nil.

Property tax simply has no loss concept - the 20% statutory allowance and owner's rates can reduce the assessable value to nil but never below it, and there is nothing to carry forward within property tax. The only route to any further relief is for the individual to elect personal assessment, which is a different tax mechanism entirely.

s.5
D · Property tax Assessable value Hard

Q244. A property is let to a relative at a nominal rent well below the market rate. On what value is property tax charged?

Correct: D — The market rent that would have been charged to an unconnected tenant, not the token rent actually paid.

Section 5B(2A) charges the property tax on the consideration that would have been payable if the letting were at arm's length, where the actual rent is less than the market rent because of the relationship between the parties.

s.5B(2A)
D · Property tax Lease renewal Medium

Q245. A tenancy is renewed at a materially higher rent partway through the year. How is the assessable value affected?

Correct: A — As if a new letting had started - a fresh assessable value is set based on the new agreed rent from the renewal date.

The assessable value simply follows whatever consideration is actually payable for each part of the year - the old rent up to renewal, the new, higher rent from the renewal date - exactly as any change in the rent under the lease would be reflected.

s.5B(2)
D · Property tax Deductions Medium

Q246. How does Government rent (as distinct from general rates) affect the property tax computation?

Correct: B — The government rent is not deductible by the owner, whether paid by the owner or the tenant.

Only rates paid by the owner are a specific deduction under s.5(1A). Government rent is not separately deductible at all - like mortgage interest and repair costs, it is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance, however much is actually paid.

s.5(1A)
D · Property tax Vacant periods Medium

Q247. A property let at $20,000 a month stood genuinely vacant, with no tenant and no rent receivable, for 2 months of the year. What is the property tax payable for the year?

Correct: C — $24,000.

No rent accrues for a period the property is genuinely vacant between tenancies, so the assessable value covers only the 10 months it was actually let: $20,000 × 10 = $200,000. Charging property tax on a full 12 months' notional rent, as if vacancy made no difference, is the error to avoid - property tax is not a tax on ownership, only on consideration actually receivable.

s.5B(2)
D · Property tax Vacant periods Medium

Q248. A property let at $35,000 a month stood genuinely vacant, with no tenant and no rent receivable, for 3 months of the year. What is the property tax payable for the year?

Correct: D — $37,800.

No rent accrues for a period the property is genuinely vacant between tenancies, so the assessable value covers only the 9 months it was actually let: $35,000 × 9 = $315,000. Charging property tax on a full 12 months' notional rent, as if vacancy made no difference, is the error to avoid - property tax is not a tax on ownership, only on consideration actually receivable.

s.5B(2)
D · Property tax Charge Easy

Q249. Does it make any difference to the owner's property tax whether the tenant uses the property for a business, as a residence, or as a charity's office?

Correct: A — It has no bearing on property tax at all - property tax is a separate charge on the owner regardless of the tenant's own tax position.

None. Property tax is charged on the owner by reference to the rent receivable, entirely independent of what the tenant does with the property or the tenant's own tax status.

s.5
E · Personal assessment Nature Easy

Q250. What is personal assessment?

Correct: B — It is a relief, not a separate head of charge.

Personal assessment is an election that re-computes income already chargeable under the three heads at progressive rates after allowances. It never makes non-chargeable income chargeable, and it is never automatic.

s.41
E · Personal assessment When it helps Medium

Q251. For which of the following can electing personal assessment produce no benefit at all?

Correct: C — A taxpayer whose only income is employment income.

Salaries tax already applies progressive rates and personal allowances, so there is nothing for the election to unlock. Personal assessment helps only where there is property income or unincorporated business profit charged at the standard rate with no allowances.

s.41
E · Personal assessment Eligibility Easy

Q252. What is the age requirement for electing personal assessment?

Correct: D — 18, or under 18 if both parents are dead.

The elector must be 18 or over, or under that age if both parents are dead.

s.41(1)
E · Personal assessment Eligibility Hard

Q253. What makes a person a 'temporary resident' for personal assessment?

Correct: A — More than 180 days in the year, or more than 300 days in two consecutive years including the year of election.

Either limb suffices. Contrast 'ordinarily resident', which is a factual test about residing voluntarily and for a settled purpose with sufficient continuity - a permanent identity card is evidence of it, not the test.

s.41(4)
E · Personal assessment Eligibility Hard

Q254. From the year of assessment 2018/19, how is the residence condition satisfied?

Correct: B — The elector must personally be ordinarily resident or a temporary resident.

From 2018/19 the elector must qualify on their own residence. Up to 2017/18 a married person could rely on the spouse's status; that route is closed.

s.41(1)
E · Personal assessment Married couples Hard

Q255. From the year of assessment 2018/19, how may a married person elect for personal assessment?

Correct: C — Either spouse may elect separately, or they may elect jointly.

The Inland Revenue (Amendment) (No. 9) Ordinance 2018 introduced separate election from YA 2018/19. Before that a joint election was mandatory where both had income, so one spouse could veto it.

Inland Revenue (Amendment) (No. 9) Ordinance 2018
E · Personal assessment Married couples Hard

Q256. A couple are jointly assessed under salaries tax. How must any personal assessment election be made?

Correct: D — The election must be made by them jointly.

Where the couple is already jointly assessed under s.10(2), the personal assessment election must also be joint. They cannot split for one and not the other.

s.41(1A)
E · Personal assessment Married couples Hard

Q257. Where a couple elect jointly, how is the total tax apportioned between them?

Correct: A — In the ratio of each spouse's reduced total income.

In proportion to each spouse's reduced total income - after interest and concessionary deductions, not gross. Each then receives their own notice of assessment.

s.42(2)
E · Personal assessment Time limits Medium

Q258. By when must an election for personal assessment be made?

Correct: B — The later of 2 years after the end of the year of assessment and 2 months after a notice of assessment.

For YA 2026/27 that means not later than 31 March 2029, or two months after a notice of assessment or additional assessment, whichever is later.

s.41(2)
E · Personal assessment Time limits Hard

Q259. By when must an election for personal assessment be withdrawn?

Correct: C — Within 6 months of the date the personal assessment is issued.

Six months, or such longer period as the Commissioner considers reasonable. Where the election was joint, the withdrawal must be joint too. After withdrawal the taxpayer may not elect again for that year without the Commissioner's agreement.

s.41(3)
E · Personal assessment Deceased taxpayer Medium

Q260. A person eligible to elect for personal assessment dies before doing so. What happens to the right of election?

Correct: D — His executor has the same right of election.

The executor has the same right over the deceased's total income as the deceased would have had.

s.41
E · Personal assessment Computation Hard

Q261. Which figures are aggregated to arrive at total income under personal assessment?

Correct: A — Net assessable value, net assessable income, and net assessable profits.

Property enters at net assessable value - after rates and the 20% allowance - employment at net assessable income, and business at net assessable profits after losses brought forward and donations already relieved. Bringing property in at gross rent is a reported error.

s.42
E · Personal assessment Interest deduction Hard

Q262. How much interest on money borrowed to produce property income may be deducted under personal assessment?

Correct: B — Restricted to the net assessable value of that property.

Capped at the net assessable value of that individual property (Board of Review D51/04). The excess lapses; it cannot create or increase a loss. This is a different relief from home loan interest under ss.26E/26F, which is capped at $100,000 and relates to a dwelling the taxpayer occupies.

s.42(1); D51/04
E · Personal assessment Computation Hard

Q263. Tax under personal assessment is the lower of the progressive rates on net chargeable income and what?

Correct: C — The standard rate on reduced total income.

The standard rate applies to reduced total income - before personal allowances. Applying it to net chargeable income uses the wrong base and understates the cap.

s.43
E · Personal assessment Computation Hard

Q264. Total income under personal assessment is $1,420,000, interest to produce property income is $0, and allowances total $145,000. What is the tax payable?

Correct: D — $198,750.

Reduced total income $1,420,000; less allowances = net chargeable income $1,275,000. Progressive rates give $198,750; the standard rate on reduced total income gives $213,000. The lower is $198,750.

s.43
E · Personal assessment Computation Hard

Q265. Total income under personal assessment is $1,058,400, interest to produce property income is $200,000, and allowances total $290,000. What is the tax payable?

Correct: A — $78,628.

Reduced total income $858,400; less allowances = net chargeable income $568,400. Progressive rates give $78,628; the standard rate on reduced total income gives $128,760. The lower is $78,628.

s.43
E · Personal assessment Computation Hard

Q266. Total income under personal assessment is $884,000, interest to produce property income is $42,000, and allowances total $145,000. What is the tax payable?

Correct: B — $100,490.

Reduced total income $842,000; less allowances = net chargeable income $697,000. Progressive rates give $100,490; the standard rate on reduced total income gives $126,300. The lower is $100,490.

s.43
E · Personal assessment Business losses Medium

Q267. What is the effect of electing personal assessment on a sole proprietorship loss of the year?

Correct: C — It can be set against the taxpayer's other income in the same year.

This is one of the two main reasons to elect. Without the election the loss is stranded in the profits tax computation and merely carried forward; personal assessment lets it shelter current-year salary and property income.

s.42(1)
E · Personal assessment Business losses Hard

Q268. Can an offshore business loss be brought into a personal assessment computation?

Correct: D — It cannot be brought in - offshore profits were never chargeable.

No. Personal assessment aggregates income chargeable under the three heads. Profits that were never chargeable bring no loss relief either - the rule cuts both ways.

s.42
E · Personal assessment When it helps Hard

Q269. A taxpayer with substantial salary income also owns an unmortgaged let property. Is personal assessment likely to be beneficial?

Correct: A — No - the marginal progressive rate exceeds the standard rate.

Above roughly $200,000 of net chargeable income the marginal progressive rate is 17%, against a 15% standard rate. Aggregating the property income drags it up to 17%, and there is no mortgage interest or loss for the election to unlock. Compute both ways - never assume.

s.43
E · Personal assessment Eligibility Medium

Q270. Which of the following cannot elect for personal assessment?

Correct: B — A company.

Personal assessment is available to individuals only. A corporate partner is assessed on its share at corporate rates and that is the end of it.

s.41
E · Personal assessment Making the election Easy

Q271. How must an election for personal assessment be made?

Correct: C — In writing, in the tax return or on Form IR76C.

The election must be in writing - in practice by completing the relevant section of the tax return, or on Form IR76C.

s.41(2)
E · Personal assessment Computation Medium

Q272. A married couple elect for personal assessment. What allowance may they claim between them for their marital status?

Correct: D — The higher of the two allowances - not both.

The married person's allowance under personal assessment works the same way as under salaries tax - one married couple gets one married person's allowance (or, unmarried, each their own basic allowance), never both a basic and a married allowance stacked together.

s.42A
E · Personal assessment Computation Medium

Q273. Are child, dependent parent, dependent sibling, and disability allowances available under a personal assessment computation?

Correct: A — Yes - each qualifying child allowance, dependent parent allowance and so on is available under personal assessment exactly as under salaries tax.

The full suite of personal allowances under Part V (basic, married, child, dependent parent, dependent sibling, single parent, disabled dependant, personal disability) is available to reduce reduced total income to net chargeable income, exactly as in a salaries tax computation.

s.42A
E · Personal assessment Computation Medium

Q274. Are the concessionary deductions available under salaries tax (self-education expenses, home loan interest, elderly residential care expenses, MPF contributions, approved charitable donations) also available under personal assessment?

Correct: B — Yes - the same concessionary deductions (self-education expenses, home loan interest, MPF contributions, elderly residential care expenses, approved charitable donations, and so on) are all available.

Yes, at the same statutory caps, deducted from total income before arriving at reduced total income - alongside the personal-assessment-specific deductions for business losses and interest to produce property income that salaries tax alone does not offer.

s.42
E · Personal assessment Computation Medium

Q275. Does electing personal assessment change how income from each individual source (property, employment, business) is itself computed?

Correct: C — No - each source of income keeps its own basis; property income is still computed on an accruals basis and business profits on the normal profits tax basis, merely aggregated afterwards.

Personal assessment is purely a re-aggregation and re-rating mechanism. Each source's net assessable value, net assessable income or assessable profits is computed exactly as it would be under the ordinary property tax, salaries tax or profits tax rules, and only then are the results added together and taxed afresh.

s.42
E · Personal assessment When it helps Hard

Q276. In which of the following is personal assessment LEAST likely to produce any tax saving?

Correct: D — A property is jointly owned by a married couple; only the spouse who elects personal assessment includes their own share.

Where a property is solely owned and let for the whole year with no mortgage, there is nothing for personal assessment to unlock - no loss to use, no interest to deduct beyond what property tax itself already sets off against rates, and the standard rate on that income alone is likely to beat the progressive computation once it is aggregated with other income. Always compute the tax both ways rather than assuming.

E · Personal assessment Practical approach Medium

Q277. In an exam question asking whether a married couple should elect for personal assessment, what should the answer actually compare?

Correct: A — The whole family's tax position, computed both with and without the election, for each spouse separately and jointly.

Compute the total family tax bill under each realistic combination - no election, each spouse electing separately, and a joint election - and recommend whichever gives the lowest total. There is no shortcut rule that always wins; election is a comparison exercise, not an automatic saving.

E · Personal assessment Business losses Hard

Q278. A sole trader's business made a loss last year (say YA 2024/25), which was simply carried forward under the profits tax computation because no election was made at the time. Can personal assessment still be used now to relieve that loss against last year's other income?

Correct: B — The loss is still relievable, since personal assessment for a year can be elected up to two years after that year ends.

The time limit for electing personal assessment for a given year runs for two years after that year of assessment ends (or longer following a late assessment), so there is still time to go back and elect for YA 2024/25 itself, setting that year's loss against that year's other income, rather than only being able to use the loss against future profits.

s.41(2)
E · Personal assessment Computation Medium

Q279. In the personal assessment computation, what does 'total income' mean before it becomes 'reduced total income'?

Correct: C — It is the total income of the individual, before deducting interest, concessionary deductions or losses - the starting point of the computation.

Total income is simply the sum of the individual's net assessable value, net assessable income and assessable profits from all sources - the starting point, before any of the personal-assessment-specific deductions (interest, concessionary deductions, losses) are subtracted to arrive at reduced total income.

s.42
E · Personal assessment Partnership interaction Medium

Q280. An individual partner in a mixed partnership elects personal assessment. What happens to the corporate partner's share of the same partnership's profit?

Correct: D — It is included in full, since a corporate partner's own separate assessment is unaffected by what an individual partner elects.

Each partner's share is assessed independently of what any other partner elects. The corporate partner's share of profit continues to be assessed under ordinary profits tax at the corporate rate, entirely unaffected by the individual partner's personal assessment election.

s.41
E · Personal assessment Eligibility Medium

Q281. Must a taxpayer have more than one source of chargeable income before personal assessment is worth considering?

Correct: A — Yes - a non-Hong Kong-sourced loss cannot be brought in, but Hong Kong-sourced property, employment and business income can all still be aggregated even where some of it individually would be modest.

There is no such requirement in the legislation - even a taxpayer with a single source can elect - but as a matter of practical benefit, personal assessment tends only to help where there is property or business income (with a loss, or mortgage interest, or no allowances of its own) to combine with something else; a single salary source alone gains nothing from electing.

s.41
E · Personal assessment Time limits Medium

Q282. What happens if an election for personal assessment is made after the statutory time limit in s.41(2) has passed?

Correct: B — The Commissioner may refuse to accept a late election, though in practice a reasonable excuse for the delay is usually accommodated.

The election is out of time and the Commissioner is not obliged to accept it, though there is administrative practice of accepting a late election where there is a reasonable explanation - it should never be assumed as of right.

s.41(2)

What this is

Section B mirrors the exam's real OT case format: unlike Section A's single-fact questions, each case gives one connected scenario and asks five questions against it — so an early answer (a rental value, a share of profit) often feeds directly into a later one, exactly as it would in a real case.
