Case 1 — Ms Fiona Ng (10 marks)

Fiona Ng is employed as marketing manager by Silverline Retail Ltd, a company centrally managed and controlled in Hong Kong. Her annual salary for the year of assessment 2026/27 is $960,000. Silverline provides her with a self-contained flat, rent free, for the whole year; Fiona has no outgoings deductible under s.12(1)(a) against her salary.

Separately, Fiona wholly owns a second residential flat, which she lets out (unconnected with her employer) for the whole year at $18,000 a month. She personally paid rates of $6,500 for the year on that flat. She is single and claims only the basic allowance ($145,000 for 2026/27); she has no mortgage on either property and no other income, deductions or losses.
Rental value

B001. What rental value must be included in Fiona's assessable income for the flat Silverline provides rent free?

Correct: A — $96,000.

The flat is self-contained accommodation, so the rate is 10% of income after s.12(1)(a) outgoings. With no outgoings to deduct, that base is her full salary: $960,000 × 10% = $96,000.

s.9(2)
Assessable income

B002. What is Fiona's total assessable income from her employment for the year (salary plus the rental value of the flat)?

Correct: B — $1,056,000.

$960,000 salary + $96,000 rental value = $1,056,000. Omitting the rental value entirely, or computing it at the wrong percentage (8% applies to two hotel rooms, not a self-contained flat), are the two errors this question is designed to catch.

s.9(1)(a), s.9(2)
Property tax

B003. What is the property tax payable on Fiona's own let flat for the year?

Correct: C — $25,140.

Assessable value $216,000 ($18,000 × 12); less rates paid by the owner $6,500 = $209,500; less the 20% statutory allowance $41,900 = net assessable value $167,600; × 15% = $25,140. Forgetting the rates deduction, forgetting the 20% allowance, or forgetting both and taxing the gross rent, each give one of the other three options.

ss.5, 5(1A)
Salaries tax computation

B004. Ignoring any election for personal assessment, what is Fiona's salaries tax payable for the year?

Correct: D — $136,870.

Progressive rates on net chargeable income ($1,056,000 − $145,000 allowance = $911,000) give $136,870; the standard rate on net income before allowances ($1,056,000) gives $158,400. Salaries tax payable is the lower of the two: $136,870. Applying the standard rate to income after allowances instead of before (giving $136,650) is a close-looking but wrong alternative route to this figure.

s.13
Personal assessment

B005. Should Fiona elect personal assessment for the year?

Correct: A — No — total tax without electing ($162,010) is lower than with personal assessment ($165,362): there is no mortgage interest or loss for the election to unlock, and her income already sits in the 17% marginal band.

Without electing: salaries tax $136,870 + property tax $25,140 = $162,010. Electing aggregates both incomes ($1,223,600) less the same one basic allowance, computed at progressive rates capped by the standard rate on reduced total income: $165,362. Aggregating drags the property income into her 17% marginal band, above the flat 15% property tax rate, and there is nothing else (no mortgage interest, no loss) for the election to unlock — so electing costs her $3,352 more, not less. Compute both ways; never assume personal assessment helps.

s.41-43

Case 2 — Golden Horizon Ltd (10 marks)

Golden Horizon Ltd, a Hong Kong trading company, reports an accounting profit before tax of $5,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. Its accounts include depreciation of $300,000 and a fine of $20,000 for a pollution control breach, and it paid $150,000 in approved charitable donations, all charged as expenses.

During the year Golden Horizon bought qualifying plant for $500,000 (the 20% pool's written-down value brought forward was $200,000, and there were no disposals), and incurred $1,000,000 of qualifying Type B R&D expenditure, which is included in the $1,000,000 already charged as an expense in arriving at the accounting profit above. The company has no connected entities for the two-tier regime.
Depreciation allowances

B006. What is the total depreciation allowance available on the plant pool for the year?

Correct: B — $380,000.

Initial allowance: $500,000 additions × 60% = $300,000. Reduced pool: $200,000 + $500,000 − $300,000 = $400,000. Annual allowance at 20%: $80,000. Total = IA $300,000 + AA $80,000 = $380,000. Taking the IA alone, the AA alone, or computing the AA on the pool before deducting the IA, each give one of the other three options.

s.39B; Sch. 3
R&D deduction

B007. Beyond the $1,000,000 already charged as an expense in the accounts, what additional deduction is available for the qualifying Type B R&D expenditure?

Correct: C — $2,000,000.

Type B R&D is enhanced at 300% on the first $2,000,000: $1,000,000 × 3 = $3,000,000 total allowable deduction. $1,000,000 of that is already in the accounting profit, so the additional deduction still to be made in the computation is $3,000,000 − $1,000,000 = $2,000,000. Stating the total enhanced deduction ($3,000,000) as if it were the additional amount is the commonest error - it double-counts the $1,000,000 already expensed.

s.16B
Donations

B008. What is the maximum charitable donation deduction Golden Horizon may claim?

Correct: D — $150,000.

The allowable deduction is the lower of the amount paid ($150,000) and 35% of assessable profits before donations ($1,081,500), so the full $150,000 paid is deductible — well within the $1,081,500 cap. Stating the cap itself, rather than the lower of the two, is a common error.

s.16D
Assessable profit

B009. What is Golden Horizon's assessable profit for the year?

Correct: A — $2,940,000.

$5,000,000 accounting profit + $300,000 depreciation + $150,000 donations + $20,000 fine = $5,470,000. Less the additional R&D deduction $2,000,000 = $3,470,000. Less depreciation allowances $380,000 = $3,090,000 (the base for the donation cap). Less the donation deduction $150,000 = assessable profit $2,940,000. Stopping before deducting the donation, or before deducting the depreciation allowances, gives one of the other two wrong figures.

s.14, s.16, s.17
Two-tier profits tax

B010. What is Golden Horizon's profits tax payable for the year?

Correct: B — $320,100.

The two-tier rates apply to the final assessable profit of $2,940,000: ($2,000,000 × 8.25%) + ($940,000 × 16.5%) = $320,100. Applying a flat 16.5% or flat 8.25% to the whole profit, or applying the two-tier rates to the wrong (pre-donation) profit figure of $3,090,000, each give one of the other three options.

s.14AA

Case 3 — Harbour Partners (10 marks)

Harbour Partners is a Hong Kong partnership with two partners: Mr Tam, an individual, holding a 60% profit share, and Silver Bay Ltd, a corporate partner, holding the remaining 40%. The partnership's assessable profit for the year is $4,000,000, allocated in that profit-sharing ratio, with each partner's two-tier $2,000,000 band apportioned in the same ratio.

Mr Tam's own tax on his share remained unpaid more than six months after the due date - specifically 7 months overdue when he finally settled it.
Partnership allocation

B011. What is Mr Tam's share of the partnership's assessable profit?

Correct: C — $2,400,000.

$4,000,000 × 60% = $2,400,000. Using Silver Bay's 40% share instead, using the whole partnership profit unallocated, or misapplying a 50:50 split, each give one of the other three options.

s.22
Corporate partner's tax

B012. What is Silver Bay Ltd's own profits tax payable on its 40% share, applying the two-tier rates to its apportioned band?

Correct: D — $198,000.

Silver Bay's share is $1,600,000, with an apportioned first-tier band of $800,000 ($2,000,000 × 40%) at the corporate rates: ($800,000 × 8.25%) + ($800,000 × 16.5%) = $198,000. Applying a flat 16.5% or flat 8.25% to the whole share, ignoring the apportioned band, or stating Mr Tam's figure instead, each give one of the other three options.

s.14AA; DIPN 28
Individual partner's tax

B013. What is Mr Tam's own profits tax payable on his 60% share, applying the two-tier rates to his apportioned band?

Correct: A — $270,000.

Mr Tam's share is $2,400,000, with an apportioned first-tier band of $1,200,000 ($2,000,000 × 60%) at the unincorporated rates: ($1,200,000 × 7.5%) + ($1,200,000 × 15%) = $270,000. Applying a flat 15% or flat 7.5% to the whole share, or stating Silver Bay's figure instead, each give one of the other three options.

s.14AA; DIPN 28
Total partnership tax

B014. What is the total profits tax payable in respect of Harbour Partners' profit for the year?

Correct: B — $468,000.

The partnership is not itself taxed; the total is simply the sum of what each partner pays on their own apportioned share: $270,000 + $198,000 = $468,000. Applying one flat rate to the whole $4,000,000 as if it were a single corporate taxpayer (16.5%), a single unincorporated taxpayer at the flat rate, or the two-tier corporate rates without regard to Mr Tam's individual rate, each give one of the other three - and each ignores that a mixed partnership has more than one type of partner.

s.14AA; DIPN 28
Late payment surcharge

B015. Mr Tam's own tax of $270,000 on his share was paid 7 months after the due date. What is the total amount he actually had to pay, including surcharges?

Correct: C — $311,850.

A 5% surcharge arises on the due date: $270,000 × 1.05 = $283,500. Because it remained unpaid beyond 6 months, a further 10% is charged on the tax plus that first surcharge: $283,500 × 1.10 = $311,850. Stopping at the first 5% surcharge, applying a flat 10% instead of the compounding two-step charge, or applying the second 10% to the original tax rather than to tax-plus-first-surcharge, each give one of the other three options.

s.71(5), s.71(5A)

Case 4 — Lau's Trading (10 marks)

Kenneth Lau runs Lau's Trading as a sole proprietorship. Its accounts for the year show a net profit of $1,800,000, after charging the following as expenses: a monthly “salary” of $50,000 drawn by Kenneth himself ($600,000 for the year), a salary of $240,000 paid to his wife, who works full time managing the shop, and depreciation of $80,000.

Depreciation allowances for the year have been computed at $120,000. Kenneth also made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000 in respect of himself as a self-employed person; this was not charged in the accounts above.
s.17(2) payments to the proprietor

B016. How much must be added back in respect of the salaries paid to Kenneth and to his wife?

Correct: D — $840,000.

Both are added back: $600,000 (Kenneth) + $240,000 (his wife) = $840,000. A sole proprietor cannot be their own employee, and s.17(2) extends the same treatment to a payment to the proprietor's spouse — however genuinely she works in the business, husband and wife are not treated as at arm's length for this purpose. Adding back only one of the two is the error this question tests.

s.17(2)
s.16AA MPF deduction

B017. What deduction may the business claim for Kenneth's own mandatory MPF contribution as a self-employed person?

Correct: A — $18,000.

Section 16AA allows the proprietor's own mandatory contribution as a deduction in the profits tax computation, capped at the statutory maximum of $18,000. It was not charged in the accounts, so it is deducted in the computation. Answering nil — on the reasoning that a proprietor's own payments are never deductible — confuses this with the s.17(2) salary rule; MPF is the deliberate exception.

s.16AA
Assessable profit

B018. What is Lau's Trading's assessable profit for the year?

Correct: B — $2,582,000.

$1,800,000 net profit + $840,000 salaries added back under s.17(2) + $80,000 depreciation = $2,720,000; less depreciation allowances $120,000 and the s.16AA MPF deduction $18,000 = $2,582,000. Forgetting the MPF deduction, forgetting the wife's salary, or forgetting the depreciation allowances each give one of the other three options.

ss.16, 16AA, 17(2)
Two-tier profits tax

B019. What is the profits tax payable by Lau's Trading?

Correct: C — $237,300.

A sole proprietorship is an unincorporated business, so the two-tier rates are 7.5% and 15%, not the corporate 8.25%/16.5%: (2,000,000 × 7.5%) + ($582,000 × 15%) = $237,300. Using the corporate rates gives $261,030 and is the commonest slip here.

s.14AA
Loss relief

B020. Suppose instead that Lau's Trading had made a loss for the year, and Kenneth also had salary income from a part-time job. What could he do to relieve the loss against that salary in the same year?

Correct: D — Elect personal assessment, which lets the current-year business loss be set against his salary in the same year.

Within profits tax alone the loss is simply carried forward (s.19C) and cannot touch his salary. Electing personal assessment aggregates all his chargeable income, letting the current-year business loss shelter the salary. Hong Kong has no carry-back and no transfer of losses between spouses.

ss.19C, 42(1)

Case 5 — Ms Priya Sharma (10 marks)

Priya Sharma has a Hong Kong employment with an annual salary of $1,200,000 for the year of assessment 2026/27.

During the year she exercised a share option granted to her by her employer in an earlier year. The market value of the shares on the date of exercise was $850,000 and she paid the exercise price of $500,000. On completing her fixed-term contract she also received a gratuity of $200,000, payable under the terms of that contract.

She paid $135,000 of mortgage interest on the flat she lives in herself, and made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000. She is married and her husband has no income; the married person's allowance is $290,000.
Share options

B021. What amount of the share option gain is assessable to salaries tax?

Correct: A — $350,000.

The charge falls on exercise, on the gain: market value at exercise $850,000 less the exercise price paid $500,000 = $350,000. Assessing the full market value, or treating the gain as a capital gain outside the charge, are both wrong — an employee share option gain is specifically brought into charge by s.9(1)(d).

s.9(1)(d); DIPN 38
Termination payments

B022. How is the $200,000 contract-completion gratuity treated?

Correct: B — Assessable in full — it is payable under the contract, so it rewards services.

A gratuity payable under the contract on completing it is a reward for services and is fully assessable. Contrast a genuine statutory severance or long service payment under the Employment Ordinance, which is compensation for loss of office and is not assessable — that is the distinction being tested.

s.8(1)
Home loan interest

B023. What deduction may Priya claim for the $135,000 of home loan interest?

Correct: C — $100,000.

Home loan interest on the taxpayer's own dwelling is deductible but capped at $100,000 a year (the $120,000 figure applies only where there is a qualifying child), so $100,000 of the $135,000 paid is allowed and the excess simply lapses.

ss.26E, 26F
Net income

B024. What is Priya's net income for the year, after deductions but before allowances?

Correct: D — $1,632,000.

Assessable income $1,200,000 salary + $350,000 option gain + $200,000 gratuity = $1,750,000; less the capped home loan interest $100,000 and MPF $18,000 = $1,632,000.

ss.12, 26E, 26G
Salaries tax payable

B025. What is Priya's salaries tax payable for the year?

Correct: A — $210,140.

Progressive rates on net chargeable income ($1,632,000 − $290,000 allowance = $1,342,000) give $210,140; the standard rate on net income before allowances ($1,632,000 × 15%) gives $244,800. The lower of the two is $210,140.

s.13

Case 6 — Mr Wong Kwok-keung (10 marks)

Wong Kwok-keung owns two properties in Hong Kong, both let in his own name.

Flat A was let for the whole year at $30,000 a month. Wong paid rates of $12,000 on it. The tenant defaulted and $60,000 of the year's rent was proved to be irrecoverable during the year.

Flat B was let under a new four-year lease granted at the start of the year, for which Wong received a premium of $360,000. No periodic rent is payable on Flat B, and the tenant pays the rates on it direct to the Government.
Irrecoverable rent

B026. What is the assessable value of Flat A for the year, before deducting rates and the statutory allowance?

Correct: B — $300,000.

Rent for the year $360,000 ($30,000 × 12) less the $60,000 proved irrecoverable during the year = $300,000. Section 7C(1) gives the deduction in the year the rent is recognised as irrecoverable, not the year it accrued.

ss.5B(2), 7C(1)
Flat A property tax

B027. What is the property tax payable on Flat A?

Correct: C — $34,560.

Assessable value $300,000; less rates paid by the owner $12,000 = $288,000; less the 20% statutory allowance $57,600 = net assessable value $230,400; × 15% = $34,560.

ss.5, 5(1A)
Lease premium

B028. How much of Flat B's premium falls into the assessable value for this year?

Correct: D — $120,000.

A premium is spread over the lease term or 36 months, whichever is shorter. The lease runs four years (48 months), so the 36-month cap bites: $360,000 ÷ 36 × 12 = $120,000 for the year. Spreading over the full 48 months gives $90,000 and is the error the cap exists to catch.

s.5B(4)
Total property tax

B029. What is Wong's total property tax liability for the year on both properties?

Correct: A — $48,960.

Property tax is computed property by property, each with its own rates deduction and its own 20% allowance: Flat A $34,560 + Flat B $14,400 (net assessable value $96,000 × 15%) = $48,960. Flat B has no owner's rates to deduct because the tenant pays them direct.

s.5
Corporate owners

B030. Suppose Flat B were instead owned by a Hong Kong company carrying on business here. What relief from property tax would be available?

Correct: B — Apply for exemption under s.5(2)(a), the rental income being included in its profits tax computation instead.

A corporation carrying on a trade or business in Hong Kong may apply under s.5(2)(a) for exemption from property tax where the income is brought into its profits tax computation. Without that application property tax is charged and then set off against the profits tax payable under s.25 — so the rent is not taxed twice either way, but the exemption is the cleaner route.

ss.5(2)(a), 25

Question 1 — Mr Ivan Ho (15 marks)

Scenario15 marks

Ivan Ho is employed on an annual salary of $1,020,000 for the year of assessment 2026/27. During the year he incurred $60,000 on a job-related course, qualifying as a deductible self-education expense, and made the mandatory MPF contribution of $18,000. He is married; his wife has no income of her own.

Ivan also wholly owns a separate residential flat, which he lets out unconnected with his employment. Its net assessable value for the year (after rates and the 20% statutory allowance) is $200,000. He pays mortgage interest of $150,000 a year on the loan used to acquire that flat.

(a) Compute Ivan's salaries tax liability for the year, ignoring any election for personal assessment. (10 marks)

(b) Advise, with supporting calculations, whether Ivan should elect personal assessment for the year. (5 marks)

Show model answer

Less: mandatory MPF contribution (1 mark)(18,000)

Less: married person's allowance (1 mark)(290,000)

2%/6%/10%/14% on four $50,000 bands ($16,000) + 17% on the $452,000 remainder ($76,840)		92,840
Standard rate on net income before allowances: $942,000 × 15% (2 marks)141,300
Salaries tax payable (the lower of the two) (2 marks)92,840

Total for part (a): 10 marks. Using the standard rate on net income after allowances ($652,000 × 15% = $97,800) instead of before them, is the single commonest way to lose the 2 marks on the comparison.

(b) Without electing personal assessment
Salaries tax (from part (a))92,840

Question 2 — XYZ Trading Ltd (25 marks)

Scenario25 marks

XYZ Trading Ltd, a Hong Kong company with no connected entities, reports a net profit per accounts of $8,000,000 for the year ended 31 March 2027. The accounts include depreciation of $450,000, approved charitable donations of $200,000, and legal fees of $60,000 for acquiring a new five-year retail lease.

The company's plant and machinery pool (20% pool) had a written-down value brought forward of $600,000; during the year it bought qualifying plant for $800,000 and sold plant for $100,000. Separately, it incurred $1,500,000 of qualifying Type B R&D expenditure, already charged as an expense (and so already included) in the $8,000,000 net profit above. The company also has an unrelieved trading loss of $500,000 brought forward from an earlier year.

(a) Compute XYZ Trading Ltd's profits tax payable for the year. (20 marks)

(b) XYZ Trading Ltd is considering whether the $500,000 loss could instead be surrendered to a profitable fellow group company. Advise, with reasons. (5 marks)

Show model answer
(a) XYZ Trading Ltd — Profits Tax Computation, YA 2026/27

Depreciation (1 mark)450,000
Charitable donations (1 mark)200,000
Legal fees — capital, acquiring a new lease (2 marks)60,000
8,710,000
Less: additional R&D deduction (4 marks)
Type B enhanced deduction: min($1,500,000, $2,000,000) × 300% = $4,500,000 total, less the $1,500,000 already expensed = $3,000,000 additional		(3,000,000)
Less: depreciation allowances (4 marks)
IA: $800,000 × 60% = $480,000. Pool: $600,000 + $800,000 − $480,000 − $100,000 disposal = $820,000. AA: $820,000 × 20% = $164,000. Total $480,000 + $164,000		(644,000)
Profit before loss brought forward5,066,000
Less: loss brought forward (1 mark)(500,000)
Profit before donations (Z)4,566,000
Less: approved charitable donations (2 marks)
lower of $200,000 actual and 35% × $4,566,000 = $1,598,100 — fully allowable		(200,000)
Assessable profit4,366,000
Tax payable
First $2,000,000 at 8.25% (2 marks)165,000
Remaining $2,366,000 at 16.5% (2 marks)390,390
Profits tax payable555,390

Total for part (a): 20 marks. Stating the total enhanced R&D deduction ($4,500,000) instead of the additional amount still to be deducted ($3,000,000), and computing the annual allowance on the pool before deducting the initial allowance, are the two errors this question is designed to catch.

(b) (5 marks): Hong Kong has no group loss relief of any kind. Each company, including XYZ Trading Ltd and any fellow group company, is a separate person chargeable to profits tax in its own right (2 marks). The $500,000 loss cannot be surrendered to, or set off against, a fellow group company's profits, however profitable that company is or however closely the two are connected (2 marks). The loss simply remains within XYZ Trading Ltd itself, carried forward indefinitely with no time limit, to be set off only against XYZ's own future assessable profits from the same trade (1 mark).

Question 3 — Mr Anthony Cheung (15 marks)

Scenario15 marks

Anthony Cheung owns two properties in Hong Kong, both let in his own name during the year of assessment 2026/27.

The shop was let for the whole year at $45,000 a month. Anthony paid rates of $20,000 on it. The tenant fell into difficulty and three months' rent was proved irrecoverable during the year.

The flat was let for the whole year at $22,000 a month, and Anthony also received a premium of $540,000 on granting that five-year lease at the start of the year. The flat's tenant pays the rates direct to the Government.

(a) Compute Anthony's property tax liability for the year. (11 marks)

(b) Anthony is considering transferring both properties into a Hong Kong company he owns, which carries on a trading business here. Explain the property tax consequences. (4 marks)

Spreading the premium over the full 60 months (giving $108,000) instead of applying the 36-month cap is the other error this question tests.

(b) (4 marks): A corporation carrying on a trade or business in Hong Kong may apply under s.5(2)(a) for exemption from property tax, on the basis that the rental income is instead brought into its profits tax computation (2 marks). If no such application is made, property tax is charged on the company in the ordinary way, but s.25 then sets that property tax off against the profits tax payable, so the same rent is not taxed twice either way (1 mark). Note the rate difference this creates: the rental profit would move from the flat 15% property tax charge to the corporate two-tier profits tax rates of 8.25%/16.5%, and the company could then deduct actual outgoings such as mortgage interest and repairs rather than being confined to the fixed 20% statutory allowance (1 mark).

Question 4 — Summit & Vale Partners (25 marks)

Scenario25 marks

Summit & Vale Partners is a Hong Kong partnership with two partners: Mr Vale, an individual, holding a 70% profit share, and Summit Holdings Ltd, a Hong Kong company, holding the remaining 30%.

The partnership's accounts for the year ended 31 March 2027 show a net profit of $6,400,000, after charging: a partner's salary of $900,000 paid to Mr Vale, a salary of $300,000 paid to Mr Vale's spouse (who works in the business), depreciation of $350,000, and approved charitable donations of $120,000.

The partnership's 30% plant and machinery pool had a written-down value brought forward of $500,000. During the year it bought qualifying plant for $900,000 and sold plant for $400,000.

(a) Compute the partnership's assessable profit for the year. (14 marks)

(b) Compute the profits tax payable by each partner, and in total. (8 marks)

(c) Mr Vale asks whether Summit Holdings Ltd could elect personal assessment on its share. Advise. (3 marks)

8,070,000

IA: $900,000 × 60% = $540,000. Pool: $500,000 + $900,000 − $540,000 − $400,000 disposal = $460,000. AA: $460,000 × 30% = $138,000. Total $540,000 + $138,000		(678,000)
Profit before donations7,392,000

Total for part (a): 14 marks. Both the partner's own salary and the salary to his spouse are added back under s.17(2) — a partnership cannot deduct either, and forgetting the spouse's salary is the commonest omission. Computing the annual allowance on the pool before deducting the initial allowance is the other error tested here.

Mr Vale — individual, 70%

Total for part (b): 8 marks. The $2,000,000 two-tier band is apportioned between the partners in the profit-sharing ratio, and each partner's slice is then taxed at their own rates — 7.5%/15% for the individual, 8.25%/16.5% for the corporate partner. Applying one flat set of rates to the whole $7,272,000, as if the partnership were a single taxpayer, is the error a mixed partnership is set to catch.

(c) (3 marks): No. Personal assessment is available to individuals only (1 mark). Summit Holdings Ltd is a company, so its share of the partnership's assessable profit simply stays in its own profits tax computation at the corporate rates, with no personal assessment route available to it (1 mark). Mr Vale, being an individual, could elect on his own share — but on these figures it would not help him: his share alone far exceeds the level at which the 17% marginal progressive rate overtakes the 15% standard rate, and there is no loss or interest here for the election to unlock (1 mark).

Question 5 — Mr Daniel Lau (15 marks)

Scenario15 marks

Daniel Lau is an individual resident in Hong Kong. In May 2026 he bought three adjacent mini-storage units in Kwun Tong for $3,200,000. He paid stamp duty and legal costs of $120,000 and spent $280,000 partitioning, repainting and installing access controls. He borrowed to fund the purchase and paid $180,000 interest during the holding period.

The units were never used by Daniel or let to tenants. He placed online advertisements for a resale before the renovation works were completed and sold all three units in February 2027 for $4,350,000, paying selling agency and legal costs of $90,000. Daniel says the gain is capital because he originally described the units as a "long-term store of value".

(a) Explain whether the gain is more likely to be taxable as profits from trade or non-taxable as capital. (10 marks)

(b) Assuming the gain is taxable as trading profits, compute Daniel's assessable profit and profits tax payable for YA 2026/27. (5 marks)

Show model answer

(a) (10 marks): The issue is whether Daniel was carrying on an adventure in the nature of trade, so that the profit arises from a trade, profession or business carried on in Hong Kong and is chargeable under s.14 (1 mark). Intention is relevant but is judged objectively from the facts, not merely from Daniel's label (1 mark). The subject matter points towards trade: three adjacent units are more consistent with a resale package than a personal long-term investment (1 mark). The short period of ownership, from May 2026 to February 2027, is a strong badge of trade (1 mark). The renovation and access-control works improved the units for onward sale rather than for own use or rental yield (1 mark). The early online advertisements, before completion of the works, show a pre-existing resale plan (1 mark). Borrowing and interest exposure support a need for quick realisation rather than passive holding (1 mark). There was no rental income or own use during the holding period, so there is little evidence of investment exploitation (1 mark). The buying, improving and selling activity was carried out in Hong Kong, so the source of any trading profit is Hong Kong (1 mark). On balance, the gain is more likely a taxable trading profit, and Daniel bears the practical burden of supporting any capital-gain claim if challenged (1 mark).

(b) Daniel Lau — Trading Profit and Profits Tax, YA 2026/27
Sale proceeds (1 mark)4,350,000
Less: purchase cost (1 mark)(3,200,000)
Less: stamp duty and legal costs (1 mark)(120,000)
Less: renovation and access controls(280,000)
Less: interest and selling costs(270,000)
Assessable profits (1 mark)480,000
Profits tax at the individual first-tier rate, $480,000 × 7.5% (1 mark)36,000

Total for part (b): 5 marks. This question is designed to catch the error of treating a self-serving "capital intention" statement as decisive, instead of weighing the badges of trade objectively.

Question 6 — JadeTech Manufacturing Ltd (25 marks)

Scenario25 marks

JadeTech Manufacturing Ltd is a Hong Kong manufacturing company with no connected entities. Its net profit per accounts for the year ended 31 March 2027 is $7,850,000, after charging depreciation of $740,000 and approved charitable donations of $260,000, and after crediting an accounting gain of $450,000 on the sale of its old factory.

The old factory had qualifying construction cost of $2,400,000. Before the sale, total industrial building allowances granted were $1,152,000 and the residue of expenditure was $1,248,000. The sale proceeds attributable to the building, excluding land, were $1,560,000.

The 30% plant and machinery pool had written-down value brought forward of $520,000. During the year JadeTech bought qualifying plant for cash of $900,000 and sold pooled plant for $180,000. It also acquired a machine on hire purchase: deposit paid $240,000, eight instalments paid in the year, and the capital element of each instalment was $55,000.

During the year JadeTech completed and first used a new factory. The purchase price included land of $2,100,000 and qualifying construction cost of $4,200,000.

(a) Compute JadeTech's assessable profits and profits tax payable for YA 2026/27. (22 marks)

(b) State three depreciation-allowance errors this question is designed to catch. (3 marks)

Show model answer
(a) JadeTech Manufacturing Ltd — Profits Tax Computation, YA 2026/27

Approved charitable donations added back first (1 mark)260,000
Less: accounting gain on factory sale, capital receipt(450,000)

Adjusted profit before depreciation allowances8,712,000
Less: depreciation allowances

IA: $900,000 × 60% = $540,000. Pool: $520,000 + $900,000 − $540,000 − $180,000 = $700,000. AA: $700,000 × 30% = $210,000		(750,000)
Hire-purchase machine (3 marks)
Qualifying capital paid: $240,000 + (8 × $55,000) = $680,000. IA $408,000 and AA $81,600		(489,600)
New factory industrial building allowance (3 marks)

Total for part (a): 22 marks. The tax payable is $165,000 + $693,726 = $858,726.

(b) (3 marks): The first error is giving building allowances on land: only qualifying construction cost is used (1 mark). The second is computing initial allowance on the full hire-purchase cash price instead of the capital sums actually paid in the year (1 mark). The third is omitting the balancing charge on the old factory sale and taxing the accounting gain instead (1 mark).

Question 7 — Harbor Link Sourcing Ltd (15 marks)

Scenario15 marks

Harbor Link Sourcing Ltd is incorporated and managed in Hong Kong. During the year ended 31 March 2027 it earned net sourcing commission profit of $3,200,000 from overseas customers who bought electronic components from factories in Mainland China.

Harbor Link's Hong Kong staff found suppliers, negotiated prices and specifications, arranged purchase orders and dealt with quality complaints from its office in Hong Kong. Factory visits and shipment inspections in Mainland China were carried out by independent contractors engaged job by job. Customers signed their master supply agreements outside Hong Kong and paid Harbor Link into an overseas bank account.

(a) Advise whether Harbor Link's offshore claim is likely to succeed. (10 marks)

(b) If the whole profit is taxable in Hong Kong, compute the profits tax payable. (5 marks)

Show model answer

(a) (10 marks): The charge under s.14 is on profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong from a trade, profession or business carried on here (1 mark). The company carries on business in Hong Kong: it is incorporated and managed here and its staff conduct the sourcing business from the Hong Kong office (1 mark). Source is decided by identifying the profit-producing operations and where those operations take place, not by asking where the customer is resident or where money is banked (1 mark). For a sourcing commission business, the relevant operations are finding suppliers, negotiating price and specifications, arranging purchase orders and handling performance problems (2 marks). Those core operations were performed by Harbor Link's own staff in Hong Kong (1 mark). The Mainland factory visits and inspections were ancillary execution work, and they were performed by independent contractors rather than by Harbor Link's own profit-producing team (1 mark). Signing master agreements outside Hong Kong is not decisive if the commercial work that earned the commission was done in Hong Kong (1 mark). The overseas bank account is administrative evidence, not a source rule (1 mark). Harbor Link bears the burden of proving the facts supporting an offshore claim under s.68(4); on these facts the claim is unlikely to succeed (1 mark).

(b) Harbor Link Sourcing Ltd — Profits Tax if the Offshore Claim Fails, YA 2026/27
Assessable profits3,200,000
First $2,000,000 at 8.25% (2 marks)165,000
Balance $1,200,000 at 16.5% (2 marks)198,000
Profits tax payable (1 mark)363,000

Total for part (b): 5 marks. This question is designed to catch the error of treating overseas customers, overseas signing or an overseas bank account as decisive, instead of applying the operations test to the profit-producing activities.

Question 8 — East Point Design Ltd (25 marks)

Scenario25 marks

East Point Design Ltd filed its profits tax return late after omitting a major service invoice. The Inland Revenue Department later issued an additional assessment on 15 August 2027, showing tax undercharged of $420,000, and requiring payment on 15 September 2027. East Point accepts that the invoice was taxable but says the omission was caused by a bookkeeper's spreadsheet error.

The directors are considering an objection because they also believe a separate deduction has been refused wrongly. They cannot pay the full assessment by the due date and expect cash will not be available until eight months after the due date.

(a) Explain the objection procedure and what East Point must do if it wants collection held over. (10 marks)

(b) Compute the maximum penalty under s.80 and the late-payment amount if the tax remains unpaid for eight months. (8 marks)

(c) Advise on the penalty exposure and the practical steps East Point should take now. (7 marks)

Show model answer

(a) (10 marks): A valid objection must be made in writing to the Commissioner within one month after the notice of assessment, stating precisely the grounds of objection (2 marks). Filing an objection does not by itself suspend collection: the tax remains payable unless the Commissioner orders holdover (2 marks). East Point should therefore request holdover at the same time, explaining the disputed deduction and providing supporting documents (2 marks). Holdover may be conditional, including requiring the taxpayer to purchase a tax reserve certificate or provide security (1 mark). If the objection is determined against East Point, the company may appeal to the Board of Review within one month after the determination (1 mark). The accepted omitted invoice should not be included in the objection grounds: East Point should separate the conceded undercharge from the genuinely disputed deduction (1 mark). Missing the payment date without holdover exposes the company to late-payment surcharges even while correspondence continues (1 mark).

(b) East Point Design Ltd — Penalty and Late-Payment Exposure
Tax undercharged / additional tax assessed420,000
Maximum s.80 penalty: $10,000 plus treble the tax undercharged (3 marks)1,270,000
First surcharge for late payment: 5% of $420,000 (1 mark)21,000
Further surcharge after six months: 10% of $441,000 (2 marks)44,100
Total surcharges after eight months65,100
Amount payable after eight months (2 marks)485,100

Total for part (b): 8 marks. The late-payment computation applies the second 10% surcharge to the tax plus the first surcharge, not to the original tax alone.

(c) (7 marks): The omission of taxable income creates penalty exposure even if the bookkeeper made the spreadsheet error: the company remains responsible for the correctness of its return (1 mark). A maximum s.80 penalty is not automatically imposed; IRD will consider culpability, cooperation, voluntary disclosure, previous compliance and whether prosecution or additional tax procedures are used (2 marks). East Point should make a full written disclosure of the omitted invoice, correct the computation, explain the control failure and provide evidence that the error was not deliberate (1 mark). It should pay the undisputed part as soon as possible, or at least seek instalment arrangements, because cash difficulty does not remove statutory surcharges (1 mark). It should support the disputed deduction with invoices, contracts, board approvals and accounting records, and keep the objection focused on that point (1 mark). Finally, it should improve controls over sales cut-off and return review before the next filing, since repeated errors aggravate penalties (1 mark).

Originality

All eight questions and all eight model answers on this page are original, written for this Hub in the exam's own constructed-response format. See the ACCA TX-HKG page for the fuller statement of what is and is not reproduced anywhere on this Hub.

Revision aid — one page, every format

Computation Formats

The standard pro-forma layout for each Hong Kong tax, in the order the lines belong, with what goes on each line and one worked example apiece.

計算格式五種稅的標準計算格式集於一頁：物業稅、薪俸稅、利得稅、摺舊免稅額及個人入息課稅，逐行說明並各配一條例題。格式取自教科書，並已對照稅務局核新。
Where these come from The layouts follow Hong Kong Taxation and Tax Planning (22nd ed., Ho & Mak) — Ch.7 property tax, Ch.12 salaries tax, Ch.20 profits tax, Ch.31 plant and machinery. That book states the law to 31 May 2024, so every rate and allowance has been re-checked against IRD and updated where it has moved. § What has changed lists each difference rather than silently absorbing it.

How to use these

A tax computation is marked on structure as much as on arithmetic. Getting a figure into the wrong line — or the right figure in the right line but the wrong order — loses the marks even when the final number is close. These are the skeletons to have in your head before you start writing.

ConventionMeaning
XA figure goes here. Letters (A, B, Y, ZB…) mark subtotals that a later line refers back to.
IndentationIndented lines are workings feeding the subtotal on the right; they do not themselves enter the main column.
Single ruleA subtotal.
Double ruleA figure the question asks for, or one that carries into the next stage.
Three rules that apply to every computation here
  1. Head the computation. Taxpayer name, which tax, and the year of assessment. Three lines, and they are marks.
  2. Show the working, not just the answer. ($30,000 × 12) beside the figure earns the mark even if the arithmetic slips.
  3. Name every subtotal correctly. "Assessable value", "net assessable value", "assessable profit", "net assessable profit", "net chargeable income" are defined terms with different meanings. They are not interchangeable.

1. Property Tax IRO ss.5, 5B, 7C — textbook Ch.7

Property Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 20XX/XX
Rent receivableX
Premium, spread over the lease termX
Service charges / management fees borne by the tenant and paid to the ownerX
Recovery of rent previously written off as irrecoverableX
Less: irrecoverable rent of the year(X)
Assessable valueX
Less: rates paid by the owner(X)
X
Less: statutory allowance for repairs and outgoings, 20% of the above(X)
Net assessable valueX
Property tax at the standard rate, 15%X
LineWhat belongs there
PremiumSpread evenly over the lease term, capped at 36 months (s.5B(4)). A 3-year lease premium received in one year is taxed 12⁄36 in each.
Irrecoverable rentDeducted in the year it is recognised as irrecoverable, not the year the rent accrued (s.7C(1)). Recovery later is assessable in the year of recovery, not related back.
RatesOnly rates paid by the owner. Rates paid by the tenant never enter the computation.
20% statutory allowanceFixed, automatic, and taken after rates. It is not a claim and no receipts are needed — and no more can be claimed however much was actually spent.
The four things that never get deducted Government rent, mortgage interest, actual repairs, and improvements are all non-deductible under property tax. The 20% allowance is the only relief for outgoings. Mortgage interest is exactly why a mortgaged property owner should look at Personal Assessment.
Worked example Textbook Example 7.1 (Mr Gap), p.101 — rate unchanged, so still current

Mr Gap let a Sai Kung house on a three-year lease from 1 January 2022 at $30,000 a month, with a premium of $180,000 payable on 1 January 2022. In the year ended 31 March 2024 he paid Government rent $10,800, mortgage interest $110,000, rates $18,000, and repairs and improvement $20,000.

Mr Gap — Property Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 2023/24
Rent ($30,000 × 12)360,000
Premium ($180,000 × 12⁄36)60,000
Assessable value420,000
Less: rates paid by owner(18,000)
402,000
Less: statutory deduction ($402,000 × 20%)(80,400)
Net assessable value321,600
Property tax ($321,600 × 15%)48,240

Government rent $10,800, interest $110,000 and repairs $20,000 — $140,800 of real cash cost — get no deduction at all. That is the point of the example.

2. Salaries Tax IRO ss.8–13 — textbook Ch.12

The structural point worth memorising There is no statutory format for a salaries tax computation. But the layout below puts every item affecting rental value before the rental value line — because rental value is 10% of income after allowable outgoings. Lay it out any other way and you will compute rental value on the wrong base.
Salaries Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 20XX/XX
SalariesA
Bonus, commission, gratuityB
Allowances (cash or convertible into cash)C
D
Less: allowable expenses — s.12(1)(a)
Travelling from office to officeE
Professional subscriptionF(G)
Income after allowable outgoingsH
Add: rental value of employer-provided quarters (H × 10%)J
Less: rent suffered (rent paid by employee − rent refunded)(K)L
M
Add: lump sum on termination of employmentN
Add: gain on exercise of share optionO
P
Less: self-education expenses — s.12(1)(e)(Q)
Net assessable income, before concessionary deductionsR
Less: concessionary deductions
Approved charitable donations (max 35% of P)S
Elderly residential care expensesT
Home loan interestU
Mandatory contributions to MPF / recognised schemeV
VHIS premiumsW
Qualifying annuity premiums and MPF voluntary contributionsX
Domestic rentsY
Assisted reproductive service expensesZ(ZA)
Net income (net assessable income after concessionary deductions)ZB
Less: personal allowances

Then compute the tax twice and pay the lower
(b) Progressive rates on EE: 2% / 6% / 10% / 14% on the first four $50,000 bands, then 17%b
(c) Standard rate on ZB (net income, before personal allowances) — s.13(2)c
Salaries tax liability = the lower of (b) and (c)X
Updated: the standard rate is two-tiered from 2024/25 The textbook's format shows the standard rate as a flat 15%. From YA 2024/25 the standard rate is two-tiered: 15% on the first HKD 5,000,000 of net income, 16% on the remainder. Under HKD 5,000,000 the book's line still gives the right answer; above it, the book understates. Write line (c) as the two-tier calculation.
LineWhat catches people out
Rental value base (H)10% of income after s.12(1)(a) outgoings — not of gross salary. 4% for a hotel room / shared boarding-type accommodation, 8% for two rooms in a hotel.
Rent suffered (K)Deducted from rental value, and only down to nil — it cannot create a negative.
Donations cap (S)35% of P — income after the outgoings and rental value but before self-education and the other concessionary deductions.
Order of Q and S–ZSelf-education is a s.12 deduction and comes before the concessionary block. Putting it among the concessionary deductions changes the donations cap base.
The standard-rate base (ZB)Net income before personal allowances. Applying it to EE is the single most common error in this computation.
Worked example Built on the textbook's Ch.12 layout, at YA 2026/27 rates

Mr Pak earns salary $900,000 and a bonus $100,000, pays a professional subscription of $2,000, and is provided with a rent-free flat by his employer. He donated $30,000 to an approved charity and made mandatory MPF contributions of $18,000. He is single with no dependants.

Mr Pak — Salaries Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 2026/27
Salary and bonus1,000,000
Less: professional subscription — s.12(1)(a)(2,000)
Income after allowable outgoings (H)998,000
Add: rental value ($998,000 × 10%)99,800
Net assessable income before concessionary deductions1,097,800
Less: approved charitable donations (well under the 35% cap)(30,000)
Less: mandatory MPF contributions (capped at 18,000)(18,000)
Net income (ZB)1,049,800
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000(145,000)
Net chargeable income (EE)904,800
(b) Progressive on 904,800: 1,000 + 3,000 + 5,000 + 7,000 + (704,800 × 17%)135,816
(c) Standard rate on net income 1,049,800 × 15% (under the 5,000,000 threshold)157,470
Tax payable — the lower135,816

Note the rental value is $99,800, not $100,000 — 10% of income after the subscription, not of the $1,000,000 gross. A two-dollar difference in the wrong direction, but it is the line the marks are on. Any one-off Budget reduction would come off at the end; none is assumed here.

3. Profits Tax IRO ss.14–19C — textbook Ch.20

Start from profit per the accounts — never rebuild from gross profit The textbook sets this out as an explicit WRONG vs CORRECT contrast, and it is worth the space. A profits tax computation is an adjustment of the accounting profit, not a fresh income statement.

✗ Wrong — the gross profits method

Gross profitX
Add: assessable incomeX
Less: allowable expenses under the IRO(X)
Less: depreciation allowances(X)
Less: charitable donation(X)
Assessable profitX

Rebuilding the whole profit from scratch. It loses the audit trail back to the accounts, and any expense you forget to re-add is silently allowed.

✓ Correct — adjust the accounting profit

Profit / (loss) per the accountsX
Add: non-allowable expenses chargedX
Less: non-assessable income credited, and deductible amounts not in the accounts(X)
Less: depreciation allowances(X)
Less: charitable donation (capped)(X)
Assessable profitX

Every line is a reconciling difference an assessor can trace to the accounts. This is the format to use.

Three ordering traps in this format 1. The charitable donation is added back first and relieved last, because its 35% cap is measured on Y — after depreciation allowances. Deducting it early gives the wrong cap.
2. Depreciation allowances come off before the donation, never after.
3. Only one entity in a group may claim the two-tiered first-tier rate in a year. Where the question mentions connected entities, say which one is nominated.
Worked example Built on the textbook's Ch.20 format, current rates

A Hong Kong company's accounts show a profit of $2,500,000. Charged in arriving at it: depreciation $300,000, a charitable donation $80,000, a fine $20,000, and a general provision for doubtful debts $50,000. Credited to it: dividend income $100,000 and offshore trading profit $200,000. Depreciation allowances for the year are $260,000, and there is a loss brought forward of $310,000. It is the nominated group entity for the two-tiered rate.

Profits Tax Computation · Year of Assessment 2026/27
Profit per the accounts2,500,000
Add: depreciation300,000
Add: charitable donation80,000
Add: fine20,000
Add: general provision for doubtful debts50,000
2,950,000
Less: dividend income(100,000)
Less: offshore profit(200,000)
2,650,000
Less: depreciation allowances(260,000)
Y2,390,000
Less: charitable donation — 35% of Y is 836,500, so the full $80,000 is allowed(80,000)
Assessable profit2,310,000
Less: loss brought forward(310,000)
Net assessable profit2,000,000
Profits tax: $2,000,000 × 8.25% (all within the first tier)165,000

Watch the donation: added back at $80,000 and then allowed at $80,000 — it looks like a wasted round trip, and it is, until the 35% cap bites. Had Y been $200,000, the cap would be $70,000 and only that much would come back. The round trip is what makes the cap computable.

4. Depreciation allowances — plant and machinery IRO Part 6 — textbook Ch.31

Plant and machinery is grouped into three pools by annual allowance rate — 10%, 20% and 30%. The schedule below is the standard layout; with it memorised the work becomes filling in blanks.

Depreciation Allowance Schedule · Year of Assessment 20XX/XX
10%20%30%Allowances
Written down value b/fXXX
Additions (qualifying cash purchases)XXX
Less: initial allowance, 60% of the addition(X)(X)(X)X
XXX
Less: disposal proceeds (limited to original cost)(X)(X)(X)
Reduced valueXXX
Less: annual allowance at the pool rate(X)(X)(X)X
Written down value c/fXXX
Total depreciation allowancesX
PointDetail
Initial allowance, 60%On the addition, not on the pool. Taken before the annual allowance, so the annual allowance is computed on the reduced figure.
Order: IA → disposal → AADisposals come out after the initial allowance and before the annual allowance. Reversing this changes every figure below it.
Four kinds of additionCash purchase — pooled, 60% IA on the cash price. Hire purchase — not pooled; 60% IA only on the capital portion of the deposit and instalments paid in the year. Private asset introduced into the business — pooled, but no initial allowance. Asset used partly privately — not pooled; dealt with separately and apportioned.
Balancing adjustmentArises only when the pool is emptied — proceeds exceeding the pool give a balancing charge; a residue with no assets left gives a balancing allowance. A disposal from a continuing pool creates neither.
Prescribed fixed assets100% deduction under s.16G — these never enter the pool at all. They belong in the profits tax computation, not here.
Worked example Built on the textbook's Ch.31 schedule

Pools brought forward: 10% $100,000, 20% $200,000, 30% $300,000. During the year the business bought machinery for cash $150,000 (a 20% pool item) and sold an item from the 30% pool for $50,000, below its original cost.

10%20%30%Allowances
Written down value b/f100,000200,000300,000
Additions—150,000—
Less: initial allowance (60% × 150,000)—(90,000)—90,000
100,000260,000300,000
Less: disposal proceeds——(50,000)
Reduced value100,000260,000250,000
Less: annual allowance(10,000)(52,000)(75,000)137,000
Written down value c/f90,000208,000175,000
Total depreciation allowances227,000

The 20% pool's annual allowance is $52,000, not $70,000 — 20% of $260,000 after the initial allowance, not of the $350,000 before it. The $227,000 total is the single figure that carries into the profits tax computation above.

5. Personal Assessment IRO ss.40–43

The one format that consumes the other four: it takes the net assessable value from the property computation, the net assessable income from the salaries computation and the net assessable profit from the profits computation, and re-taxes the lot at progressive rates.

Personal Assessment Computation · Year of Assessment 20XX/XX
Net assessable value — from the property tax computationX
Net assessable income — from the salaries tax computationX
Net assessable profit — sole proprietorships and share of partnershipsX
Total incomeX
Less: interest on money borrowed to produce property income (capped at that property's NAV)(X)
Less: concessionary deductions(X)
Less: business loss of the year(X)
Less: loss brought forward under Personal Assessment(X)
Reduced total incomeRTI
Less: personal allowances(X)
Net chargeable incomeNCI
(b) Progressive rates on NCIb
(c) Standard rate on RTI — before allowancesc
Tax payable — the lower of (b) and (c)X
Joint election — apportioning the tax Where a married couple elects jointly, the allowances come off the joint reduced total income and the tax is computed once, then split in the ratio of each spouse's reduced total income — not gross. Each receives their own notice of assessment.

What has changed since the textbook

The 22nd edition states the law to 31 May 2024. Every rate and figure in the formats above was re-checked against IRD. Here is what moved and what did not, so you can see that the unchanged items were checked rather than assumed.

ItemTextbook (to 31 May 2024)Current — used above
Salaries tax standard rate Flat 15% on net income (Ch.12 format, line c) changed Two-tiered from YA 2024/25: 15% on the first $5,000,000, 16% on the remainder
Personal allowances Basic $132,000 / married $264,000 / child $130,000 era changed From YA 2026/27: basic $145,000, married $290,000, child $140,000, single parent $145,000, dependent parent 60+ $55,000 (IRD pam61e)
One-off tax reduction Table runs to 2023/24, ceiling $3,000 changed A 100% reduction capped at $3,000 also applied for 2025/26. Check the current Budget — none is assumed in the examples above
Child allowance, newborns Not in this edition proposed 2026 Policy Address: $160,000 for a 2nd or subsequent child born on/after 16 Sep 2026 — needs an amendment ordinance, so not used above. details →
Property tax standard rate15%unchanged 15%
20% statutory repair allowance20% of AV after ratesunchanged
Two-tiered profits tax rates8.25% / 16.5% and 7.5% / 15%, first $2,000,000unchanged
Salaries tax progressive bands2/6/10/14% on four $50,000 bands, then 17%unchanged
Initial allowance on P&M60%unchanged
Annual allowance pools10% / 20% / 30%unchanged
Donations cap35%unchanged
Rental value percentages10% / 8% / 4%unchanged
Not reflected in the textbook's chapters at all The 22nd edition predates the 2026 stamp duty amendments, the 2026 bills on funds/FIHV/carried interest and on shipping and commodity trading, the CARF and amended-CRS legislation, and the September 2026 Policy Address measures. None of those change the five computation formats above, but they do change the surrounding rules — see IRD What's New.

Source documents

  • IRD — Allowances, Deductions and Tax Rate Table (pam61e): the 2026/27 allowance and rate figuresread 24 Sep 2026
  • IRD — A Brief Guide to Personal Assessment (pam37e)read 24 Sep 2026
  • IRD — What's New, for changes after the textbook's cut-offread 24 Sep 2026
How the textbook was read The 22nd edition is a scanned PDF with no text layer, and no OCR is available in this environment. The pages above were located through the book's own index and read by rendering each page as an image. Layouts are reproduced as structure — line order, subtotal names and captions — not as copied text, and every figure in the worked examples was recomputed independently. The one example carried over directly (Mr Gap) is labelled as the textbook's own.

Exam technique — the most heavily weighted question type

Tax Reconciliation

"Here is a computation prepared by someone who got it wrong. Here are ten notes. Produce the revised computation." How to attack it, and how to prove your answer with a reconciliation.

稅務調節考試最常見的題型：給一份錯誤的利得稅或個人入息課稅計算表及十項附註，要求重新編製。兩條完整例題，逐項分析、修正後計算表及完全吐合的調節表。

1. The question type, and what it is really testing

You are given a profits tax or personal assessment computation prepared by a bookkeeper, a client, or "the previous accountant". It is internally consistent — the arithmetic adds up — but several treatments are wrong. A set of numbered notes gives you the facts. You must produce the corrected computation.

It is not a computation question. It is a review question. A blank-page computation tests whether you can build a format. This tests something harder: whether you can look at a plausible-looking answer and find what is wrong with it. That is what tax work actually is — almost nothing arrives as a blank page, and the figure in front of you always looks reasonable.

Three consequences follow, and they drive everything on this page:

Because……therefore
The given computation looks plausibleYou cannot spot errors by eye. You must work note by note, in order, and decide an adjustment for each — including "no adjustment".
Some notes are distractorsA note that needs no adjustment still earns a mark if you say so and why. Silence earns nothing and looks like an oversight.
Errors can offset each otherThe bottom line can look close to right while several treatments are wrong. Never sanity-check by the final figure. Illustration A below is built to show this happening.

2. The six-step method

StepDo this
1Do not edit the given computation. Start a clean one from profit per the accounts (or, for personal assessment, from each source's own correct figure). Editing someone else's layout inherits their structural errors.
2Rule up a note-by-note working schedule before touching the computation: note number, treatment, adjustment, amount. Every note gets a row, including the ones needing no adjustment.
3Decide each note in isolation. Is the item chargeable / deductible? Was it already in the accounts? Those two questions together give the adjustment — an item can be deductible and still need no adjustment because it was already correctly charged.
4Build the revised computation in the standard format, feeding in the schedule's figures. Keep the donation add-back-then-relieve round trip, and keep depreciation allowances before the donation.
5Reconcile from the given figure to yours, line by line. This is the step candidates skip, and it is where the marks and the self-check both live.
6Reconcile the tax too, not just the profit. Rate errors, set-offs and reliefs live below the net assessable profit line and are easy to leave uncorrected.
Why step 5 is worth the minutes it costs The reconciliation is self-marking. If it does not arrive at your revised figure, you have made an error somewhere and you still have time to find it. If it does arrive, you have proved your answer and shown the examiner your reasoning in one compact table. It is the cheapest insurance in the paper.

3. Illustration A — Profits tax: the question

Question

Kingsway Trading Limited carries on a trading business in Hong Kong and prepares accounts to 31 December. The profit per the audited accounts for the year ended 31 December 2026 was $3,200,000.

The company's bookkeeper prepared the following profits tax computation for the year of assessment 2026/27.

REQUIRED: Using the notes below, prepare a revised profits tax computation for the year of assessment 2026/27, and reconcile the revised net assessable profit to the figure computed by the bookkeeper.

✗ As prepared by the bookkeeper — Kingsway Trading Limited, YA 2026/27
Profit per accounts3,200,000
Add: depreciation420,000
3,620,000
Less: dividend income(150,000)
Less: charitable donations(250,000)
Less: depreciation allowances(380,000)
Assessable profit2,840,000
Less: loss brought forward(240,000)
Net assessable profit2,600,000
Profits tax at 8.25%214,500
Notes
NoteInformation
1The profit is after charging depreciation of $420,000. Depreciation allowances properly computed under Part 6 of the IRO for the year amount to $505,000.
2Turnover includes $680,000 of profit on a contract negotiated and concluded entirely in Singapore by the company's Singapore branch. The Assessor has accepted this profit as offshore.
3Other income includes dividends of $150,000 from a company listed in Hong Kong.
4Other income includes $90,000 of interest on a Hong Kong dollar deposit with a licensed bank in Hong Kong.
5Administrative expenses include a fine of $35,000 imposed for a breach of licensing conditions.
6Administrative expenses include an increase in the general provision for doubtful debts of $60,000, and a specific bad debt written off of $45,000 in respect of a trade debtor who has been wound up.
7Charitable donations of $250,000 to approved charitable institutions were charged in arriving at the profit per the accounts.
8Finance costs include $120,000 of interest paid to a director on a loan to the company. The director is not chargeable to profits tax on that interest, so the conditions in s.16(2) are not satisfied.
9The company owns an office in Hong Kong which it lets to a tenant. The rental income is included in the profit per the accounts. Property tax of $48,000 for the year was paid and charged in the accounts.
10The agreed loss brought forward from the year of assessment 2025/26 is $240,000. Kingsway Trading Limited is the only Hong Kong entity in its group and is entitled to the two-tiered profits tax rates.

4. Illustration A — note-by-note working

Build this before the computation. Two questions per note: is the item chargeable or deductible? and how was it treated in the accounts? The adjustment is the difference between the two.

NoteCorrect treatmentAdjustment$
1 Accounting depreciation is not deductible; statutory depreciation allowances replace it. Add back $420,000; deduct the correct allowances of $505,000, not the bookkeeper's $380,000. Add / Deduct420,000
(505,000)
2 Offshore profit is outside the s.14 charge. The bookkeeper missed it entirely — the largest single error. Deduct(680,000)
3 Dividends from a Hong Kong company are not chargeable (s.26). Correctly deducted by the bookkeeper. Deduct(150,000)
4 Interest on a HKD deposit with a licensed bank is exempt under the Exemption from Profits Tax (Interest Income) Order. Missed. Deduct(90,000)
5 A fine is not incurred in the production of profits and is not deductible. Missed. Add back35,000
6 General provision is not deductible (s.16(1)(d)) — add back $60,000. The specific write-off of a debt of a wound-up debtor is deductible and was correctly charged — no adjustment. Add back
no adj.		60,000
—
7 Add back the $250,000 charged, then relieve it under s.16D restricted to 35% of the profit after depreciation allowances. The bookkeeper simply deducted it a second time. Add back
then relieve		250,000
(250,000)
8 Interest failing s.16(2) is not deductible. Missed. Add back120,000
9 Two separate points. Property tax charged in the accounts is not deductible — add back $48,000. Separately, it is set off against the profits tax payable under s.25, below the tax line. Both were missed. Add back

(48,000)
10 Loss brought forward is set off after the donation. The two-tiered rates apply, so 8.25% on the first $2,000,000 and 16.5% on the remainder — not 8.25% on the whole. Deduct / rate(240,000)
Note 6 is the distractor, and Note 9 is the double-barrelled one Note 6 gives you two figures where only one moves — say explicitly that the specific write-off needs no adjustment. Note 9 carries two marks in two different places: an add-back in the computation and a set-off under the tax. Answering only the add-back loses half of it.

6. Illustration A — the reconciliation

This is the part the question specifically asked for, and the part most candidates omit. It starts at the bookkeeper's figure and arrives at yours.

Reconciliation of net assessable profit
Net assessable profit per the bookkeeper's computation2,600,000
Offshore profit not excluded (2)(680,000)
Exempt bank deposit interest not excluded (4)(90,000)
Fine not added back (5)35,000
General provision not added back (6)60,000
Interest failing s.16(2) not added back (8)120,000
Property tax charged not added back (9)48,000
Donations deducted without being added back (7)250,000
Additional depreciation allowances ($505,000 − $380,000) (1)(125,000)
Revised net assessable profit2,218,000
Reconciliation of tax
Profits tax per the bookkeeper's computation214,500
Effect of the reduction in net assessable profit, at the rates properly applicable(13,530)
Revised profits tax200,970
Property tax set off under s.25, omitted (9)(48,000)
Revised profits tax liability152,970
The point of this illustration: two errors pulling in opposite directions The bookkeeper overstated the profit by $382,000 ($2,600,000 against $2,218,000) — which pushes tax up. But they also applied 8.25% to the whole profit instead of tiering at $2,000,000 — which pulls tax down. On the correct profit of $2,218,000, a flat 8.25% would have given $182,985 against the true $200,970, understating tax by $17,985.

The two errors partly cancel. That is exactly why the bottom line tells you nothing about whether a computation is right, and why the note-by-note schedule is not optional.

7. Illustration B — Personal assessment

Question

Mr and Mrs Lam have elected jointly for personal assessment for the year of assessment 2026/27. Mr Lam's net assessable income from employment is $600,000. Mrs Lam runs a sole proprietorship whose assessable profit is $180,000, and owns a Hong Kong flat let at $30,000 a month throughout the year. She paid rates of $12,000 and mortgage interest of $200,000 on that flat. Neither has any other income, deduction or dependant.

A friend prepared the computation below. REQUIRED: prepare the revised computation, show the apportionment between the spouses, and reconcile to the friend's figure.

✗ As prepared by a friend — Mr & Mrs Lam, YA 2026/27
Mr Lam — salary600,000
Mrs Lam — business profit180,000
Mrs Lam — rental income ($30,000 × 12)360,000
Total income1,140,000
Less: mortgage interest(200,000)
Less: rates paid(12,000)

Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000(145,000)
Net chargeable income783,000

ErrorWhat is wrong
1Property brought in at gross rent. Personal assessment takes the net assessable value: rates are deducted inside the property computation, and the 20% statutory allowance is then taken. Deducting rates as a separate line below total income skips the 20% entirely.
2A basic allowance claimed where a jointly electing married couple is entitled to the married person's allowance of $290,000.
3No standard-rate comparison. Tax under personal assessment is the lower of progressive rates on net chargeable income and the standard rate on reduced total income.
4No apportionment between the spouses. On a joint election each receives their own assessment for their share.

Note how the rates error works The friend deducted rates of $12,000 — and got a worse answer than ignoring them, because deducting them in the wrong place forfeited the 20% statutory allowance of $69,600. Doing something reasonable in the wrong line of a computation is not half right; it is wrong, and here it is wrong by $57,600.

8. The errors examiners plant, in rough order of frequency

Planted errorHow to catch it
Offshore profit left inAny note mentioning a place outside Hong Kong is a source question. Decide it explicitly.
Donation deducted without being added backIf it was charged in the accounts it must go back in first, or the 35% cap cannot be computed.
Donation cap on the wrong base35% of profit after depreciation allowances, not of profit per accounts.
Accounting depreciation left in, or DA figure wrongAdd back the accounts figure and deduct the Part 6 figure. They are never the same number.
General vs specific provisionGeneral is added back, specific is not. The question will give you both.
Flat rate instead of two-tieredCheck the rate line every time, and check whether the entity is the nominated group member.
Property tax: add-back or set-off missedIt is two adjustments in two places, from one note.
Interest failing s.16(2)Any interest paid to a director, shareholder or associate is a s.16(2) question.
Exempt bank interest left inHKD deposit interest from a licensed bank is exempt.
Loss brought forward in the wrong placeAfter the donation, not before.
Personal assessment: gross rent not NAVProperty always enters at net assessable value.
Personal assessment: standard-rate comparison omittedAnd when performed, on reduced total income — before allowances.
Wrong allowance for a married coupleJoint election takes the married person's allowance.

9. Marking technique

Earns marks

  • A note number against every line of the revised computation — the marker can follow your reasoning without hunting.
  • Saying "no adjustment" for a distractor, with one clause of reason.
  • Showing the cap working even when the cap does not bite: "lower of $250,000 and 35% × $2,708,000 = $947,800".
  • The reconciliation, even a rough one.
  • Correct subtotal names: assessable profit, net assessable profit, reduced total income, net chargeable income.
  • A one-line heading: taxpayer, tax, year of assessment, basis period.

Loses marks

  • Editing the given computation instead of starting clean — you inherit its structure and its errors.
  • Silence on a distractor note. Indistinguishable from missing it.
  • Netting several adjustments into one unexplained figure.
  • Stopping at net assessable profit when the question asked for the liability — rate, set-offs and reliefs are marks.
  • Checking your work against the bottom line. Offsetting errors make a wrong answer look right.
  • Correct treatment written in the wrong line, as with the rates in Illustration B.
If you run short of time Produce the note-by-note schedule and stop. It carries most of the technical marks, since it shows the decision on every item. A beautifully formatted computation with three treatments wrong scores less than a rough schedule that gets all ten notes right.

Business — Profits Tax

Profits Tax

Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112), Part 4 — charged on assessable profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong from a trade, profession or business carried on in Hong Kong.

利得稅涵蓋香港來源原則、兩級制稅率、應課稅收入、扣稅開支、虧損、FSIE、Patent Box 及基本計算格式。

1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.14

Hong Kong taxes profits on a territorial source basis, not on residence. Section 14(1) charges profits tax on every person (including a corporation) carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong, on assessable profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong for that trade/profession/business — profits from the sale of capital assets are expressly excluded from the charge.

Statutory text — s.14(1) "...profits tax shall be charged for each year of assessment on every person carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong in respect of his assessable profits arising in or derived from Hong Kong for that year from such trade, profession or business (excluding profits arising from the sale of capital assets) as ascertained in accordance with this Part."

Three conditions must all be met for a charge to arise: (1) the person carries on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong; (2) the trade/profession/business produces profits other than from the sale of capital assets; (3) the profits are sourced in Hong Kong. Locality of profits is a question of fact determined by what the taxpayer did to earn the profit and where — see DIPN 21 (Locality of Profits) for the "broad guiding principle" drawn from Hang Seng Bank, HK-TVB International, Kwong Mile, and other leading cases.

2. Rates & Recent Changes Schedule 8B

Two-tiered profits tax rates (from YA 2018/19, current)
Taxpayer typeFirst HKD 2,000,000 of assessable profitsRemainder
Corporations8.25%16.5%
Unincorporated businesses (sole proprietors / partnerships)7.5%15%

Legislated via s.14(2)/(3) referring out to Schedule 8B (two-tiered rates) — Schedule 8 sets the flat standard/corporate rate that continues to apply where a group of connected entities has more than one entity in Hong Kong (only one connected entity per group may be nominated each year to access the discounted first-tier rate; s.14AAC deals with connected entities generally).

Recent changes to watch
  • Refined FSIE regime — effective 1 January 2023 (Division 3A of Part 4, added by 17 of 2022) — see §6 below.
  • Patent Box concession — 5% concessionary rate on qualifying IP income from YA 2023/24 (Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Tax Concessions for Intellectual Property Income) Ordinance 2023).
  • Pillar Two — Income Inclusion Rule + Hong Kong Minimum Top-up Tax for in-scope MNE groups, effective for fiscal years beginning on/after 1 January 2025.
  • One-off relief — Inland Revenue (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 (gazetted 22 May 2026): 100% profits tax reduction for YA 2025/26, capped at HKD 3,000 per taxpayer. (Source: PwC Tax Summaries, reviewed 22 Jul 2026 — verify against the gazetted ordinance before relying on this for a filing.)
Bills in progress — not yet law (as at 24 September 2026)
  • Funds / FIHV / carried interest — Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Preferential Tax Regimes for Funds, Family-owned Investment Holding Vehicles and Carried Interest) Bill 2026, gazetted 12 June 2026, first reading 24 June 2026. Widens the definition of "fund", broadens the schedule of qualifying assets (notably to support private credit), removes the 5% cap on incidental transactions, relaxes the exemption conditions for special purpose entities and family-owned SPEs, and enhances the carried interest regime — but adds a tax reporting mechanism and economic substance requirements modelled on the FIHV regime. (Gazettal press release, 12 Jun 2026; FSTB response on carried interest, 12 Aug 2026.)
  • Shipping & physical commodity trading — Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Tax Concessions for Shipping-related Activities and Physical Commodity Trading) Bill 2026, gazetted 12 June 2026. Offers shipping-related companies an elective 15% concessionary rate (elected annually) as a BEPS 2.0-aware alternative to the existing 0%/8.25% concessions, and creates a new half-rate (8.25%) concession for physical commodity trading. (Press release, 10 Jun 2026.)
  • Corporate treasury centres — the Government published an Action Plan to Promote Development of Corporate Treasury Centres (9 Jun 2026) and launched a consultation on enhancing the CTC tax concession regime (27 Jul 2026). Expect the qualifying-activity and safe-harbour conditions for the 8.25% CTC rate to change — check before advising a group treasury structure.
  • Qualifying debt instruments — the list of debt instruments and sovereign bonds eligible for profits tax concession or exemption was refreshed on 30 June 2026. The list is the operative test — do not rely on an older copy.
  • Pillar Two filing — IRD published the GIR XML schema and user guides for the GloBE Information Return on 8 June 2026. In-scope MNE groups now have the machine-readable filing format. (IRD BEPS 2.0 page.)

3. Taxable / Non-Taxable Receipts IRO s.15

Section 15(1) deems certain sums to be Hong Kong-source trading receipts even though they might not otherwise be so regarded — this closes gaps the general s.14 source test would otherwise leave open (e.g. royalties, hire charges). Combine this with the general case-law source principle (DIPN 21) and the FSIE deeming rule (§6) to classify any receipt.

StatusReceiptBasis
TaxableRoyalties / sums for the use of, or right to use in Hong Kong, any patent, trade mark, copyright, design, secret process/formula or similar IPs.15(1)(b)
TaxableSums for use outside Hong Kong of IP where the payer claimed a Hong Kong deduction for the payments.15(1)(ba)
TaxableGrants, subsidies or similar financial assistance connected with carrying on the HK trade/business (other than towards capital expenditure)s.15(1)(c)
TaxableHire, rental or similar charges for use of movable property in Hong Kongs.15(1)(d)
TaxableInterest derived from Hong Kong received by a corporation carrying on a HK trade/businesss.15(1)(f)
TaxableSums from exhibition/use in HK of film, tape, sound recording or related advertising materials.15(1)(a)
Non-taxableProfits from the sale of capital assetss.14(1) (excluded from the charge)
Non-taxableInterest on a Hong Kong bank deposit earned by a person other than a financial institutionExemption from Profits Tax (Interest Income) Order 1998 — see DIPN 34; lost if the deposit secures a loan whose interest is tax-deductible (no partial exemption)
Non-taxableSpecified foreign-sourced income that satisfies the FSIE economic substance / nexus / participation conditionsDivision 3A, Part 4 (s.15H onward) — see §6
Taxable (deemed)Specified foreign-sourced income (interest, dividends, IP income, disposal gains on equity interests) that fails the FSIE conditionss.15I — deemed to arise in/derive from Hong Kong

4. Deductible / Non-Deductible Expenses IRO ss.16–17

The general test (s.16(1)) is that outgoings and expenses are deductible to the extent incurred in the basis period in the production of chargeable profits (the "Ronpibon Tin" apportionment principle — see DIPN 3 for apportioning mixed-purpose expenses). Section 17 then carves out specific exclusions even where the general test would otherwise be met.

StatusItemBasis / conditions
DeductibleInterest on money borrowed for producing chargeable profits, plus related legal/procuration fees and stamp dutys.16(1)(a), subject to the anti-avoidance conditions in s.16(2)–(2C) (see DIPN 13A)
