4A. Research and Development — the enhanced deduction IRO s.16B, Schedule 45

Qualifying R&D expenditure splits into two types with very different treatment. Getting the split wrong, or applying the enhanced rate to the whole of Type B, is the error the June 2026 examining team reported on the question fewest candidates answered correctly.

TypeWhat falls in itDeduction
Type A Qualifying R&D expenditure that is not Type B — including plant and machinery bought for R&D, fees paid to an outside expert or consultant, and testing fees 100% — a normal full deduction, no uplift
Type B Staffing costs of employees directly and actively engaged in qualifying R&D, and consumable items used up in it. Also payments to a designated local research institution. 300% on the first $2,000,000, then 200% on the remainder — no cap on the 200% tier
Three ways to get this wrong 1. Applying 300% to all Type B expenditure instead of only the first $2,000,000.
2. Treating everything as Type B — plant and machinery, consultancy fees and testing fees are Type A and get 100% only.
3. Leaving plant and machinery out altogether because it is capital. Under s.16B it is deductible at 100%; it does not go into the depreciation allowance pools.
Worked example Original; mechanics verified against the June 2026 examiner's report worked answer

Delta Ltd incurred the following on qualifying R&D in the year: plant and machinery $0.6m, a consultancy fee to an independent expert $0.4m, staffing costs of the research team $1.5m, and consumable items $0.9m.

Type A — plant and machinery $0.6m + consultancy $0.4m = $1.0m, at 100%1.0m
Type B — staffing $1.5m + consumables $0.9m = $2.4m
First $2.0m at 300%6.0m
Remaining $0.4m at 200%0.8m
Total deduction7.8m

$3.4m was actually spent and $7.8m is deducted. Common wrong answers on these facts: $8.2m (300% on all $2.4m of Type B), $7.2m (plant and machinery omitted as capital), and $3.4m (no enhancement at all).

5. Basis Period & Loss Relief IRO ss.18, 18C, 19C

Assessable profits are normally computed on the accounting year ending within the year preceding the year of assessment (s.18(1)). Where a business commences or ceases partway through a year, ss.18C–18H set special opening/closing basis periods. Trading losses are carried forward indefinitely and set off against future assessable profits from the same source (s.19C) — there is no time limit, but no carry-back and no group relief between separate legal entities in Hong Kong (each company is assessed on its own profits).

Where a taxpayer has both "normal" and "concessionary rate" trading receipts (e.g. under a qualifying debt instrument or reinsurance concession), s.19CA/19CB impose a cross-set-off formula using a statutory adjustment factor rather than a straight one-for-one offset — see DIPN 8.

6. Foreign-Sourced Income Exemption (FSIE) Part 4, Division 3A

Division 3A (ss.15H onward, added by the Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Taxation on Specified Foreign-sourced Income) Ordinance 2022, effective 1 January 2023) deems specified categories of foreign-sourced income — interest, dividends, disposal gains on equity interests, and IP income — received in Hong Kong by an MNE entity to be Hong Kong-sourced unless the entity meets an economic substance requirement (for interest/dividends/disposal gains) or complies with the nexus approach (for IP income), or qualifies for the participation exemption (for dividends/disposal gains on substantial equity interests).

Practical effect A Hong Kong holding or treasury company receiving offshore dividends, interest, or IP royalties that would otherwise be treated as offshore (non-taxable) under the ordinary source principle may now be taxed on that income unless it can document adequate economic substance in Hong Kong or a qualifying participation/nexus position. This is a common trap in tax computations for group treasury/holding entities — always check FSIE before treating offshore passive income as automatically non-taxable.

11 worked illustrations back this page — DIPN-sourced (lease premiums, interest deduction restrictions, service company fee caps, foreign tax deductibility, bank interest exemption, prepaid expenses) plus Module 9 textbook examples (basis periods, loss relief, secured loan/interest flow-back tests), all cross-checked against current law.

Illustration — Interest deduction restricted by a tax-free secured deposit DIPN 13A

Taxpayer F borrows $1,000,000 at 5% interest, secured by a $1,000,000 deposit earning tax-exempt interest at 4%. Because the loan is secured on a deposit generating tax-free income, s.16(2A)/(2B) restrict the deduction: the $40,000 tax-free interest earned reduces the otherwise-deductible $50,000 loan interest, leaving only $10,000 deductible.

Business — Profits Tax

Profits Tax by Entity

The same charge under s.14, but three materially different computations: sole proprietorship, partnership, and corporation. The partnership carries allocation mechanics on top, and only individuals can carry their share into personal assessment.

利得稅：三種實體同一條段，三種不同計算：獨資、合夥及法團。涵蓋 s.17(2) 對業主及其配偶的支付、合夥利潤分配與重新分配、法團合夥人與兩級制稅階的攝分，以及哪類業主可將分潤納入個人入息課稅。

1. Why the entity changes the computation

Profits tax has one charging section for all three. What differs is the rate, what counts as a deductible payment to the owner, and what happens after the assessable profit is struck.

The idea underneath all of it An unincorporated business is not separate from its owner. A sole proprietor cannot employ himself, and a partner cannot be an employee of his own partnership — so a "salary" to them is an appropriation of profit, not an expense. A company is a separate person, so it genuinely can employ its director and genuinely does pay them a salary.

Nearly every difference below follows from that one point. Once you see it, you do not have to memorise the table — you can derive it.

The second consequence is who bears the tax. A company pays its own profits tax and the director separately pays salaries tax on the salary. A sole proprietor's profit is taxed once, in the business — but the proprietor may then elect personal assessment to have it re-taxed at progressive rates after allowances. A company cannot elect at all.

2. The three side by side

PointSole proprietorshipPartnershipCorporation
Two-tiered rates 7.5% on the first $2m, 15% above 7.5% / 15% — but see §2b where a partner is a company 8.25% on the first $2m, 16.5% above
Salary to the owner Not deductible s.17(2) — an appropriation Not deductible s.17(2) Deductible — a director is an employee
Salary to the owner's spouse Not deductible s.17(2), even if genuinely employed Not deductible s.17(2) Deductible if genuine employment at a commercial rate
Owner's own mandatory MPF Deductible s.16AA, capped at $18,000 — self-employed contributions Deductible s.16AA for each partner n/a — the company's contributions for the director are ordinary staff costs
Interest on a loan from the owner Not deductible s.17(2) Not deductible s.17(2) Conditional — deductible only if s.16(2) is satisfied
Allocation between owners n/a Required — see §2 n/a
Personal assessment Available — the assessable profit enters the proprietor's PA Available to individual partners on their allocated share Not available — companies cannot elect
Losses Carried forward indefinitely, or set against other income under PA Allocated to partners; a corporate partner's share can shelter its own other profits Carried forward indefinitely against the company's own profits only
Return form BIR60 (individual), with the business schedule BIR52 BIR51
s.17(2) reaches the spouse, and that surprises people A salary to a sole proprietor's or partner's spouse is not deductible even where the spouse works full time for a commercial wage. Worse, the spouse is still chargeable to salaries tax on what they receive — so the same money is taxed in the business and again in the spouse's hands. The equivalent payment in a company is deductible. This is one of the sharper practical differences between the forms.

3. Sole proprietorship

One computation, one taxpayer. The whole assessable profit belongs to the proprietor, and the only question after that is whether personal assessment improves on it.

Illustration

Fiona carries on a design studio as a sole proprietor. The accounts for the year ended 31 March 2027 show a profit of $960,000, after charging a salary of $360,000 to Fiona, a salary of $180,000 to her husband (who works full time in the business at a commercial wage), and Fiona's own mandatory MPF contributions of $18,000. Depreciation allowances are $80,000.

Fiona — Profits Tax Computation · YA 2026/27
Profit per accounts960,000
Add: salary to the proprietor — s.17(2)360,000
Add: salary to the proprietor's spouse — s.17(2)180,000
Proprietor's own mandatory MPF — deductible, s.16AA0
1,500,000
Less: depreciation allowances(80,000)
Assessable profit1,420,000
Profits tax, unincorporated: $1,420,000 × 7.5% (within the first $2,000,000)106,500

Then two further consequences that are easy to forget:

The husband is still taxed His $180,000 is disallowed to the business but remains his employment income. Salaries tax: $180,000 − $145,000 basic allowance = $35,000 net chargeable income, at 2% = $700. The money is taxed twice.
Personal assessment is available — but here it is worse Fiona could elect PA on the $1,420,000. Net chargeable income would be $1,275,000, giving $198,750 at progressive rates (the standard-rate comparison on $1,420,000 gives $213,000, so progressive wins). That is well above the $106,500 profits tax she already pays. Do not elect.
The general shape Personal assessment helps a sole proprietor whose profit is low — where allowances and progressive rates beat a flat 7.5% — or who has property income or a loss to bring in. At $1.4m of profit the 17% marginal rate is already above 7.5%, so it costs money. Compute both; never assume.

4. Partnership

One assessment is raised on the partnership, not on the partners. But the profit must still be allocated partner by partner — because the allocation drives loss relief, personal assessment, and (where a partner is a company) the rate itself.

StepWhat happens
1Compute the partnership's assessable profit or adjusted loss in the ordinary way, adding back salaries and interest to partners and to partners' spouses under s.17(2).
2Allocate prior allocations first — the salaries and interest just added back go to the partner they relate to, not into the profit-sharing ratio.
3Share the balance in the profit-sharing ratio. The balance is often negative once the prior allocations are taken out.
4Reallocate so that no partner is left on the wrong side of zero: where the partnership has assessable profits, a partner cannot keep a loss share, and vice versa.
5Apply the rates — by partner if their natures differ (§2b).
Step 4 is the one candidates miss If the partnership's bottom line is a profit, no partner may be allocated a loss: any negative share is reallocated to the profit-making partners in proportion. If the partnership's bottom line is a loss, the mirror applies — any partner allocated a profit has it reallocated to the loss-making partners. The June 2025 examiner's report names this explicitly.

A full worked partnership allocation, with a loss per the accounts that adjusts to a profit, is Question 9 on the ACCA TX-HKG page →

5. Partnerships with a corporate partner

A company can be a partner. When it is, the partnership contains partners taxed at different rates, and the two-tiered threshold has to be shared out.

The rule Each partner's share of the assessable profits is taxed at that partner's own rate — 8.25%/16.5% for a corporate partner, 7.5%/15% for an individual. And the $2,000,000 first-tier band is itself apportioned between the partners in their profit-sharing ratio. The partnership does not get one $2,000,000 band at a single rate.

Illustration

Novena Trading is a partnership with assessable profits of $3,000,000 for YA 2026/27. The partners share profits equally: Carol, an individual, and Elm Holdings Limited, a company.

Novena Trading — profits tax by partner · YA 2026/27
Carol (individual)Elm Holdings LtdTotal
Share of assessable profits, 50 : 501,500,0001,500,0003,000,000
Share of the $2,000,000 first-tier band
apportioned in the profit-sharing ratio		1,000,0001,000,0002,000,000
First tier, at the partner's own rate1,000,000 × 7.5%
= 75,000		1,000,000 × 8.25%
= 82,500		157,500
Balance, at the partner's own rate500,000 × 15%
= 75,000		500,000 × 16.5%
= 82,500		157,500
Profits tax150,000165,000315,000
What the answer would have been in a uniform partnership
CompositionProfits tax on $3,000,000
All partners individuals300,000
Mixed, 50 : 50 as above315,000
All partners corporate330,000

The mixed partnership lands exactly between the two — which is the point. A single blended rate applied to the whole $3,000,000 would not produce $315,000, and computing the first tier once at either rate would be wrong for one of the partners.

Loss relief for a corporate partner Where the partnership makes a loss, a corporate partner's allocated share can be set against that company's own other assessable profits — the loss is not trapped in the partnership. An individual partner's share goes into their personal assessment or is carried forward against future shares of the same partnership. The examining team noted that candidates were "not familiar with the loss relief for corporate partners".

6. How a partner's share flows into personal assessment

This is the link between this page and Personal Assessment, and it only exists for individual partners.

Partnership — assessable profits computed and allocated→
Individual partner's allocated share enters their personal assessment as net assessable profits, alongside their salary and property income✓
Corporate partner's allocated share — no personal assessment; the company is assessed on its share at corporate rates and that is the end of it✗

Carol's position, continuing §5. Her $1,500,000 share has already borne $150,000 of profits tax within the partnership assessment. If she elects personal assessment, that $1,500,000 becomes part of her total income:

Share of partnership assessable profits1,500,000
Less: basic allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $132,000(145,000)
Net chargeable income1,355,000
Progressive rates212,350
Standard-rate comparison: $1,500,000 × 15%225,000
Tax under personal assessment212,350
Against her share of the partnership profits tax already charged150,000
Electing would cost her62,350
The pattern, across both illustrations on this page Fiona at $1.42m and Carol at $1.5m both find personal assessment worse. That is not a coincidence. Business profits are taxed at 7.5% in an unincorporated business, and the progressive marginal rate reaches 17% once net chargeable income passes $200,000. For a profitable business with no other reliefs to unlock, PA is usually a cost.

It turns beneficial when there is something for it to unlock: mortgage interest on a let property, a business loss to set against salary, or allowances going unused because the income is not employment income. Those are the cases to look for — not size of profit.

7. Corporation

The standard case, and the one the general profits tax format is written for. The company is a separate person, so payments to its directors are real expenses.

Illustration — the same business as §3, incorporated

Fiona Ltd carries on the same design studio. The accounts show the same profit of $960,000 after the same salary of $360,000 to Fiona, now a director, and $180,000 to her husband, a genuine employee. Depreciation allowances are $80,000.

Fiona Ltd — Profits Tax Computation · YA 2026/27
Profit per accounts960,000
Director's salary — deductible, no add-back0
Salary to the director's spouse, genuinely employed — deductible0
Less: depreciation allowances(80,000)
Assessable profit880,000
Profits tax, corporation: $880,000 × 8.25%72,600

The salaries are then taxed in the recipients' hands, which the sole-proprietorship version largely avoided for Fiona:

Fiona — salaries tax on $360,000 ($215,000 net chargeable income)18,550
Husband — salaries tax on $180,000 ($35,000 net chargeable income)700

8. Same business, three forms — the figures side by side

The identical trade, earning $1,500,000 before remunerating the owner and spouse
Sole proprietorshipCorporation
Profit per accounts960,000960,000
Add back: owner's and spouse's salaries — s.17(2)540,000—
Less: depreciation allowances(80,000)(80,000)
Assessable profit1,420,000880,000
Profits tax106,500 @ 7.5%72,600 @ 8.25%
Owner's salaries tax— no salary in law18,550
Spouse's salaries tax700700
Total tax borne107,20091,850

The company pays tax at the higher headline rate and still comes out $15,350 lighter, because $540,000 of remuneration moves out of the 7.5%-plus-nothing charge and into the progressive salaries tax bands, where the first $145,000 is covered by an allowance and the next slices are taxed at 2%–14%.

Read that as a structural point, not as advice The comparison isolates one variable to show how s.17(2) drives the difference. A real incorporation decision turns on much more — limited liability, audit and filing costs, business registration, stamp duty on any transfer of the business, how profits are actually extracted, and what happens on a later sale. The figures above are an illustration of a mechanism, not a recommendation. And the answer reverses at other profit levels: push the profit high enough and the 17% salaries tax band overtakes the 8.25% corporate rate.

9. Exam checklist

Before you startAsk
Which entity is it?Sole proprietorship, partnership or company. This sets the rate before anything else. Answering an unincorporated question at 8.25% loses the rate marks and every figure after them.
Is anyone paid who is the owner, or married to one?In an unincorporated business both are disallowed under s.17(2). In a company both are deductible if genuine.
Whose MPF is it?The proprietor's or partner's own mandatory contributions are deductible under s.16AA, capped at $18,000. Their spouse's are not.
Is there a corporate partner?Then the rates differ by partner and the $2,000,000 band is apportioned in the profit-sharing ratio.
Does anyone have a share on the wrong side of zero?Reallocate. No loss share when the partnership is in profit; no profit share when it is in loss.
Has the question asked about personal assessment?Only an individual can elect. Compute it both ways and say which is better — the answer is often "do not elect", and saying so with figures is the mark.
Is the spouse's disallowed salary still taxed?Yes, on the spouse. If the question gives their personal circumstances, it wants that computation too.

Individual — Salaries Tax

Salaries Tax

Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112), Part 3 — charged on Hong Kong-source income from an office, employment of profit, or pension.

薪俸稅涵蓋香港受僱工作、入息、福利、可扣除支出、個人免稅額、標準稅率上限及個人入息課稅銜接。

1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.8

Salaries tax is charged on income arising in or derived from Hong Kong from an office, employment of profit, or pension (s.8(1)) — again a territorial-source tax, not a residence-based one. Whether employment income is "Hong Kong employment" or "non-Hong Kong employment" is decided on the "totality of facts" test from Goepfert — the three key factors are: (1) where the employment contract was negotiated and is enforceable, (2) the residence of the employer, and (3) where the employee's remuneration is paid (see DIPN 10).

The 60-day rule — s.8(1A)(b)/(1B) Income from services rendered wholly outside Hong Kong by a person not employed by the Government (and not ship/aircraft crew) is excluded from the charge — unless the person visited Hong Kong for more than 60 days in the basis period, in which case services rendered during those visits are brought back into charge.

Directors' fees from a Hong Kong resident company are always Hong Kong-sourced regardless of where the director renders services. Income taxed in a DTA territory that gives a s.50 credit is excluded from the s.8(1A)(c) exemption route (must use the credit mechanism instead, not double relief).

2. Rates & Standard Rate Cap IRO s.13, Schedule 2

Progressive rates on net chargeable income (2025/26 and continuing into 2026/27 basis) — Schedule 2
BandRate
First HKD 50,0002%
Next HKD 50,000 (50,001–100,000)6%
Next HKD 50,000 (100,001–150,000)10%
Next HKD 50,000 (150,001–200,000)14%
Remainder (above 200,000)17%

Under s.13, tax computed progressively on net chargeable income (i.e. after allowances) is capped at a standard-rate calculation applied to net total income (i.e. before personal allowances, but after concessionary deductions): 15% on the first HKD 5,000,000, 16% on the remainder. The taxpayer pays whichever of the two computations is lower — this matters most for higher earners with large personal allowances.

One-off relief Inland Revenue (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 (gazetted 22 May 2026): 100% reduction of salaries tax/personal assessment tax for YA 2025/26, capped at HKD 3,000. (Source: PwC, reviewed 22 Jul 2026 — verify against the gazetted ordinance.)

4. Deductible / Non-Deductible Items IRO s.12

The general test (s.12(1)(a)) is stricter than the profits tax test — expenses must be "wholly, exclusively and necessarily" incurred in producing the assessable income (not merely "to the extent"), and domestic/private expenses and capital expenditure are excluded outright. In practice very few ordinary employment expenses pass this test (see DIPN 9).

6. Personal Assessment IRO s.41

Personal Assessment is an election (not automatic) available to individuals (and, if both elect, jointly for married couples under s.41(1A)) that aggregates all sources of income — including property tax and profits tax from an unincorporated business — into one computation, deducting personal allowances and applying salaries-tax-style progressive rates. It is beneficial mainly where the taxpayer has property tax or unincorporated-business profits tax that would otherwise get no benefit from personal allowances, or has losses in one source that can offset income in another.

Joint assessment (s.10(2), distinct from Personal Assessment) lets a married couple be taxed as one for salaries tax where beneficial — typically where one spouse has income below the value of their own allowances (DIPN 18).

Personal Assessment has its own page This summary is here because Personal Assessment is where Salaries Tax meets the other two heads of charge. The full treatment — eligibility and the residence tests, the 2018/19 change letting married persons elect separately, election and withdrawal time limits, the three-step computation and the standard-rate cap, what is deductible, and four worked illustrations including one where electing costs money — is on the Personal Assessment page.

Business — Property Tax

Property Tax

Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112), Part 2 — charged on the owner of land or buildings in Hong Kong, on the net assessable value.

物業稅說明物業稅的納稅人、租金收入、差餉、20% 法定修葺免稅額、不可收回租金及公司業主與利得稅的互動。

1. Overview & Charging Basis IRO s.5

Property tax is charged for each year of assessment on every person who owns land or buildings in Hong Kong, computed at the standard rate on the net assessable value — regardless of whether the owner carries on any trade or business. It is a tax on ownership + letting, not on trading profit as such.

Statutory text — s.5(1) "Property tax shall...be charged for each year of assessment on every person being the owner of any land or buildings or land and buildings wherever situate in Hong Kong and shall be computed at the standard rate on the net assessable value of such land or buildings..."
Current rate
Standard rate applied to net assessable value15%

Owner-occupied property generates no rental consideration and therefore has no assessable value — no property tax arises. Where the owner of the land is not the owner of the buildings on it, separate assessments are made for each (s.5(1)(b)).

Traps in the property tax computation

Three points the June 2026 examining team reported as weak 1. Compute each property separately. Where a taxpayer owns more than one let property, property tax is computed property by property, not on the aggregate. Each gets its own assessable value, its own rates deduction and its own 20% allowance.

2. Repairs and replacements get no separate deduction. Actual spending on repairs, redecoration or replacing fittings is deemed to be covered by the 20% statutory allowance — however much was really spent. Candidates could say the cost was not deductible but could not explain why.

3. There are no depreciation allowances under property tax. Replacing air-conditioners or other plant in a let property attracts no depreciation allowance, because Part 6 does not apply to the property tax charge. If the owner is a company carrying on business the position differs — the income is then within profits tax, where allowances are available.
The rental deposit — two different things A deposit taken at the start of a lease is not assessable income; it is security held for the tenant. A deposit later forfeited and retained is set off against irrecoverable rent. The June 2026 report names both including the deposit as income and failing to set off a forfeited deposit as common errors.

2. Net Assessable Value IRO s.5(1A), s.5B, s.7C

Assessable value (s.5B(2)) is the consideration in money or money's worth payable for the right to use the land/buildings during the year — i.e. rent and other consideration receivable, not merely received. Net assessable value (s.5(1A)) then deducts:

Assessable value (rent/consideration receivable for the year)X
Less: irrecoverable consideration proved bad during the year (s.7C)(X)
Less: rates paid by the owner, if the owner agreed to bear them(X)
Less: statutory 20% allowance for repairs and outgoings (on the balance after rates)(X)
Net assessable valueX

The 20% repairs/outgoings allowance is flat and statutory — it applies regardless of the owner's actual repair costs, and cannot be varied by claiming higher actual expenditure. Consideration recovered in a later year, having previously been written off as irrecoverable under s.7C, is brought back into that later year's assessable value (s.7C(2)).

Lease premiums paid up front are deemed under s.5B(3)/(4) to be payable in equal monthly instalments spread over the period of the right of use, capped at a maximum of 3 years — even if the actual lease term is longer. See the DIPN 4/DIPN 14 illustrations below.

3. Taxable / Non-Taxable Items

StatusItemBasis
TaxableRent receivable for the year (whether or not actually received)s.5B(2)
TaxableLease premiums / non-returnable deposits / key money, spread over up to 3 yearss.5B(3)/(4); DIPN 4, DIPN 14
TaxableConsideration for services/benefits connected with the right of use (e.g. furniture, management services bundled into rent)s.5B(6)
Non-taxableOwner-occupied property (no rent receivable)No assessable value arises — s.5(1)
Non-taxableRent/consideration proved to have become irrecoverable during the years.7C(1)
Deduction (fixed)Rates paid by owner + flat 20% repairs/outgoings allowances.5(1A)(b)

4. Corporate Interaction with Profits Tax IRO s.25, s.5(2)(a)

For a corporation carrying on a trade, profession or business in Hong Kong, property tax and profits tax can otherwise double-tax the same rental income. Two relief mechanisms apply:

  • Set-off (s.25): where the rental profits form part of the corporation's trading profits (or the property is used to produce chargeable profits), profits tax payable is reduced by the property tax already paid on that property. If property tax paid exceeds the profits tax payable, the excess is refunded (s.25, proviso (b), via s.79).
  • Upfront exemption (s.5(2)(a)): instead of paying property tax and later claiming the set-off, a corporation entitled to the s.25 set-off may apply in writing to the Commissioner for the property to be exempted from property tax altogether. The corporation must notify the Commissioner within 30 days of any change in ownership/use affecting the exemption (s.5(2)(c)).
Practical note Non-corporate owners (individuals, partnerships) do not get the s.25 set-off/exemption against profits tax in the same way — they may instead elect Personal Assessment (IRO s.41) to have property tax effectively absorbed into a single personal-assessment computation where advantageous. See the Salaries Tax page for Personal Assessment.

On this page

What Personal Assessment is Who may elect Married couples Time limits: election & withdrawal The computation, step by step What is deductible When it helps — and when it does not Worked illustrations Common pitfalls Source documents
Individual — Personal Assessment

Personal Assessment

Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112), Part 7 (ss.40–43) — not a tax, but an election that re-computes Property Tax, Profits Tax and Salaries Tax together at progressive rates, after allowances.

個人入息課稅並非稅種，而是一項選擇：把物業、業務及受僱入息合併計算，按累進稅率並扣除免稅額。涵蓋資格、2018/19 年起可分開選擇的改動、時限、標準稅率上限，以及甚麼情況下選擇反而更貴。

1. What Personal Assessment is IRO s.41

Hong Kong levies direct tax under three separate heads — Salaries Tax, Profits Tax and Property Tax. Personal Assessment (PA) is not a fourth head of charge. It is a relief: an individual may elect to have all three sources aggregated into one computation, taxed at salaries-tax progressive rates after personal allowances, instead of being taxed separately at the standard rate on each source.

The one-line test for whether PA can possibly help Property Tax and Profits Tax are charged at the standard rate with no personal allowances. Salaries Tax already gets progressive rates and allowances. So PA can only help someone with property income or unincorporated-business profits. A taxpayer whose only income is employment income cannot benefit from electing — there is nothing for the election to unlock.

The election is annual, must be made in writing, and is not automatic. IRD will not apply it for you, though where an election has been made and turns out to be disadvantageous, the assessor will raise the separate assessments instead and note on the demand that PA was not to your benefit.

Distinguish from Joint Assessment Joint assessment (s.10(2)) is a Salaries Tax mechanism for married couples — it pools employment income only. Personal Assessment (s.41) pools all three heads of charge. They are different elections under different sections, and the exam trap is treating them as the same thing. See Salaries Tax §6.

2. Who may elect IRO s.41(1), s.41(4)

The conditions changed from YA 2018/19. Both are set out because the older rule still governs any earlier year still under assessment or objection.

Year of assessmentConditions
2018/19 onwards
current		 The individual is 18 or over (or under 18 if both parents are dead); and the elector is personally either ordinarily resident in Hong Kong or a temporary resident.
Up to 2017/18 Same age test; but the residence test could be satisfied by the spouse — the elector, or if married their spouse, had to be ordinarily resident or a temporary resident.

The substantive change is that from 2018/19 the elector must qualify on their own residence. Piggy-backing on a spouse's residence status no longer works.

TermMeaning
Ordinarily resident
s.41(4)		 Resides in Hong Kong voluntarily and for a settled purpose (education, business, employment, family) with a sufficient degree of continuity — habitually and normally resident apart from temporary or occasional absences, living here as an ordinary member of the community for all the purposes of daily life. Ultimately a question of fact. The Ordinance does not define it further; the case law is Lysaght v CIR (regular visits of substantial duration year to year) and Cooper v Cadwalader (maintaining a place of abode).
Temporary resident Stays in Hong Kong for more than 180 days during the year of assessment for which the election is made, or more than 300 days in two consecutive years of assessment, one of which is the year of election.
Not the same as a permanent identity card "Ordinarily resident" is a factual test about how and where someone actually lives. Holding a Hong Kong permanent identity card is evidence, not the test, and someone can hold one while no longer ordinarily residing here. Conversely a non-permanent resident who is physically here for enough days qualifies as a temporary resident and may elect.

Deceased taxpayers. Where a person who was eligible to elect dies, the executor has the same right of election over the deceased's total income as the deceased would have had.

3. Married couples IRO s.41(1A), s.42(2)

Separate election has been available since YA 2018/19 The Inland Revenue (Amendment) (No. 9) Ordinance 2018 relaxed what had been a hard joint-election requirement. From YA 2018/19, a married person may elect for Personal Assessment separately from, or jointly with, their spouse.
SituationWho elects
2018/19 onwards, general ruleEither spouse may elect on their own. A joint election remains available where either or both are eligible and both have income assessable under the Ordinance.
Already jointly assessed under Salaries TaxThe PA election must be made jointly. A couple who elected joint assessment under s.10(2) cannot then split for PA.
Up to 2017/18Where both spouses had assessable income and were not living apart, the election had to be made by both. If one refused, neither could elect.

Where a joint election is made, each spouse's total income as appropriately reduced is aggregated into a joint reduced total income, the married person's allowance and other allowances are deducted from the joint figure, and the tax is computed once. The total tax is then apportioned between the spouses in the ratio of their respective reduced total incomes, and each receives their own notice of assessment and demand for payment.

Why the 2018/19 change matters in practice Under the old joint-election rule, electing meant each spouse necessarily learned the other's income and business losses. A spouse who wanted to keep that private could simply refuse, and the couple lost the relief entirely. Separate election removes that veto.

4. Time limits — election and withdrawal IRO s.41(2), s.41(3)

ActionDeadline
Election The later of:
  • 2 years after the end of the year of assessment concerned — so for YA 2026/27, not later than 31 March 2029; or
  • 2 months after the issue of a notice of assessment or additional assessment for that year.
Withdrawal Within 6 months of the date the Personal Assessment is issued, or such longer period as the Commissioner considers reasonable. Where the election was made jointly, the withdrawal must also be joint.

An election is made in writing — in practice by completing the relevant section of the Tax Return (BIR60), or on Form IR76C.

Withdrawal is close to one-way Once an election is withdrawn, the taxpayer may not elect again for that same year unless the Commissioner considers a re-election appropriate. Because the two-year election window is generous but the six-month withdrawal window is short, the safer sequence is to compute both outcomes before electing rather than electing speculatively and unwinding it later.

5. The computation, step by step IRO s.42, s.42A, s.43

Three steps: aggregate, deduct, then compare against the standard rate.

StepWhat happens
1Aggregate income chargeable to Property Tax, Salaries Tax and Profits Tax into total income.
2Deduct, in order: interest on money borrowed to produce property income → concessionary deductions → business losses of the year → PA losses brought forward. This gives reduced total income. Then deduct personal allowances to give net chargeable income.
3Compute tax as the lower of: progressive rates on net chargeable income, or the standard rate on reduced total income.
The standard-rate cap applies to PA too — and on the right base The cap compares progressive tax on net chargeable income (after allowances) against standard rate on reduced total income (before allowances). Applying the standard rate to the post-allowance figure is a classic error: it uses the wrong base and understates the cap.

What goes into "total income"

SourceFigure brought in
Property
Net assessable value		 Rental income + recovered bad rent − irrecoverable rent = assessable value; less rates agreed and paid by the landlord; less the 20% statutory deduction. See Property Tax §NAV.
Employment
Net assessable income		 Assessable income less s.12(1)(a) outgoings, s.12(1)(b) depreciation allowances and s.12(1)(e) self-education, plus any s.12(5) balancing charge. Note this is after self-education but before concessionary deductions — those are taken later, at step 2. See Salaries Tax §4.
Business
Net assessable profits		 Profits of every sole proprietorship, plus the individual's share from each partnership — after offsetting losses brought forward and after approved charitable donations already allowed in the profits tax computation. See Profits Tax §5.
Only Hong Kong-source income enters PA aggregates income chargeable under the three heads. Offshore profits that were never chargeable to Profits Tax do not become chargeable by electing PA — and correspondingly an offshore business loss cannot be brought in to shelter Hong Kong income.

6. What is deductible under Personal Assessment

StatusItemBasis / cap (2026/27)
DeductibleInterest on money borrowed to produce property income — the deduction PA exists forCapped at the net assessable value of that individual property; no excess relief and no carry-forward (Board of Review D51/04)
DeductibleApproved charitable donationss.26C — aggregate min. HKD 100, capped at 35% of income after other deductions
DeductibleElderly residential care expensess.26D — HKD 110,000 per parent/grandparent; mutually exclusive with the dependent parent allowance
DeductibleHome loan interestss.26E/26F — HKD 100,000 (120,000 with a qualifying child); up to 20 years of assessment
DeductibleVHIS qualifying premiumsss.26H–26M — HKD 8,000 per insured person
DeductibleQualifying annuity premiums + MPF voluntary contributionsss.26N–26U — combined cap HKD 60,000
DeductibleDomestic rentsHKD 100,000 (120,000 with a qualifying child)
DeductibleAssisted reproductive service expensesHKD 100,000
DeductibleBusiness losses of the year, and PA losses brought forwardThe other reason to elect — a sole-proprietorship loss can shelter salary and property income in the same year
DeductiblePersonal allowancesBasic 145,000 / married 290,000 for YA 2026/27 (132,000 / 264,000 on the D26 exam basis) — the full table is on Salaries Tax §5
Non-deductiblePrivate and domestic expenses generallyPA does not open up deductions that no head of charge allows. It only lets you take, against aggregated income, the reliefs the Ordinance already grants.
Non-deductibleOffshore business lossesNever chargeable, so never available for set-off
Non-deductibleMortgage interest exceeding that property's NAVThe excess lapses — it cannot create or increase a loss
Don't confuse the two interest deductions Interest to produce property income (this section, capped at that property's NAV) is a different relief from home loan interest under ss.26E/26F (capped at HKD 100,000, for a dwelling the taxpayer occupies). A let property that is also mortgaged attracts the first; an owner-occupied home attracts the second. They are not interchangeable and a single property will not normally attract both.

7. When it helps — and when it does not

PA is likely to help where

  • Property is mortgaged — Property Tax gives no relief at all for loan interest.
  • There is a business loss to set against salary or property income in the same year.
  • Total income is low enough that the progressive rates average out below the standard rate.
  • Personal allowances are unused because the income is property or business income rather than salary.
  • Concessionary deductions (donations, elderly care) are being wasted against income that gets no relief for them.

PA is unlikely to help where

  • The only income is employment income — Salaries Tax already applies progressive rates and allowances, so there is nothing to gain.
  • Total income is high: the 17% marginal rate exceeds the 15% standard rate, so aggregating drags property or business income up to 17%.
  • The property is unmortgaged and allowances are already fully absorbed elsewhere.

Because the marginal progressive rate (17%) is above the standard rate (15%), PA is a relief that reverses into a cost once income is large enough. It must be computed both ways, not assumed.

8. Worked illustrations

Adapted from IRD's own worked examples in A Brief Guide to Personal Assessment (pam37e). IRD's leaflet computes them at YA 2025/26 allowances; every figure below has been recomputed at YA 2026/27 rates (basic allowance 145,000, married person's allowance 290,000), so the answers deliberately differ from the leaflet's.

One-off Budget reductions excluded IRD's examples net off a 100% tax reduction capped at HKD 3,000 for 2025/26. No equivalent has been assumed here for 2026/27 — check the current Budget before treating any figure below as the final net tax payable.

As Illustration 1, but Miss Chan also earns $500,000 from employment.

Electing costs $540 more ($100,490 against $99,950). Miss Chan is already at the 17% marginal rate on salary, so aggregating the property income taxes it at 17% rather than the 15% standard rate — and that outweighs the mortgage-interest deduction the election unlocks. This is the illustration to remember: the same taxpayer, the same property, the same mortgage, opposite answer, purely because of the other income. Under IRD's 2025/26 figures the election was similarly disadvantageous.

Illustration 4 — Married couple electing jointly, and how the tax is split IRD pam37e Example 4, recomputed at 2026/27

Mr Cheung's sole-proprietorship profit is assessed at $480,000. Mrs Cheung receives monthly rent of $20,000 from a mortgaged property and paid $72,000 of loan interest.

Business profits (Mr Cheung)480,000
Property, net assessable value (Mrs Cheung) ($20,000 × 12 × 80%)192,000
Less: mortgage interest(72,000)
Mrs Cheung's reduced total income120,000
Joint reduced total income600,000
Less: married person's allowance D26 exam (YA 2025/26): $264,000(290,000)
Net chargeable income310,000
Tax at progressive rates (standard-rate cap 15% × 600,000 = 90,000, not binding)34,700
Apportionment — in the ratio of each spouse's reduced total income
Mr Cheung: $34,700 × 480,000 / 600,00027,760
Mrs Cheung: $34,700 × 120,000 / 600,0006,940

Each spouse receives their own notice of assessment and demand for the apportioned amount. Note the apportionment base is reduced total income — Mrs Cheung's share is computed on $120,000 after her mortgage interest, not on the $192,000 NAV before it. IRD's 2025/26 version, using a $264,000 married person's allowance and the $3,000 reduction, gives $36,120 split $28,896 / $7,224.

Three further Personal Assessment election scenarios from Module 9 →

9. Common pitfalls

TrapWhat is actually right
Treating PA as a fourth head of chargeIt is a relief and an election. It changes how existing chargeable income is taxed; it never makes non-chargeable income chargeable.
Assuming PA always saves taxAbove roughly the point where the 17% marginal rate bites, it costs money — Illustration 3. Always compute both ways.
Recommending PA to a salary-only taxpayerThere is nothing to gain: progressive rates and allowances already apply.
Applying the standard-rate cap to net chargeable incomeThe cap is the standard rate on reduced total income, before personal allowances.
Deducting mortgage interest above the property's NAVCapped at that property's NAV. The excess lapses; it cannot create a loss.
Bringing in an offshore business lossOffshore profits were never chargeable, so the loss is not available.
Citing the mandatory joint electionOut of date. Separate election has been available since YA 2018/19. It remains mandatory to elect jointly only where the couple is already jointly assessed for Salaries Tax.
Relying on a spouse's residence to qualifyOnly for years up to 2017/18. From 2018/19 the elector must satisfy the residence test personally.
Apportioning joint tax by gross incomeThe ratio is each spouse's reduced total income.
Missing the withdrawal windowElection runs to 2 years after the year end; withdrawal is only 6 months from the assessment, and re-election afterwards needs the Commissioner's agreement.

Business — Stamp Duty

Stamp Duty

Stamp Duty Ordinance (Cap. 117) — a separate ordinance from the Inland Revenue Ordinance. Charged on share transfers, immovable property transactions, and leases.

印花稅說明印花稅以文書為課稅對象，涵蓋物業、股票、租約、BSD/SSD、關聯公司寬免及上訴程序。
Source note Stamp duty sits in the Stamp Duty Ordinance (Cap. 117), not Cap. 112 — the consolidated Cap. 117 text (current to 26 Feb 2026) is saved in Data/CAP117/. Section numbers below have been cross-checked directly against that text; where earlier SOIPN-based drafting of this page used outdated numbering or a superseded rate structure (notably the old flat-15% description of AVD Scale 1), it has been corrected below.

1. Overview

Stamp duty is a transaction tax, not an income tax — it is charged on specific categories of instruments (documents), not on profit. The three main heads for a Hong Kong company are: (1) Hong Kong stock transfers, (2) immovable property conveyances/agreements, and (3) leases. Hong Kong has no capital gains tax, estate duty, gift tax, or VAT — stamp duty is the main transaction-based levy filling that gap.

2026 amendment Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 (gazetted 29 May 2026, effective retrospectively from 26 February 2026) revised the residential/non-residential AVD rate bands — figures below reflect the post-26-Feb-2026 rates per PwC (reviewed 22 Jul 2026). Verify against the gazetted schedule before relying on a specific banding for a transaction.

2. Share Transfers SDO s.19 (contract notes), First Schedule Head 2(1)

Ad valorem duty on transfer of Hong Kong stock0.2% of consideration or market value, whichever is higher (split 0.1% buyer / 0.1% seller, plus a small fixed contract note duty)

Contract notes are charged under s.19 (First Schedule Head 2(1)); s.21 prohibits stock being passed through without duty on the intervening step, s.22 covers consideration paid in stock/securities, and s.23 covers periodical-payment consideration. s.20 (formerly a related contract-note provision) has been repealed (33 of 2024 s.5) — do not cite it. Reliefs exist for stock borrowing/lending transactions (s.19(11) excludes a stock borrowing/return from the charge; s.19(12A) sets the borrower's return conditions; registration fee currently $270, must register within 30 days) and for intra-group ("associated companies") transfers under s.45 (§6 covers this in more detail) — see SOIPN 2.

New — RMB settlement of stamp duty on dual-counter stock The Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 2) Ordinance 2026 (Bill passed 8 July 2026, gazetted 17 July 2026) lets stamp duty on a transfer of dual-counter stock traded at the RMB counter be calculated and paid in Renminbi, so an investor settles the trade and the duty in the same currency at the same counter. The 0.2% rate is unchanged — this is a settlement-currency and administration change only. Commencement is on a day to be appointed by the Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury, pending HKEX system readiness, so it is not yet in force.
Source: Government welcomes passage of Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 2) Bill 2026, 8 Jul 2026.

2A. Conveyances & Agreements for Sale — Charging Mechanics SDO s.4, Part IIIA (ss.29A–29DV)

The general charge is s.4 ("Charging of, liability for, and recovery of stamp duty") read together with the First Schedule, which sets out each "Head of charge" and its rate. For immovable property, Part IIIA (originally ss.29A–29I, now expanded to ss.29A–29DV across 7 Divisions covering interpretation, conveyances, agreements for sale, refunds, and the AVD scale machinery) supplies the detailed mechanics — including the provisional/formal agreement stamping rules illustrated in DIPN/SOIPN 1 below.

3. Property Transfers — Ad Valorem Duty (AVD) First Schedule Head 1(1)/(1A); ss.29AI, 29AJ, 29AK

Correction vs. common assumption AVD Scale 1 is not a flat 15% on residential property. The flat-15% Scale 1 that applied from 5 Nov 2016 was superseded by a 2023 reform that made Scale 1 a graduated table matching Scale 2's bands (top rate 4.25%) — the only remaining difference is a new top band the Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 added above ~$109.57M (see below). If your prior understanding was "flat 15% for non-HKPR/company buyers," that is now out of date except at the very top of the market.

AVD has three rate tables, all graduated (not flat), all sharing the same lower bands:

ScaleApplies toTop rate
Scale 1 (First Schedule Head 1(1)/(1A), default table — s.29AI)Residential property, buyer not qualifying for the Scale 2 concession (incl. companies, non-HKPRs)4.25% up to $100,000,000; a transitional band charging $4,250,000 + 30% of the excess from $100,000,000–$109,574,470; 6.5% flat above $109,574,470 (new top bands added by the Stamp Duty (Amendment) Ordinance 2026, s.14)
Scale 2 (s.29AJ concession)Hong Kong Permanent Resident buying their sole residential property, or a qualifying closely-related-person reassignment4.25% — unchanged by the 2026 amendment
Scale 3 (s.29AI(b) default for non-residential; also s.29AK for a car park bought alongside a Scale-2 residential purchase)Non-residential property4.25% — unchanged by the 2026 amendment

All three scales start at a flat $100 for low-value transactions and climb through the same intermediate bands (1.5% / 2.25% / 3% / 3.75%) before reaching their respective top rate. Duty is charged on consideration or market value, whichever is higher. "Closely related persons" (for Scale 2 eligibility and for the close-relative exemptions on BSD/SSD) is defined at s.29AD — broadly parent/spouse/child/sibling. Reliefs: replacement of a sole residential property (refund window), exchange/partition ("equality money" only), court orders, mortgagee sales, associated-company transfers under s.45 (§6) — see SOIPN 8, though note SOIPN 8 (Nov 2018) predates the 2023 Scale 1 reform and the 2026 amendment.

4. Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) & Special Stamp Duty (SSD) First Schedule Head 1(1AAB)/(1C) [BSD]; Head 1(1AA) [SSD]

Correction vs. common assumption There is no "Part IIIAA" or "Part IVA" for BSD/SSD in the current ordinance structure — Part IVA is actually the unrelated Unit Trusts/Open-ended Fund Companies part (ss.37A–41). BSD and SSD are instead defined as separate Heads of charge in the First Schedule, cross-referenced from Part IIIA.
DutyApplies toRate
Buyer's Stamp Duty (BSD) — Head 1(1AAB) conveyance / Head 1(1C) agreement for saleResidential property acquired by a non-HKPR (companies are always treated as non-HKPR); subject to ss.29C, 29CB, 29CC0% — reduced from 15% in stages (L.N. 148 of 2023; 3 of 2024 s.14; L.N. 26 of 2024; 8 of 2024 s.6)
Special Stamp Duty (SSD) — Head 1(1AA), Part 4 (property disposed of on/after 28 Feb 2024)Residential property resold within the holding-period window; subject to ss.29D, 29DA0% — reduced from up to 20% (L.N. 26 of 2024; 8 of 2024 s.6)
Note BSD and SSD remain fully defined in the First Schedule with their mechanics unchanged (liable party, timing, holding-period tiers for SSD) — only the rate was reduced to 0% as a market-support measure from 28 February 2024. Head 1(1AA)'s historical Parts 1–3 are preserved verbatim for legacy holding-period windows still being assessed (20 Nov 2010–27 Oct 2012 at 15/10/5%; 27 Oct 2012–25 Oct 2023 and 25 Oct 2023–28 Feb 2024, both at 20/15/10%) — relevant only if assessing an old disposal that hasn't yet been finalised. Both duties could in principle be reactivated at a non-zero rate by future amendment — see SOIPN 5 (SSD) and SOIPN 7 (BSD), noting both predate the current 0% rate and Head numbering nuances above.

5. Leases SDO Head 1(2)

Lease termDuty
Not defined or uncertain / ≤ 1 year0.25% of average annual rent (plus any premium, taxed as a sale)
Between 1 and 3 years0.5% of average annual rent
Over 3 years1% of average annual rent

A premium paid for a lease is chargeable as if it were a sale consideration, separately from the rent-based duty above — see the interaction with Property Tax/Profits Tax premium-spreading rules on the Property Tax page.

6. Reliefs SDO s.45; s.29AD

Associated bodies corporate relief (s.45) — relieves a conveyance from one associated body corporate to another from AVD, SSD, BSD, and HK-stock contract-note duty (it spans Heads 1(1), 1(1AA), 1(1AAB), 2(1) and 2(3)), where a ≥90% common-ownership test is met. A clawback applies under s.45(5A) if the ≥90% association ceases within 2 years of the relieved conveyance.

Bill before LegCo — do not apply yet · 法案仍待立法會審議 The Stamp Duty (Amendment) (No. 3) Bill 2026 (announced 29 Sep 2026, gazetted 2 Oct 2026, first reading 14 Oct 2026) would relax this relief: the association test would fall from 90% to 75%, association could be established through direct or indirect beneficial interests or voting rights rather than issued share capital alone, and the relief would extend to entities with no share capital — limited liability partnerships and companies limited by guarantee. The Bill proposes to apply to instruments executed on or after 25 February 2026.
The enacted test remains ≥90%. Quote 90% for any instrument being stamped now. The retrospective date is the part to watch: if enacted as drafted, transfers already executed since 25 Feb 2026 that met 75% but not 90% would become relievable. See IRD What's New §2.

Closely related persons (s.29AD) — defines the parent/spouse/child/sibling relationships that qualify for the Scale 2 AVD concession (§3) and are also picked up by the close-relative exemption notes applied to the BSD/SSD sub-heads (co-purchasers who are closely related are treated as "the same person" for ownership-counting purposes).

Proposed — newborn-family stamp duty concession, 2026 Policy Address (16 Sep 2026) A family with a child born in Hong Kong on or after 16 September 2026, where at least one parent is a Hong Kong permanent resident, would get a stamp duty waiver capped at HKD 20,000 on a residential property purchased in the window running from one year before to two years after the birth. To take effect on enactment of the amendment ordinance — not yet law, so do not apply it to a current transaction. Note it is a capped waiver, not a rate change: on any purchase where AVD exceeds HKD 20,000 the relief is a flat HKD 20,000.
Source: IRD — 2026 Policy Address, Tax-related Policy Measures (on Individuals), published 16 Sep 2026.

7. Partnership Admission & Retirement

Where a partner is admitted to, or retires from, a partnership that holds Hong Kong stock or immovable property, the change in each partner's proportionate interest can itself be a chargeable "sale and purchase" of the underlying property/stock for stamp duty purposes (the incoming/continuing partners are treated as acquiring the outgoing/diluted partners' fractional interest). This is assessed using the same AVD/stock-transfer rules above, applied to the fractional interest that changes hands — always check partnership deeds and capital-account movements for a hidden stamp duty trigger whenever partners change.

8. Illustrations

10 worked illustrations back this page — SOIPN-sourced (agreement timing, AVD/SSD/BSD mechanics) plus Module 9 textbook examples. This is the topic needing the most correction: both source books predate the 2023 AVD Scale 1 reform and/or the 2024 BSD/SSD rate cut, so most headline rates in the older material are wrong — corrected figures are shown alongside the originals throughout.

Illustration — Current graduated Scale 1 vs. Scale 2 Corrected from Cap. 117 First Schedule, post-2026 amendment

A $13,000,000 residential property bought by a non-HKPR (or corporate) buyer with no Scale 2 concession available: Scale 1 is graduated exactly like Scale 2 at this value band (3.75%), giving $487,500 — not a flat-15% $1,950,000 as older material describes. The two scales only diverge for a single residential property with consideration above $100,000,000, where the 2026 amendment gives Scale 1 a new 6.5% flat top band that Scale 2 does not get.

Common — Depreciation & Allowances

Depreciation & Allowances

Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112), Part 6 & related provisions — capital allowances replace accounting depreciation for tax purposes; accounting depreciation itself is never deductible (IRO s.17(1)(c)).

折舊及免稅額整理工業/商業建築物免稅額、機械及設備、初期/每年免稅額、結餘課稅/免稅額及特定資產即時扣除。

1. Overview

Because capital expenditure and accounting depreciation are non-deductible under Profits Tax (s.17(1)(c)/(d)), Part 6 of the IRO substitutes a separate, statutory system of capital allowances for four categories of qualifying capital expenditure: (1) industrial buildings, (2) commercial buildings, (3) plant & machinery, and (4) a growing list of 100%/5-year write-off regimes for specific asset types (ss.16C–16L) that sit alongside, and interact with, Part 6.

Key mechanic — add-back and allowance in the same computation In every profits tax computation: add back accounting depreciation (non-deductible), then deduct the correct statutory allowance instead. The two numbers are almost never equal — this is the single most common adjustment in a Hong Kong tax computation.

2. Industrial & Commercial Buildings IRO ss.33A, 34, 36, 37

Building typeInitial allowanceAnnual allowanceBalancing allowance/charge
Industrial building or structure (mills, factories, docks, utility undertakings, qualifying storage/farming/R&D buildings)20% (1/5) of cost, year of first use4% (1/25) straight-line on costOn sale/lease termination/demolition — balancing charge capped at total allowances previously granted
Commercial building or structure (all other non-excluded buildings)None4% (1/25) straight-line on cost, from 1998/99Same balancing mechanism as industrial buildings, from 1998/99

"Industrial building or structure" is narrowly defined (DIPN 2) — it excludes dwellings, retail shops, showrooms, hotels, and offices. Where a building is used partly for a qualifying industrial purpose and partly not, a 10% de-minimis rule applies: if the non-qualifying use is no more than 10% of the whole, the building is treated as wholly industrial. On a sale, the buyer's future annual allowance is recalculated as the residue of expenditure after sale, spread over the remaining years to the building's 25th year from first use.

Historical note Before 1998/99, commercial buildings only qualified for a much smaller "rebuilding allowance" (0.75% pre-1990/91, then 2% from 1990/91–1997/98) rather than the modern 4% annual allowance — relevant only when tracing the residue of expenditure on a very old building still being written down today.

3. Plant & Machinery — Pooling System IRO ss.39B–39E

Since YA1980/81, plant and machinery of the same annual-allowance rate class is pooled together rather than tracked asset-by-asset (the old asset-by-asset method under ss.37–39 survives only for hire-purchase assets, mixed business/private-use assets, and a few other special cases).

Initial allowance60% of cost, given once on acquisition
Annual allowanceReducing-balance on the pool's "reducing value," at 10%, 20% or 30% depending on asset class (Board of Inland Revenue rates)
Common annual allowance rate classes (Appendix A(i), DIPN 7)
RateAsset examples
10%Air-conditioning plant, lifts, cables, ships
20%Furniture, fixtures, domestic/room air-conditioners — the general residual rate for unlisted items
30%Motor vehicles, computer/EDP equipment, textile/electronics manufacturing plant, tractors/bulldozers

Balancing allowances only arise when the trade/pool ceases altogether. Balancing charges can arise at any time disposal proceeds exceed the pool's reducing value, but are capped at the total allowances previously granted for that asset (you can never be charged more than you were originally allowed). Hire-purchase assets, and assets moved between private and business use, are excluded from pooling and calculated separately with notional allowance adjustments.

4. 100% / 5-Year Write-Off Regimes IRO ss.16C, 16F, 16G, 16H–16L

RegimeBasisTreatment
Technical education payments to approved institutionss.16CDeductible when paid
Refurbishment/renovation of non-domestic buildingss.16F5 equal annual instalments (20%/year)
Prescribed fixed assets — manufacturing plant, standalone computer hardware/software (excludes leased assets)s.16G100% one-off in year of payment
Environmental protection machinery & environment-friendly vehiclesss.16H, 16I100% one-off (from 2018/19; previously 5-year spread)
Environmental protection installations (buildings)ss.16J–16L100% one-off (from 2018/19; previously 5-year spread)

A taxpayer with unallowed instalments from pre-2018/19 environmental expenditure could elect under s.16I(3A) to accelerate the remaining instalments to a single 100% deduction in 2018/19 (see the DIPN 5 illustration below).

5. Patents, Know-How & Specified IP Rights IRO ss.16E, 16EA–16EC

AssetBasisTreatment
Patent rights / know-hows.16E100% one-off, year of purchase — no spreading
Specified IP Rights (copyright, registered trade marks/designs, plant variety rights, layout-design/topography rights, performer's economic rights)ss.16EA–16EC5 equal annual instalments (or shorter, to match remaining legal protection period)

Expenditure deductible under s.16E/16EA/16G/16I is excluded from Part 6 depreciation allowances — the regimes are mutually exclusive per asset, not cumulative. Anti-avoidance carve-outs deny the deduction for sale-and-license-back arrangements, purchases from associates, and IP used exclusively outside Hong Kong by another person under a leveraged licensing structure.

6. Illustrations

6 worked illustrations back this page — DIPN-sourced (industrial building sale, plant & machinery pooling, balancing charges, IP amortisation) plus a Module 9 textbook example spanning two years of pooling with disposals and additions.

Illustration — Industrial building sale: buyer/seller allowance split DIPN 2

A factory is built for $500,000 in February 1992. Initial allowance 20% = $100,000; annual allowance 4% = $20,000 in the first year, continuing for 3 more years, leaving a residue of expenditure of $320,000. The building is then sold for $420,000. The seller faces a balancing charge of $100,000 (sale price exceeds residue by $100,000, capped at allowances previously granted). The buyer's future annual allowance is recalculated as 1/21 (years remaining to the 25th year) × $420,000 = $20,000/year.

Common — IRD Administration

IRD Administration

Inland Revenue Ordinance (Cap. 112) — filing, assessment, objections, appeals, provisional tax and penalty mechanics that apply across Profits, Property and Salaries Tax.

稅務局行政涵蓋報稅、評稅、估計評稅、反對、上訴、暫繳稅緩繳、罰則、稅務調查，以及自動交換財務帳戶資料與加密資產申報。
Source note The section numbers on this page reflect the IRO's long-standing, stable administration framework, but this build's local CAP112 text extraction did not cleanly surface the Part 9–14 body text for direct verification (see §7). Cross-check exact wording against a fresh Cap. 112 download before citing a subsection in a formal position.

1. Overview

These provisions are common infrastructure across Profits Tax, Property Tax and Salaries Tax — a computation is only complete once you know how it gets filed, assessed, and (if needed) disputed or paid provisionally.

2. Returns & Filing IRO s.51

The Commissioner issues annual returns (profits tax, salaries tax, property tax, employer's return) which must be completed and filed by the stated due date — extensions are routinely available for corporate profits tax returns filed through a tax representative under the Block Extension Scheme. Every person carrying on a trade, profession or business must keep sufficient records (s.51C) for at least 7 years to enable profits/losses to be readily ascertained.

Practical note For a newly incorporated company, the first profits tax return is usually issued around 18 months after incorporation or commencement of business — but a company must still notify the Commissioner of chargeability (s.51(2)) within 4 months after the end of the basis period if no return has been issued, even where no return has yet been received.
Block Extension Scheme — 2025/26 returns, "D" code extended By circular letter of 14 July 2026, the Commissioner further extended the due date for 2025/26 profits tax returns with Accounting Date Code "D" (accounting date falling between 1 and 31 December 2025):
  • Paper filing: 17 August 2026 → 31 August 2026
  • Electronic filing: 17 September 2026 → 2 October 2026
The extension was granted to help businesses and practitioners adapt to new compliance requirements; the circular still urges representatives to file well before the extended date. Codes "N" and "M" were not changed by this circular. Source: Circular Letter to Tax Representatives — Block Extension Scheme for Lodgement of 2025/26 Tax Returns, 14 Jul 2026.
Business Tax Portal — new Responsible Person capacities (8 Jun 2026) IRD expanded the capacities in which a Responsible Person may register a business for the Business Tax Portal (BTP). Check the registration capacity before opening a BTP account for a client entity — an account opened in the wrong capacity has to be redone.

3. Assessment & Estimated Assessment IRO ss.59–60

The assessor assesses the return as filed, or — where no return is filed, or the assessor is not satisfied with a return — issues an estimated assessment based on the best information available. Estimated assessments are commonly issued precisely to protect the statutory time limit for assessment where a return is outstanding; they are not a final determination and are superseded once the actual figures are agreed (usually via an objection, §4).

Additional assessments may be raised within the statutory time limit (generally 6 years from the end of the relevant year of assessment, extended to 10 years in cases involving fraud or wilful default) where profits/income have been understated or under-assessed.

4. Objections & Appeals IRO s.64 (objections), s.66 (Board of Review), s.69 (case stated)

StageTime limitForum
Notice of objection1 month from the date of the assessmentCommissioner of Inland Revenue
Appeal against the Commissioner's determination1 month from the determinationBoard of Review
Case stated appeal on a point of law1 month from the Board's decisionCourt of First Instance, then Court of Appeal / Court of Final Appeal

An objection must state precisely the grounds of objection — a bare, unparticularised objection can be rejected as invalid. Tax under dispute is not automatically suspended; the taxpayer must separately apply to hold over payment of the tax in dispute (or the portion in dispute) pending resolution.

5. Provisional Tax & Holdover IRO ss.63A–63U, 71

Provisional profits tax, provisional salaries tax, and provisional property tax are each charged in advance, generally based on the immediately preceding year's assessable profits/income, and later set off against the final assessment for that year once it issues. A taxpayer may apply to hold over payment of the whole or part of provisional tax where, for example, the current year's profits/income are objectively likely to be significantly lower than the prior year's, or personal allowances have increased, or an objection is pending on the immediately preceding year's assessment.

Practical note Holdover applications have their own strict statutory deadlines (broadly, the later of 28 days before the provisional tax is due, or 14 days after the provisional tax notice is issued) — missing the window forfeits the holdover regardless of the merits.

6. Late Payment of Tax — Surcharge and Recovery IRO s.71; Part 12

The consequence almost every taxpayer actually meets, and the one most often confused with the penalties in §7. A surcharge under s.71 is not a penalty for an offence — it is automatic, needs no intent, no reasonable-excuse enquiry and no hearing. Miss the date and it is imposed.

WhenWhat happensProvision
The due date passes A 5% surcharge is imposed on the tax unpaid. Recovery action may begin immediately and without prior notice. s.71(5)
6 months after the due date A further 10% surcharge on the amount still unpaid — including the 5% already imposed. s.71(5A)
The 10% is charged on the tax plus the first surcharge — so it is not 15% On tax of $100,000 left unpaid for over six months:
Tax due100,000
Add: 5% surcharge — s.71(5)5,000
Amount unpaid after the due date105,000
Add: further 10% on $105,000 — s.71(5A)10,500
Total payable115,500
Total surcharge $15,500 — 15.5% of the original tax, not 15%. The second surcharge compounds on the first.

The instalment trap

Where a demand note is split into two instalments, missing the first makes the second immediately due, and the 5% is then charged on the whole outstanding balance — not just on the instalment that was missed.

Demand note of $100,000: first instalment $70,000, second $30,000
First instalment paid on time, second missed — 5% × $30,0001,500
First instalment missed — the second accelerates, so 5% × $100,0005,000
Cost of missing the earlier date rather than the later one3,500

Left unpaid for six months, that same note reaches $115,500.

Recovery of tax in default IRO Part 12

IRD does not wait for the six-month mark before acting. Its own notice states that other than imposing the 5% surcharge it "will also immediately commence other recovery actions without prior notice":

ActionWhat it means in practice
Recovery notice to a third party
s.76		 Served on anyone who owes or holds money for the defaulter — employer, bank, tenant, debtor, customer. That person must pay the money to IRD instead, and is discharged to the extent they do. This is why a tax default can become visible to an employer or banker.
Civil proceedings
s.75		 Tax in default is recoverable as a civil debt in the District Court. A judgment carries the usual consequences, including costs and interest on the judgment debt.
Departure prevention order
s.77		 The Commissioner may apply to a District Judge for a direction stopping a defaulter from leaving Hong Kong until the tax is paid or security given.
Joint and several liability
property tax co-owners		 Co-owners are liable jointly and severally: IRD may pursue any one of them for the whole amount, not merely their share. Once one pays in full, recovery against the others stops. Tax is never collected twice, and any overpayment is refunded.
Applying to pay by instalments does not stop the surcharge A taxpayer in genuine financial difficulty may apply to settle by instalments. But IRD is explicit that even where the application is approved, surcharges are still imposed on tax remaining unpaid after the due date. An instalment arrangement buys time and heads off recovery action; it is not a waiver. Conditional waiver schemes have been offered in particular years as a relief measure, but they are exceptional and year-specific — never assume one applies.
Keep the two regimes apart — this is the distinction to have straight
Surcharge, s.71Penalty, ss.80 / 82A / 82
Triggered byPaying lateFailing to file or notify, filing an incorrect return, or evading tax
Fault requiredNone — automatic on the dateAbsence of reasonable excuse; for s.82, wilful intent
Amount5%, then a further 10% on the totalUp to treble the tax undercharged, plus a fine and, under s.82, imprisonment
Who imposes itThe Commissioner, administrativelyThe Commissioner (s.82A) or a court (ss.80, 82)
A taxpayer who files a correct return on time but pays late faces the surcharge only. One who files late and pays late faces both.

Source: IRD, Pay Tax On Time to Avoid Penalty and Recovery Actions, and GovHK Consequences of Not Paying Tax On Time and Recovering Tax in Default.

7. Penalties IRO ss.80, 82, 82A

ContraventionConsequence
Failure to file a return, or filing late, without reasonable excuseSummary conviction fine and/or additional tax (s.80)
Making an incorrect return, or omitting income, without reasonable excuseAdditional tax up to treble the tax undercharged (s.82A) — an administrative penalty assessed by the Commissioner, distinct from criminal prosecution
Wilfully with intent to evade, or assisting another to evade, taxCriminal prosecution (s.82) — fine up to treble the tax undercharged plus imprisonment up to 3 years

Additional tax under s.82A is an administrative sanction (no need to prove criminal intent) and can be settled by way of a compound penalty offer from the Commissioner in less serious cases — this is the mechanism most commonly encountered in routine tax computation corrections and voluntary disclosures.

8. Double Taxation Relief & Tax Clearance IRO ss.49, 50, 51D

Where Hong Kong has a comprehensive double taxation agreement (CDTA) with another jurisdiction, s.50 provides a tax credit for foreign tax paid on income also taxed in Hong Kong (interacting with the s.16(1)(c)/(2J) deduction restriction on the Profits Tax page). Employers must comply with tax clearance obligations (s.51D) before an employee who is about to leave Hong Kong permanently, or for a substantial period, ceases employment — including withholding final payments until IRD confirms clearance or a specified period has elapsed.

CDTA network (as at 24 September 2026): Hong Kong signed its 60th comprehensive double taxation agreement with Slovenia on 4 September 2026, following Nigeria (13 July 2026) and Cyprus (12 June 2026). Each enters into force only after both sides complete ratification — check the IRD CDTA list for the in-force date before claiming treaty relief.

9. Automatic Exchange of Information & Crypto-Asset Reporting IRO Part 8A

Two separate 2026 measures extend Hong Kong's information-exchange obligations, and both change what a reporting financial institution has to collect:

  • Amended CRS — enacted. The Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Automatic Exchange of Information) Bill 2026 passed on 17 June 2026, implementing the OECD's amended Common Reporting Standard.
  • CARF — bill stage. The Inland Revenue (Amendment) (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework and Amended Common Reporting Standard) Bill 2026 was introduced into LegCo on 1 June 2026, and IRD published its Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework page on 22 June 2026. CARF brings crypto-asset service providers into the reporting net — a genuinely new population of reporting entities, not just a new field on an existing return.
Policy watch The Advisory Committee on Tax Policy held its first meeting on 29 June 2026 — the standing forum now shaping medium-term HK tax policy. IRD also responded to an Ombudsman direct investigation report on 31 August 2026, and published its Annual Report on Performance Pledge 2025-26 on 9 July 2026 (useful for expected turnaround times on objections and refunds).
Fraud alerts — tell clients IRD issued fraudulent-email alerts on 6 July, 22 July, 4 September and 15 September 2026 (fake prosecution notices, fake tax audit notices, and phishing for email passwords), plus a 25 August 2026 warning not to download the eTAX Mobile Application from unofficial channels. IRD does not request passwords or payment by email link.

10. Source Documents

CAP112 Parts referenced above: Part 9 (Returns and Information), Part 10/10A–10C (Assessment, Provisional Tax), Part 11 (Objections and Appeals), Part 12 (Payment and Recovery), Part 14 (Penalties). Consolidated text: Data/CAP112/. As noted at the top of this page, re-verify exact subsection wording against a fresh, fully-extractable copy of Cap. 112 before relying on a specific citation.

Recommended additions to Data/IRD-Administration/: IRD's "A Guide on the Objection and Appeal Procedures under the Inland Revenue Ordinance," and the annual Block Extension Scheme circular (both published on ird.gov.hk).
