Profits Tax Return Guide

Box-by-box walkthrough of BIR51 (current revision 4/2025) — bridging "what the law says" (the Profits Tax and Depreciation & Allowances pages) with "what you actually type into the form." Use the Box Finder to search by keyword instead of reading start to end.

利得稅報稅表指南把 BIR51/52/54 的欄位與稅務計算邏輯連接，說明哪些資料要填在報稅表，哪些屬於另附稅務計算。
Key structural point BIR51 does not contain a line-by-line add-back/deduction schedule as boxed items. Part 1 only captures the three final results — Assessable Profits, Adjusted Loss, Loss brought forward (boxes 1–3). The actual add-backs and deductions (depreciation, capital expenditure, non-deductible items, etc.) are worked out separately in a "tax computation with supporting schedules" that you attach as a Supporting Document — it is not printed on the form itself. That computation is exactly what the Computation Template on the Profits Tax page walks through.

1. Which Form Applies

FormWho files it
BIR51Corporations — the primary form for HK incorporated companies, and the focus of this guide.
BIR52Persons other than corporations — sole proprietorships, partnerships, limited partnership funds, bodies of persons. See §9 below for how it differs from BIR51.
BIR54Not a second "persons other than corporations" form — filed by a Hong Kong resident payer/agent to report a non-resident's HK-sourced profits under ss.20A/20B. See §10 below.

All three are issued annually and must be filed within the deadline stated on the Notice to File (IRC1952 for corporations, IRC1953 for others) — typically extended under the Block Extension Scheme where a tax representative is on record. Since 1 April 2023, all supplementary forms (S1–S22) must be filed electronically via www.ird.gov.hk/e_pfr.

2. Part 1 — Statement of Assessable Profits or Adjusted Loss

BoxLabelMaps to
1Assessable Profits (before loss brought forward)The bottom line of your computation — see the Computation Template.
2Adjusted Loss (before loss brought forward)Fill instead of box 1 if the year produced a loss.
3Loss brought forward from prior years.19C carry-forward — see Basis Period & Loss Relief.

3. Parts 2–3 — Tax Liability, Rate Election & Specified Matters

Part 2 computes Tax Payable/Repayable (IRD-computed, no entry box) and asks:

Box 4Chargeable at two-tiered rates? — the two-tiered rate election. If Yes, upload Form S1 (Part 9, box 42).

Part 3 is a run of Yes/No disclosure questions (boxes 5–15) covering non-resident IP payments (s.15(1)), fund/carried-interest deeming provisions, short/medium-term debt instruments, DTA relief claims, advance rulings, alternative bond schemes, regulatory capital securities, permanent-establishment status, and the s.51AAB e-filing mandate. None of these require a computed figure — they flag which supplementary forms and disclosures apply.

4. Parts 4–8 — Company Details & General Matters

Parts 4–6 are administrative: principal business activity + HSIC code (box 16), return-language preference, and an optional authorized representative section.

Part 7 (General Matters, boxes 17–36) is the section most likely to interact with your tax computation:

BoxWhat it asks
17–19Whether accounts are audited by law, by a HK practice unit, and the signing CPA's practising certificate number.
20Basis period From/To — feeds the basis-period rules (s.18/18C).
21–24Commencement/cessation of business, and what happened to the business/assets on cessation.
25Election to align financial-instrument tax treatment with accounting treatment (ss.18I–18L) — see the DIPN 42 illustration.
26–27Foreign-currency financial statements; private company status.
28Change in shareholders during the basis period — relevant to loss-carry-forward anti-avoidance (DIPN 15).
29Party to a court-free amalgamation (s.680/681 Companies Ordinance) — see DIPN 63.
30Contract/import processing arrangement in the Chinese Mainland — the 50:50 apportionment convention (DIPN 21).
31–36Insurance RBC-regime transition, family-owned SPE/single-family-office status.

Part 8 (Transactions For/With Non-Residents, boxes 37–41) covers acting as an agent for a non-resident, IP value-creation contributions, and HK$ amounts for hire charges/professional fees paid to non-residents.

5. Part 9 — Supplementary Forms Uploaded (S1–S22)

A checkbox per supplementary form, boxes 42–63 (BIR51). Every S-form must be e-filed via www.ird.gov.hk/e_pfr, signed, and submitted with a Control List.

FormCovers
S1Two-tiered profits tax rates election
S2Transfer pricing and international tax obligations
S3Expenditure on research & development (DIPN 55)
S4Expenditure on energy efficient building installation
S5Ship-owner

S11Qualifying ship lessor (DIPN 62)
S12Qualifying ship leasing manager
S13Specified insurer
S14Licensed insurance broker company
S15Persons deriving eligible carried interest
S16Qualifying ship agent
S17Qualifying ship manager
S18Qualifying ship broker
S19Taxation on specified foreign-sourced income — the FSIE regime
S20Tax concessions for family-owned investment holding vehicle
S21Tax certainty enhancement scheme for onshore gain on disposal of equity interests
S22Tax concessions for intellectual property income — the Patent Box concession

BIR52 only lists 10 of these (S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S15, S19, S20, S21, S22) — the shipping/aircraft-leasing/insurance/treasury-centre forms are corporation-only concessions. BIR54 only references S1 and S5.

6. Part 10 — Tax Data (boxes 64–93)

HK$ amount fields (enter "0" if nil) for offshore profits excluded from Part 1, capital-asset sale profits, exempt interest/securities income, and — most relevant to a typical computation — the deduction items that mirror the Depreciation & Allowances page's write-off regimes:

BoxDeduction
74Approved charitable donations
75Building refurbishment expenditure (s.16F)
76Computer hardware/software expenditure (s.16G)
77Prescribed manufacturing machinery/plant expenditure (s.16G)
78–80Environmental protection machinery / installation / environment-friendly vehicles (ss.16H–16L)
81–82Patent rights / rights to know-how (s.16E)
83–88Specified IP Rights — copyrights, performer's rights, layout-design, plant variety rights, registered designs, registered trade marks (ss.16EA–16EC)
89–91DTA relief / unilateral foreign tax credit (s.50 vs s.16(1)(c) — see the DIPN 28 illustration)
92Interest to non-HK associated corporations, intra-group financing business
93Leased premises reinstatement costs

All of boxes 75–88 correspond directly to write-off regimes on the Depreciation & Allowances page — if you've already worked out that page's computation template, these boxes are just transcribing the same figures.

7. Part 11 — Depreciation Allowances Claimed (boxes 94–104)

CategoryInitialAnnualBalancing AllowanceBalancing Charge
Industrial Building94959697
Commercial Building—9899100
Machinery or Plant101102103104

This is a direct transcription target for the Depreciation & Allowances computation template — work out the allowance there, then drop the totals into these boxes.

8. Parts 12–13 — Financial Data & Declaration

Part 12 (boxes 105–127) asks for headline financial-statement figures — gross income, turnover, inventories, gross profit/loss, dividend/interest income and expense, remuneration, commission, IP payments, management/consultancy fees, bad debts, net profit/loss per account, receivables/payables, issued share capital, and total assets. This is IRD cross-checking your return against the shape of your accounts, not a separate computation.

Part 13 (boxes 128–129) is the declaration — tick exactly one: box 128 for a Secretary/Manager/Director/Investment Manager/Provisional Liquidator/Liquidator declaring the return is complete and accurate, or box 129 for a Service Provider declaring it was prepared per the taxpayer's confirmed instructions (IR1476).

9. BIR52 — How It Differs from BIR51

Structurally parallel but shorter (129 boxes → ~111) and reorganized. The headline differences:

  • Part 1 extras (boxes 4–5): whether the proprietor/spouse/partner received emoluments or interest on capital from the business — such payments are non-deductible under s.17(2), and box 5 confirms the tax computation adjusts for it. The two-tiered rate election is box 6 here, not box 4.
  • Part 6 is entirely new: "Personal Particulars of Proprietor or Partners and Allocation of Profits/Loss and Claim for Deduction of Mandatory Contributions" (boxes 18–37) — per-partner HKID/BR number, profit/loss sharing ratio, a Personal Assessment election flag (the actual election is made on the individual's own BIR60, not here), allocated Assessable Profits/Adjusted Loss, and MPF contributions claimed. The allocation total must equal Part 1's box 1/2. See the Personal Assessment section.
  • Part 7 drops the corporation-only items (RBC regime, Companies Ordinance amalgamation, private-company/shareholder-change questions) and adds business-specific ones: cessation by death of the proprietor, and property purchase for building allowance purposes.
  • Part 9 lists only 10 supplementary forms (the corporation-only concessions S6–S14, S16–S18 don't apply).
  • Part 10 swaps BIR51's "interest to non-HK associated corporations" box for a "mandatory MPF contributions for proprietor/partners" deduction.
  • No separate depreciation-allowances Part — Financial Data shifts one part earlier, and the corporation-only "share-based payments"/"issued share capital" fields are dropped.
  • Declaration title varies by entity type: sole proprietorship → "person"; partnership → "precedent partner"; limited partnership fund → "general partner" / "investment manager"; body of persons → "principal officer"; no resident proprietor/partner → "agent"/"manager"; deceased estate → "executor."

10. BIR54 — What It Actually Is

Common misconception, corrected BIR54 is not a second "persons other than corporations" return. Its actual title is "Profits Tax Return — In Respect of Non-Resident Persons." It is filed under ss.20A/20B by the Hong Kong resident payer or agent, in the non-resident's own name, to report that non-resident's Hong Kong-sourced trade/business profits — most commonly royalty/IP payments, or income received via a Hong Kong agent. It's bilingual (Chinese/English) and far shorter than BIR51/52 (~22 boxes).

Key sections: a two-tiered rate election made on behalf of the non-resident (box 3, with the same connected-entity disclosure logic as BIR51/S1); an IP use/assignment block (boxes 11–17) determining whether the deemed-profit computation under s.21A(1)(a) applies 100% or 30% of the royalty receipt as assessable profit; a section on the agent's role in Hong Kong; and a reciprocal shipowner exemption block (boxes 18–20, s.23B(4A)) for non-resident shipowners.

Business — Profits Tax

Profits Tax — Worked Illustrations

Every worked example backing the Profits Tax page, in one place — drawn from IRD's DIPNs and from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.). Figures are cross-checked against current law; any outdated textbook figure is corrected and flagged.

利得稅例題以改寫例題展示來源地、資本/收益性質、壞帳、知識產權、虧損及兩級制計算等常見考點。
Sources & attribution Two kinds of source, labelled inline on every illustration. DIPN/SOIPN examples are paraphrased from IRD's own published notes — never reproduced verbatim; each links to the DIPN Index, where the Official column points to IRD's authoritative PDF. Textbook examples are adapted from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.), a professional qualification manual: the fact patterns are restated in our own words, the numbers are independently recomputed against current law, and where the book's figure is now stale it is shown alongside the corrected one. No textbook text is reproduced. These are study notes — see the licence: readable and linkable, not licensed for redistribution.

A. From IRD DIPNs

Illustration — Lease premium: Profits Tax vs Property Tax interaction DIPN 4

Company H grants a 6-year lease of its property for a premium of $1,200,000, paid up front. As a person carrying on a property-dealing/letting business, the premium is a revenue receipt taxable under Profits Tax — s.15C spreads it evenly over the lease term, so 1/6 = $200,000 is assessed each year for 6 years. Separately, s.5B(4) deems the premium payable in equal monthly instalments for Property Tax purposes but capped at 3 years, so 1/3 = $400,000 is assessed for Property Tax in each of Years 1–3 only.

YearProperty Tax paid
($400,000 × 80% × 16%)		Profits Tax
($200,000 × 17.5%)		Net position
1–3 (each)$51,200$35,000Refund of $16,200 (Property Tax set off against Profits Tax under s.25)
4–6 (each)—$35,000$35,000 payable

Grand total tax over 6 years = $210,000, i.e. exactly 17.5% of the $1,200,000 premium (the historical standard rate used in the DIPN's example year) — the set-off mechanism ensures the premium is not taxed twice under both heads.

Illustration — Interest deduction restricted by a tax-free secured deposit DIPN 13A

Taxpayer F borrows $1,000,000 at 5% interest, secured by a $1,000,000 deposit earning tax-exempt interest at 4%. Because the loan is secured on a deposit generating tax-free income, s.16(2A)/(2B) restrict the deduction: the $40,000 tax-free interest earned reduces the otherwise-deductible $50,000 loan interest, leaving only $10,000 deductible.

Illustration — Service company "Type II" management fee cap DIPN 24

A professional firm pays $4,000,000 in management fees to a related service company whose actual attributable cost of providing those services is $3,000,000. The deduction is capped at cost plus a 12.5% mark-up: $3,000,000 × 112.5% = $3,375,000. The $625,000 excess is added back, increasing assessable profits from $1,000,000 (per accounts) to $1,625,000.

Illustration — Foreign tax deductible only where no DTA credit is available DIPN 28

Bank-HK pays income tax on interest income in Jurisdiction F. If Hong Kong has no double tax agreement with Jurisdiction F, the foreign tax is deductible under s.16(1)(c). If Hong Kong does have a DTA with Jurisdiction F, s.16(2J) denies the deduction — Bank-HK must instead claim a tax credit under s.50, since double relief (deduction plus credit) is not permitted.

Illustration — Hong Kong bank deposit interest exemption straddling the exemption date DIPN 34

A taxpayer has $10,000,000 trading profits plus $4,000,000 of local bank deposit interest, of which $1,000,000 accrued before 22 June 1998 (the exemption's effective date) and $3,000,000 accrued after. Only the pre-exemption $1,000,000 is taxable; total 1998/99 assessable profits = $11,000,000 rather than $14,000,000.

Illustration — Prepaid expenses follow accounting treatment, not cash timing DIPN 40, following CIR v Secan

Following the Secan case, a full cash prepayment (e.g. 3 years' rent or insurance paid up front) is no longer deductible in full in the year of payment if the applicable accounting standard requires it to be amortised over the period it relates to — the tax deduction now follows the accounting/matching treatment, reversing the Department's older cash-basis practice.

B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim; every figure has been checked against current Hong Kong tax law and corrected where the textbook is outdated (noted per illustration).

Illustration — Basis period on commencement: first accounts cover 18 months Module 9, Ch.3 §3.9.2 — s.18C(1)(b)

A company commences business on 1 July 2018 and adopts a 31 December accounting date, but its first set of accounts is not closed until 31 December 2019 — an 18-month period. Adjusted profits: $90,000 for the 18 months to 31 Dec 2019, then $68,000 for the 12 months to 31 Dec 2020.

Where the first accounting period exceeds 12 months, s.18C(1)(b) gives the Commissioner discretion to take the second year of assessment as the 12 months counted back from the end of the first accounting period, with the commencement year taking the remaining stub — both by time-apportioning the 18-month profit.

Year of assessmentBasis periodAssessable profitsBasis
Commencement year1/7/2018 – 31/12/2018 (6 mo.)$30,000 (= $90,000 × 6/18)s.18C(1)(b)
Following year1/1/2019 – 31/12/2019 (12 mo.)$60,000 (= $90,000 × 12/18)s.18B(2)
Third year1/1/2020 – 31/12/2020 (12 mo.)$68,000s.18B(2)

Check: $30,000 + $60,000 = $90,000 — the full 18-month profit is accounted for exactly once. No tax rate is involved in this mechanic, so no currency correction was needed.

Illustration — Retirement scheme contribution cap (s.17(1)(h)) Module 9, Ch.3 §3.5.4

An employee earns an annual salary of $100,000. The employer makes an ordinary annual contribution to a recognised retirement scheme equal to 20% of salary, i.e. $20,000.

s.17(1)(h) disallows the deduction of ordinary retirement-scheme contributions to the extent they exceed 15% of the employee's total emoluments: cap = 15% × $100,000 = $15,000 deductible; the remaining $5,000 is non-deductible.

The 15% cap is unchanged in current law — no correction needed.

Illustration — Loss relief: carry-forward vs. surrender on change of trade Module 9, Ch.3 §3.11 — s.19C

Part A — corporation, multi-year carry-forward: a company realises losses of $25M (2016/17) and $75M (2017/18), giving $100M carried forward. It then realises a profit of $80M in 2018/19.

Accumulated losses available$100,000,000
Less: set off against 2018/19 profit($80,000,000)
Assessable profit after set-offNil
Unrelieved loss carried forward$20,000,000

Part B — sole proprietor, same trade vs. changed trade: a sole proprietor has an unrelieved loss of $1,000,000 brought forward from a wine-distribution trade.

ScenarioResult
Continues the same wine trade, earning $1,200,000 in the current year$1,200,000 − $1,000,000 loss b/f = $200,000 taxable
Ceases the wine trade and starts an unrelated fruit-trading business, earning $500,000Loss is tied to the ceased trade and is surrendered — full $500,000 taxable, no relief

Losses only carry forward against future profits of the same source (s.19C) — changing to an unrelated trade forfeits the loss. No tax rate is involved in either part, so no correction was needed.

Illustration — Secured loan test: interest deduction restricted by a tax-free deposit Module 9, Ch.3 §3.5.3.8 — s.16(2A), adapted from DIPN 13A

A taxpayer borrows $1,000,000 from a bank at 5% p.a. ($50,000 interest) for general business use, secured by an overseas deposit earning tax-free interest. The allowable deduction depends on how the security is structured:

CaseSecurityTax-free interest earnedDeduction reduced byInterest allowed
1Deposit $1,000,000 only$40,000$40,000 (full match)$10,000
2Deposit $500,000 + shares $500,000$20,000 (deposit only)$20,000 (shares ignored — not a deposit)$30,000
3Deposit $2,000,000 (exceeds loan)$80,000Pro-rated: $1,000,000/$2,000,000 × $80,000 = $40,000$10,000
4Deposit $1,000,000 + shares $500,000$40,000 (deposit only)Pro-rated by security mix: $1,000,000/$1,500,000 × $40,000 = $26,667$23,333

Only deposits/loans generating tax-free interest trigger this restriction — other security (shares, property, guarantees) is ignored for this test. No profits tax rate is involved, so no correction was needed.

Illustration — Interest flow-back test: debenture interest paid to an untaxed associate Module 9, Ch.3 §3.5.3.8 — s.16(2C), adapted from DIPN 13A

A Hong Kong company issues $10,000,000 of debentures to fund its HK trading business, paying $1,000,000 total interest for the year. $8,000,000 of the debentures is held all year by its overseas subsidiary, an associate not taxed in Hong Kong on the interest it receives.

Proportion held by the untaxed associate$8,000,000 / $10,000,000 = 8/10
Interest disallowed (flows back untaxed)$1,000,000 × 8/10 = $800,000
Allowable interest deduction$200,000

If the associate held the debentures for only 6 of the 12 months, the disallowance is further time-apportioned: $800,000 × 6/12 = $400,000 disallowed instead.

Exception: no restriction applies if the associate is a market maker holding the debentures in the ordinary course of its business (s.16(2G)). No profits tax rate is involved, so no correction was needed.

Note A plant & machinery pooling illustration and a full two-tier-rate computation exercise were also reviewed from this chapter but are presented on the Depreciation & Allowances illustrations page instead, where they fit topically.

Individual — Salaries Tax

Salaries Tax — Worked Illustrations

Every worked example backing the Salaries Tax page — drawn from IRD's DIPNs and from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.). Figures are cross-checked against current YA 2026/27 allowances/rates; any outdated textbook figure is corrected and flagged.

薪俸稅例題以服務地點、僱傭關係、福利、股份獎勵及個人入息課稅情境強化考試判斷。
Sources & attribution Two kinds of source, labelled inline on every illustration. DIPN/SOIPN examples are paraphrased from IRD's own published notes — never reproduced verbatim; each links to the DIPN Index, where the Official column points to IRD's authoritative PDF. Textbook examples are adapted from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.), a professional qualification manual: the fact patterns are restated in our own words, the numbers are independently recomputed against current law, and where the book's figure is now stale it is shown alongside the corrected one. No textbook text is reproduced. These are study notes — see the licence: readable and linkable, not licensed for redistribution.

A. From IRD DIPNs

Illustration — Joint assessment saves tax vs separate taxation DIPN 18

Mr A earns $680,000, Mrs A earns $100,000. Taxed separately, their combined liability is $23,030. Electing joint assessment under s.10(2) — pooling income and allowances — reduces the combined liability to $17,505, because Mrs A's unabsorbed allowances/deductions offset Mr A's higher-rate income.

Illustration — Home loan interest apportionment by ownership type DIPN 35

Mr C is sole owner, pays $120,000 interest — allowable deduction capped at $100,000. Mr & Mrs D are joint tenants, pay $100,000 total interest between them — each gets $50,000. Mr E (1/4 share) and Mr F (3/4 share) are tenants in common on a $100,000 interest bill — Mr E gets $25,000, Mr F gets $75,000 (apportioned strictly by ownership share, not by who actually paid).

Illustration — VHIS premium cap applied per insured person DIPN 56

Mr J pays VHIS premiums for himself ($5,000), spouse ($4,000), grandmother ($16,000), father ($12,000), mother ($11,000), son ($3,000) — total $51,000 paid. Because the cap is HKD 8,000 per insured person, the grandmother/father/mother claims are each capped at $8,000: allowable deduction = $5,000 + $4,000 + ($8,000 × 3) + $3,000 = $36,000. The $15,000 excess simply lapses — no carry-forward.

Illustration — Charitable donation cap at 35% of reduced assessable income DIPN 37

Mr A has salary $500,000, deductible expenses $10,000 (reduced assessable income $490,000), and made donations of $210,000. Since $210,000 exceeds 35% of $490,000, the deduction is capped at $490,000 × 35% = $171,500 — the remaining $38,500 of donations gives no further tax benefit.

Illustration — Share option gain apportioned by vesting days in Hong Kong DIPN 38

An employee's share option has a 730-day vesting period, of which 292 days were spent working in Hong Kong. At exercise, only 292/730 = 40% of the gain is assessable to Hong Kong salaries tax — the remainder relates to non-Hong Kong employment and falls outside the charge.

B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim; every allowance/rate figure has been checked against current Hong Kong tax law and corrected where the textbook was using a stale amount (noted per illustration).

Illustration — The 60-day rule: two early departures tip the count over the line Module 9, Ch.4 §4.1 — s.8(1B)

An employee holds a Hong Kong employment contract but works full-time in Mainland China, returning to Hong Kong only periodically. His visits (quarterly meetings plus connecting travel) total 59 "ordinary" days for the year. On two occasions, however, he leaves Hong Kong very early in the morning to connect onward (once via Osaka, once via London) rather than flying straight back to China. Under the counting convention, both the day of arrival and the day of departure count as a full day each — even for a same-day transit.

Days in HK from ordinary visits59
Extra day — early departure via Osaka+1
Extra day — early departure via London+1
Total days in Hong Kong61

61 > 60, so the s.8(1B) exemption fails entirely — his full Hong Kong-employment income becomes chargeable, even though he worked in China almost all year. It's a hard cliff-edge test on days present, not days worked, and transit days count in full. No allowance/rate figures involved, so no correction was needed.

Illustration — Rent-free housing benefit: the "rental value" method Module 9, Ch.4 §4.2 — s.9(2)

An employee on a $600,000 salary gets a company-leased apartment rent-free; the employer also reimburses $16,800 of medical insurance (a taxable perquisite). Rental value = 10% of (salary + taxable perquisites) for a self-contained flat/house.

Salary + taxable perquisite$616,800
Rental value (10% × $616,800)$61,680

Contrast — two staff sharing one room in a company flat (boarding-house-type arrangement, not a self-contained flat) use the lower 4% rate instead of 10%:

EmployeeIncomeRental value (4%)
Staff A$150,000$6,000
Staff B$120,000$4,800

Rate scale (s.9(2)): flat/house = 10% of net employment income; hotel/hostel/boarding-house of ≤2 rooms = 8%; ≤1 room / shared-room = 4%. These percentages sit in the Ordinance itself (not an annually-adjusted allowance) — no update needed, but worth a one-line confirmation against IRD's current housing-benefit guide before relying on it for a filing.

Illustration — Share option gain: OMV at exercise, less strike price and option cost Module 9, Ch.4 §4.3 — s.9(1)(d)/(4)

An employee is granted an option (by virtue of employment) to buy 5,000 shares at a strike price of $12/share, paying $6,000 for the option itself. Open market value (OMV) at grant was $24/share; two years later he exercises when OMV has risen to $30/share.

OMV at exercise (5,000 × $30)$150,000
Less: consideration paid on exercise (5,000 × $12)($60,000)
Less: cost of the option itself($6,000)
Chargeable gain, assessed in year of exercise$84,000

The gain is taxed at exercise, not at eventual sale — any share-price movement after exercise is a capital (non-taxable) matter. No allowance/rate figures involved, so no correction was needed.

Illustration — Termination gratuity "related back" over a 36-month window Module 9, Ch.4 §4.6 — s.11D(b)(i)

An employee made redundant after 7 years 11 months of service receives a $140,400 contract-end gratuity and elects to have it "related back" under s.11D(b)(i). Because total service exceeded 3 years, the law spreads the gratuity evenly over the 36 months ending on the earlier of the payment date or last day of employment — not over the full 7-year service period.

Year of assessmentMonths in the 36-month windowGratuity allocated
Year 1 (partial)8$31,200
Year 212$46,800
Year 312$46,800
Year 4 (partial)4$15,600
Total36$140,400

Contrast: for service of 3 years or less, the gratuity spreads only over the actual contract/service period, not artificially capped at 36 months. Pure time-apportionment mechanic — no correction needed.

Illustration — Child allowance depends on "full-time education," not just age Module 9, Ch.4 §4.9 — s.31

Twins both turn 19 partway through a year and finish secondary school that same year — the allowance still applies for that year since both were in full-time education for part of it (age >18 doesn't disqualify a student). The following year, one twin enrols in a full-time vocational diploma (still qualifies); the other instead starts a technician apprenticeship structured as an employment contract — drawing a wage as an employee rather than being a student — which fails the "full-time education" condition.

YearChildren qualifyingChild allowance claimable (YA 2026/27: $140,000/child; D26 exam basis YA 2025/26: $130,000)
Year twins turn 19Both twins2 × $140,000 = $280,000
Following yearDiploma student only1 × $140,000 = $140,000

Original book figure used $100,000/child (correct for YA 2018/19, now stale); updated above to the current YA 2026/27 rate of $140,000/child. Mechanic: no age cap while a child remains in full-time education; a paid apprenticeship/employment contract breaks eligibility even though the person is still "training." Watch: the 2026 Policy Address (16 Sep 2026) proposes HKD 160,000 for a second or subsequent child born on or after 16 September 2026 — twins born years earlier stay at HKD 140,000, so this illustration is unaffected even once the amendment ordinance passes.

Illustration — Full computation: salary, housing benefit, share option gain, deductions, allowances, tax payable Module 9, Ch.4 §4.11 — the "master" illustration

A bank compliance director receives salary $1,500,000, bonus $200,000, a rent-free company flat (taxed via the 10% rental-value method), and a gain on exercising vested overseas stock options. He deducts a professional subscription, self-education fees, a charitable donation, and mandatory MPF, and claims the basic and child allowances (married, assessed as an individual).

Salary + bonus$1,700,000
Add: rental value = 10% × (salary+bonus − professional subscription)$169,882
Add: share option exercise gain (FX-converted)$25,476
Assessable income$1,895,358
Less: professional subscription($1,179)
Less: self-education expenses($77,100)
Net assessable income$1,817,079
Less: approved charitable donation($50,000)
Less: mandatory MPF contribution (capped)($18,000)
Net income$1,749,079
Less: basic allowance (YA 2026/27; D26 exam: $132,000)($145,000)
Less: child allowance × 1 (YA 2026/27; D26 exam: $130,000)($140,000)
Net chargeable income$1,464,079
Tax at progressive rates vs. standard rate — pay the lower
Progressive rates on $1,464,079 net chargeable income (2%/6%/10%/14% on the first four $50,000 bands, 17% on the $1,264,079 remainder)$230,893
Standard rate: 15% × $1,749,079 net income (well under the $5,000,000 cap)$262,362
Tax payable = lower of the two$230,893

Original book figures used a basic allowance of $132,000 (YA 2019/20 rate) and child allowance of $120,000 — both stale; updated above to the current YA 2026/27 rates of $145,000 and $140,000, which cascades through to a different net chargeable income and tax payable than the book's original answer. Note: a one-off percentage tax reduction (capped at a fixed HKD amount) is announced in most Budgets and would further reduce this figure for the specific year being computed — check the current year's Budget measure before treating $230,893 as the final "net tax payable" (see the one-off relief callout on the main Salaries Tax page).

C. Personal Assessment — from Module 9 (Textbook)

Personal Assessment (§6 of the main page) aggregates salaries, property, and unincorporated-business income into one computation. These three illustrations, adapted from Module 9's running "Chan/Lip family" case study, are recomputed against current allowances/rate bands throughout.

Illustration — Should a sole proprietor with rental property elect Personal Assessment? Module 9, Ch.6 §6.3 — s.41

A taxpayer runs a sole-proprietorship business (profit $800,000, of which he donates $400,000 to charity) and separately owns a rental property (rental income $400,000), while paying $400,000 mortgage interest on his own home. Without election, profits tax and property tax are assessed separately with no relief for the home loan interest at all, and the charitable donation is capped at 35% of the business profit alone.

ItemWithout electionWith Personal Assessment
Business profit, after donation capped at 35% of $800,000 ($280,000 used, $120,000 of the $400,000 paid gets no relief)Profits tax @15% on $520,000 = $78,000Combined income $840,000, less a recomputed donation ceiling (35% of grossed-up income — $112,000 more becomes usable), less home loan interest (capped at $100,000/yr), less married allowance ($290,000) → net chargeable income $338,000 → tax at progressive rates = $39,460
Rental property, NAV after 20% allowanceProperty tax @15% on $320,000 = $48,000
Total$126,000
Tax saved by electing$86,540

Original book figures used the 2017/18 married allowance ($264,000) and old 4-band rates; updated above to current allowances/bands. Key trap: under Personal Assessment, the charitable donation ceiling is recomputed as 35% of the grossed-up combined income, not simply 35% of the post-donation business profit — this typically unlocks extra donation relief. Home loan interest also becomes claimable for the first time once there is a combined computation to set it against, even though the taxpayer has no salaries income. Figures exclude any one-off Budget tax reduction for the specific year being computed — check the current year's measure before treating either total as final.

Illustration — Married couple, joint election: salaries + property + business + partnership loss Module 9, Ch.6 §6.4 — s.41(1A)

Husband has salaries income $520,000 plus a $120,000 share of a partnership loss. Wife owns a rental property (NAV $192,000, mortgage interest ≥ $192,000) and runs a business (net profit $400,000 after an approved donation already used at business level). One 15-year-old child.

Husband's income − partnership loss share$520,000 − $120,000 = $400,000
Wife's income − mortgage interest (capped at NAV) − extra donation relief$692,000 − $192,000 − $160,000 = $340,000
Combined reduced total income$740,000
Less: married allowance (current rate)($290,000)
Less: child allowance × 1 (current rate)($140,000)
Net chargeable income$310,000
Tax at progressive rates$34,700

Tax is then apportioned back to each spouse in proportion to their own net contribution to the combined income: husband $400,000/$740,000 × $34,700 ≈ $18,757; wife $340,000/$740,000 × $34,700 ≈ $15,943.

Original book figures used the 2017/18 married allowance ($264,000) and child allowance ($100,000); updated above to current rates ($290,000 / $140,000). Mechanic: aggregating income across both spouses, capping loan interest at the property's own NAV (not the higher amount actually paid), and apportioning the joint tax bill back to each spouse by their share of net income — not a 50/50 split.

Illustration — Dependent parent allowance, elderly care deduction, and a business loss driving one spouse's share to zero Module 9, Ch.6 §6.5 — ss.26D, 31

Husband has employment income (incl. a share option gain), pays for his elderly mother's support (not living with him) and his elderly father's residential care home fees. Wife has no employment, runs a business at a loss for the year, and owns a rental property with mortgage interest exceeding its NAV.

Husband's net assessable income + Wife's NAV$1,368,000 + $105,600 = $1,473,600
Less: mortgage interest (capped at wife's NAV)($105,600)
Less: approved donation, MPF (capped)($10,000 + $18,000)
Less: elderly residential care expenses (current cap $120,000/parent)($120,000)
Less: wife's business loss for the year($450,000)
Reduced total income$770,000
Less: married allowance (current rate)($290,000)
Less: dependent parent allowance (60+, not co-residing — current rate)($55,000)
Net chargeable income$425,000
Tax at progressive rates$54,250

Original book figures used 2017/18 rates throughout (married allowance $264,000, dependent parent allowance $46,000, elderly care cap $92,000); all updated above to current rates. Because the wife's own income is more than wiped out by her mortgage interest, donation, and business loss, her apportioned share of the joint tax floors at nil — the husband bears the entire $54,250. Note the dependent parent allowance (mother, not co-residing) and the elderly care deduction (father, in a care home) apply to different dependants — you cannot double-claim both reliefs for the same parent, but can use different reliefs for different parents in the same year.

Figures to re-verify before publishing The elderly residential care expenses cap and any one-off percentage tax reduction (with its HKD cap) are announced fresh in most annual Budgets — confirm both against the current year's Budget measure before treating any "final tax payable" figure above as authoritative. The MPF mandatory-contribution cap ($18,000) and 35%-of-income donation ceiling are carried through from established practice; a quick check against current IRD guidance is still worthwhile before publishing.

Business — Property Tax

Property Tax — Worked Illustrations

Every worked example backing the Property Tax page — drawn from IRD's DIPNs and from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.). The 15% standard rate and 20% statutory allowance are unchanged in current law, so these textbook figures needed no correction.

物業稅例題用租金、差餉、租客代付開支、不可收回租金及公司持有物業情境練習 NAV 計算。
Sources & attribution Two kinds of source, labelled inline on every illustration. DIPN/SOIPN examples are paraphrased from IRD's own published notes — never reproduced verbatim; each links to the DIPN Index, where the Official column points to IRD's authoritative PDF. Textbook examples are adapted from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.), a professional qualification manual: the fact patterns are restated in our own words, the numbers are independently recomputed against current law, and where the book's figure is now stale it is shown alongside the corrected one. No textbook text is reproduced. These are study notes — see the licence: readable and linkable, not licensed for redistribution.

A. From IRD DIPNs

Illustration — Premium spread over the statutory 3-year cap DIPN 14

A $60,000 premium is paid for a 5-year lease running from 1 June 2006 to 31 May 2011 (60 months). Because s.5B(4) caps the spreading period at 3 years (36 months) even though the lease itself runs 5 years, the premium is spread over 36 months only:

Year of assessmentMonths falling in yearAssessable value included
2006/0710 of 36$16,667
2007/0812 of 36$20,000
2008/0912 of 36$20,000
2009/102 of 36$3,333

Nothing is assessed for 2010/11 or 2011/12 even though the lease itself continues — the 3-year statutory cap has already fully absorbed the premium.

Illustration — Net assessable value computation chain DIPN 14

The DIPN sets out the standard computation chain: Consideration receivable, plus rent recovered previously written off, less irrecoverable rent, gives Assessable Value; deduct rates paid by the owner (if any); deduct the flat 20% statutory allowance on the balance, to arrive at Net Assessable Value — the figure to which the 15% standard rate is applied.

Illustration — Premium taxed twice under two different spreading rules DIPN 4 (see also Profits Tax page)

Where the property owner is also carrying on a property-dealing/letting trade, the same premium is spread differently for the two taxes: over the full lease term (no cap) for Profits Tax purposes as a trading receipt, but capped at 3 years for Property Tax purposes under s.5B(4). The s.25 set-off then reconciles the two — see the full worked example on the Profits Tax illustrations page.

B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual, following its running "Tong family" case study. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim. The 15% standard rate and 20% statutory allowance used throughout already match current law — no correction was needed for this topic.

Illustration — Premium spreading: lease term shorter than, equal to, and longer than the 3-year cap Module 9, Ch.5 §5.2 — s.5B(3)/(4)

Three properties are let on different lease terms, each with a lump-sum premium spread evenly over the lease period or 3 years, whichever is shorter:

PropertyLease termPremiumSpreading
A5 years (60 months)$360,000Capped at 36 months → $10,000/month for 3 years, then nil for the remaining 2 years
B3 years (36 months, exactly)$240,000Full term used (36 = cap) → $6,667/month throughout
C2 years (24 months)$144,000No cap needed → $6,000/month throughout

Property A shows the cap actually biting: the $360,000 premium is fully exhausted at month 36, and nothing further is assessed for the lease's remaining 24 months even though the tenancy continues.

Illustration — Full net assessable value computation, three properties Module 9, Ch.5 §5.3 — DIPN 14 template

Three commonly-tested variations on the NAV computation chain (all at the current 15%/20% rates):

Property A (jointly owned)Property BProperty C
Rent for the year$600,000$240,000$120,000
Add: premium instalment$80,000$80,000$60,000
Add: other consideration (furniture/repairs borne by tenant/rent recovered/management fee, as applicable)—$37,000$14,000
Assessable value$680,000$357,000$194,000
Less: rates paid by owner($16,000)— (tenant pays rates)—
Less: 20% statutory allowance($132,800)($71,400)($38,800)
Net assessable value$531,200$285,600$155,200
Tax @ 15%$79,680 (split 50/50: $39,840 each)$42,840$23,280

Key traps illustrated: (1) rates are only deductible if the owner agreed to bear them — Property B's tenant pays rates, so no deduction; (2) government rent, management fees, mortgage interest, and repair costs actually paid by the owner are never separately deductible — the flat 20% allowance is deemed to cover all of them regardless of actual spend.

Illustration — Irrecoverable rent exceeding the year's own rent, carried back Module 9, Ch.5 §5.4 — s.7C

A 2-year tenancy at $10,000/month runs from 1 July 2016; the tenant stops paying from 1 January 2017 and disappears on 1 May 2017, with the assessor accepting the outstanding rent as bad.

Original YA1 (filed before default known, 9 months' rent)YA2 (year debt confirmed bad)
Rent / assessable value$90,000$10,000
Less: bad debt confirmed irrecoverable (4 months, Jan–Apr)—($40,000)
Result for YA2—($30,000) — a loss

Since the $40,000 bad debt exceeds YA2's own $10,000 rent, the $30,000 excess is carried back under s.7C(3) to amend YA1:

YA1 revised: $90,000 rent − $30,000 carried-back loss$60,000
Less: 20% statutory allowance($12,000)
Revised NAV$48,000
Revised tax @15% ($7,200) vs. originally paid ($10,800)Refund of $3,600

Mere non-payment (without the debt being proved bad) gives no deduction at all — this only applies once the assessor accepts the rent as genuinely irrecoverable.

Illustration — Property tax set off against profits tax for a corporation Module 9, Ch.5 §5.6 — s.25

A company's rental income is already included in its accounts and taxed under profits tax. It did not apply for the s.5(2)(a) upfront exemption, and separately paid $3,000 property tax on the same property.

Profits tax payable for the year$10,000
Less: property tax already paid on the same property($3,000)
Net profits tax payable$7,000

A straight set-off, unaffected by rate levels — if property tax paid had exceeded the profits tax bill, the excess would be refundable instead.

Business — Stamp Duty

Stamp Duty — Worked Illustrations

Every worked example backing the Stamp Duty page — drawn from IRD's SOIPNs and from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.). This is the chapter needing the most correction of any topic: both source books were written before the 2023 AVD Scale 1 reform and/or the 2024 BSD/SSD rate cut, so most of their headline rates are now wrong — corrected figures are shown alongside the originals throughout.

印花稅例題以物業買賣、公司買樓、香港股票轉讓及關聯公司重組練習印花稅分析。
Sources & attribution Two kinds of source, labelled inline on every illustration. DIPN/SOIPN examples are paraphrased from IRD's own published notes — never reproduced verbatim; each links to the DIPN Index, where the Official column points to IRD's authoritative PDF. Textbook examples are adapted from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.), a professional qualification manual: the fact patterns are restated in our own words, the numbers are independently recomputed against current law, and where the book's figure is now stale it is shown alongside the corrected one. No textbook text is reproduced. These are study notes — see the licence: readable and linkable, not licensed for redistribution.

A. From SOIPNs

Illustration — Provisional vs formal agreement timing SOIPN 1

Provisional agreement signed 1 March 2014, formal agreement signed 8 March 2014 (within 14 days) → only the formal agreement needs stamping, by 7 April 2014; the provisional agreement is duty-free. If the formal agreement instead follows more than 14 days later (e.g. 17 March), the provisional agreement itself becomes chargeable at full AVD by 31 March 2014, and the formal agreement is separately chargeable at a fixed $100 by 16 April 2014.

Illustration — AVD on a multi-asset instrument (residential + car parks) SOIPN 8, historical figures — pre-2023 flat-15% Scale 1

An HKPR buyer purchases a $13,000,000 residential property plus two car parking spaces worth $2,000,000 in one instrument. Scale 2 (3.75% at that value band) applies to the residential portion: $487,500. The car parks (non-residential, Scale 3) at the equivalent band: $150,000. Total AVD = $637,500. Historically (SOIPN 8, Nov 2018), a non-HKPR buyer paid a flat 15% Scale 1 on the residential portion instead: $1,950,000 + $150,000 = $2,100,000 — but Scale 1 is no longer flat; see illustration B1 below for how the same fact pattern is taxed today.

Illustration — Current graduated Scale 1 vs. Scale 2 Corrected from Cap. 117 First Schedule, post-2026 amendment

Same $13,000,000 residential property, non-HKPR (or corporate) buyer, no Scale 2 concession available: Scale 1 is graduated exactly like Scale 2 at this value band (3.75%), giving the same $487,500 — not a flat-15% $1,950,000. The two scales only diverge for a single residential property with consideration above $100,000,000: at $150,000,000, Scale 2 (HKPR sole property) still applies its 4.25% top rate = $6,375,000, while Scale 1 hits the new 6.5% flat band = $9,750,000 — a HKD 3.375 million difference driven entirely by the 2026 amendment's new top bands.

Illustration — SSD tiered by holding period SOIPN 5

Under the (now 0%-rated but still operative) post-27-Oct-2012 regime: a $3,000,000 residential property resold within 6 months would attract SSD at 20% ($600,000); resold within 6–12 months, 15% ($450,000); a $4,000,000 property resold within 12–36 months, 10% ($400,000). At the current 0% rate none of this is actually payable, but the tiering logic remains the statutory mechanism.

Illustration — BSD ignores which joint owner actually paid SOIPN 7

A Hong Kong permanent resident buys a $4,000,000 residential property jointly with an unrelated non-HKPR co-buyer. Because one joint owner is a non-HKPR and the two are not close relatives, BSD (at the applicable rate) applies to the full $4,000,000 value — it is not pro-rated to only the non-HKPR's share.

B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim. This textbook predates the 2023 Scale 1 reform and the Feb 2024 BSD/SSD rate cut — every AVD/BSD/SSD figure below has been recomputed against current (2026) law, with the book's original figure shown for contrast.

Illustration B1 — AVD on residential + non-residential property in one purchase Module 9, Ch.7 §7.4

A Hong Kong company (never a HKPR) buys two properties on the same day: a commercial warehouse for $25,000,000, and a residential flat for $20,000,000 (consideration assumed to equal market value in both cases).

PropertyScaleBook figure (flat 15% on residential)Current law (graduated)
Warehouse (non-residential)Scale 3, 4.25% band$1,062,500$1,062,500 (unchanged)
Residential flatScale 1, "$6.72M–$20M" band, 3.75%$3,000,000 (flat 15%)$750,000

Original book figure used $3,000,000 (flat 15% Scale 1, the 2016–2023 rule); current law figure is $750,000 — a 75% reduction. The flat-15% Scale 1 was replaced by the same graduated table Scale 2 uses back in 2023; the 2026 amendment only adds new top bands above $100,000,000, irrelevant to a $20M deal.

Illustration B2 — Full AVD + SSD + BSD stack on a quick resale to a non-HKPR buyer Module 9, Ch.7 §7.6 — ss.24, 27

A residential flat is bought on 1 March 2018 and sold on 1 March 2019 (12 months + 1 day later) to a Mainland Chinese buyer who resides in HK ~183 days/year but holds no HK permanent ID — so he is not a HKPR for stamp duty purposes despite the residence. The stated price is $2,000,000 "subject to" an existing $5,000,000 mortgage, but market value at the (earlier, binding) contract date was $8,000,000. Because the transfer is at an undervalue and the debt is assumed, s.24 and s.27 deem the full $8,000,000 market value as the stampable amount for all three duties — that valuation mechanic is unaffected by any rate change.

DutyBook figureCurrent law (2026)Why
AVD$1,200,000 (flat 15%)$300,000 (3.75% graduated)Flat-15% Scale 1 superseded 2023
SSD (holding >12mo, ≤36mo tier)$800,000 (10% tier)$0SSD rate cut to 0% from 28 Feb 2024 (tier logic itself unchanged)
BSD$1,200,000 (flat 15%)$0BSD rate cut to 0% from 28 Feb 2024
Fixed duty on assignment$100$100 (unchanged)—
Total$3,200,100$300,100Over 90% lower today

Residence alone (183 days/year) does not confer HKPR status — the buyer here is a non-HKPR by ID/citizenship regardless of how much time he spends in Hong Kong.

Illustration B3 — Gift between close relatives: Scale 2 applies regardless of the recipient's residency Module 9, Ch.7 §7.6 — s.27, s.29AJ

A father gifts a residential flat (market value $10,000,000) to his son, a Canadian citizen with no HK permanent ID. Nil consideration is disregarded as a voluntary disposition — full market value is used. Because the transfer is between close relatives (parent–child), Scale 2 applies regardless of the son's residency status, and both BSD and SSD are exempt on the same close-relative basis.

AVD, Scale 2, "$6.72M–$20M" band, 3.75%$375,000
SSDExempt (close relative)
BSDExempt (close relative)

No correction needed — Scale 2 rates were not touched by the 2026 amendment, so the book's $375,000 figure is still correct today. Included deliberately as a contrast case: not every textbook figure in this chapter is wrong.

Illustration B4 — Hong Kong share transfer with failed group relief Module 9, Ch.7 §7.2 — s.45

A Hong Kong holding company transfers a 10% stake in an HKSE-listed (but overseas-incorporated) company to its 80%-owned subsidiary for $400,000, though market value is $500,000. Because the shares are HKSE-listed, they are Hong Kong stock for stamp duty purposes regardless of the issuer's place of incorporation. Group relief under s.45 fails — the parent only owns 80% of the subsidiary (below the 90% threshold), and an individual co-owner's personal stake cannot count toward that 90% test. The transfer at an undervalue is a voluntary disposition, so duty is charged on the higher $500,000 market value.

Stamp duty: $500,000 × 0.2%$1,000
Plus: fixed duty on the instrument of transfer$5

No correction needed — the 0.2% rate (0.1% buyer / 0.1% seller) matches current law exactly. Flag: elsewhere in the same textbook chapter, a rate of 0.26% is quoted — that was only correct for the temporary uplift period 1 Aug 2021–16 Nov 2023 and is now obsolete; 0.2% (as used in this illustration) is the figure to rely on.

Illustration B5 — Lease duty by term band (constructed — the textbook gives only the rate table, no worked figures) Module 9, Ch.7 §7.5, rate table only

A 5-year shop lease at $50,000/month rent, no premium. Term exceeds 3 years, so the 1% rate applies to average yearly rent.

Average yearly rent ($50,000 × 12)$600,000
Lease duty (1% of average yearly rent)$6,000

Rate bands (unchanged, current): 0.25% (≤1yr/undefined), 0.5% (1–3yr), 1% (>3yr) of average annual rent. If the lease is first executed as an "agreement for lease," that instrument bears this duty; a later formal lease on the same terms bears only a nominal $3 fixed duty.

Bottom line for this chapter Every AVD/BSD/SSD figure quoted in older study material — this textbook included — should be treated as showing the mechanic (which band, which test, which exemption) correctly, but the rate itself needs a fresh check against the Stamp Duty page's corrected tables before use in any real computation.

Common — Depreciation & Allowances

Depreciation & Allowances — Worked Illustrations

Every worked example backing the Depreciation & Allowances page — drawn from IRD's DIPNs and from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.). The 60% initial / 10%-20%-30% annual plant & machinery rates are unchanged in current law, so this topic needed no rate corrections.

折舊及免稅額例題透過池制、出售資產、商業建築物、翻新及指定固定資產練習折舊免稅額。
Sources & attribution Two kinds of source, labelled inline on every illustration. DIPN/SOIPN examples are paraphrased from IRD's own published notes — never reproduced verbatim; each links to the DIPN Index, where the Official column points to IRD's authoritative PDF. Textbook examples are adapted from Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.), a professional qualification manual: the fact patterns are restated in our own words, the numbers are independently recomputed against current law, and where the book's figure is now stale it is shown alongside the corrected one. A. From IRD DIPNs

Illustration — Industrial building sale: buyer/seller allowance split DIPN 2

A factory is built for $500,000 in February 1992. Initial allowance 20% = $100,000; annual allowance 4% = $20,000 in the first year, continuing for 3 more years, leaving a residue of expenditure of $320,000. The building is then sold for $420,000. The seller faces a balancing charge of $100,000 (sale price exceeds residue by $100,000, capped at allowances previously granted). The buyer's future annual allowance is recalculated as 1/21 (years remaining to the 25th year) × $420,000 = $20,000/year.

Illustration — Plant & machinery pooling across two rate classes DIPN 7

A taxpayer buys a motor car for $150,000 and 3 cookers for $50,000 (both 30% pool), plus office furniture for $20,000 and air-conditioning for $28,000 (both 20% pool). Year 1: 30% pool — cost $200,000, initial allowance 60% = $120,000, annual allowance on the remaining $80,000 at 30% = $24,000. 20% pool — similar mechanics give a smaller annual allowance. Total first-year depreciation allowance across both pools: $176,640.

Illustration — Balancing charge capped at allowances previously granted DIPN 7

On cessation of a business, a 30% pool with a reducing value brought forward of $21,000 (original cost $75,000) is sold for $80,000. Although sale proceeds ($80,000) exceed the reducing value ($21,000) by $59,000, the balancing charge is capped at $54,000 — the total allowances previously granted ($75,000 cost − $21,000 residue) — never more than was originally allowed.

Illustration — Accelerating pre-2018/19 environmental instalments to 100% DIPN 5

Company-HK pays $15M, $20M and $30M in May 2016/2017/2018 respectively for environmental protection installations, under the pre-2018/19 5-instalment (20%/year) regime. Electing under s.16I(3A) to accelerate all remaining instalments to 100% in 2018/19 gives total cumulative deductions of $3,000,000 (2016/17) + $7,000,000 (2017/18) + $55,000,000 combined by 2018/19 (remaining instalments on the first two payments, plus 100% of the third).

Illustration — Specified IP Right deduction spread to match remaining protection DIPN 49

A copyright costing $400,000 has protection expiring in YA2022/23. Rather than the standard 5 equal instalments, the deduction is compressed into the 4 years actually remaining: $100,000/year for YA2019/20–2022/23.

B. From Module 9: Principles of Taxation (4th ed.)

Adapted from a professional taxation qualification manual. Facts are paraphrased, not reproduced verbatim. The plant & machinery pooling rates (60% initial; 10%/20%/30% annual) are unchanged in current law — no correction was needed.

Illustration — Plant & machinery pooling across two years, with disposals and additions Module 9, Ch.3 §3.7.1 — adapted from DIPN 7

A business starts trading on 2 February 2018. In its first year it buys a car ($150,000) and 3 electric cookers ($50,000) — both 30% pool — plus office furniture ($20,000) and 2 air-conditioning units ($28,000) — both 20% pool.

Year 1 (YA 2018/19)
30% pool20% pool
Cost$200,000$48,000
Less: initial allowance (60%)($120,000)($28,800)
Less: annual allowance (30% / 20% of remainder)($24,000)($3,840)
Reducing value carried forward$56,000$15,360

Total Year 1 depreciation allowance across both pools: $120,000 + $28,800 + $24,000 + $3,840 = $176,640.

In Year 2: the car is written off in an accident (insurance + scrap recovery $31,000); a new van is bought for $180,000; a cooker is sold for $3,000 (total 30%-pool disposal proceeds $34,000); an air-conditioning unit is sold for $2,000 and replaced with a new one for $8,000.

Year 2 (YA 2019/20)
30% pool20% pool
Reducing value brought forward$56,000$15,360
Add: new assets$180,000$8,000
Less: initial allowance (60% of new assets)($108,000)($4,800)
Less: disposal proceeds($34,000)($2,000)
Less: annual allowance($28,200)($3,312)
Reducing value carried forward$65,800$13,248

Total Year 2 depreciation allowance: $108,000 + $4,800 + $28,200 + $3,312 = $144,312. Disposal proceeds simply reduce the pool's reducing value — they don't trigger a balancing charge unless they exceed it (see the DIPN 7 illustration above for that scenario). Rates used (60% initial, 30%/20% annual) match current law exactly — no correction needed.

Module 9 Extra Practice Q&A

Additional paraphrased illustrations and exam-style questions based on the HKICPA Module 9 Principles of Taxation textbook, 4th edition. These are study notes, not copied textbook answers. Check the current IRO, SDO, Budget measures, and IRD guidance before using any figure in a filing position.

Module 9 額外練習問答改寫練習庫，按利得稅、薪俸稅、物業稅、個人入息課稅、印花稅及跨境預扣稅分類。

Source and copyright note This section uses the Module 9 textbook as a learning source and rewrites the material into new practice prompts, short answers, and compact computations. It does not reproduce full textbook questions or worked examples.

1. Profits Tax - Trading, Source, Deductions

Illustration PT-1 Badges of trade

Question. A company buys a shop unit with short-term bank finance, renovates it lightly, advertises it for resale within three months, and sells at a gain. Is the gain likely capital or trading?

中文題目：一間公司以短期銀行貸款購入商舖，簡單裝修後三個月內放售並賺取收益。該收益較可能屬資本性質，還是營業買賣收益？

Answer. It is likely trading. Short holding period, financing arranged for quick turnover, resale activity, and commercial organization all point toward an adventure in the nature of trade. The label in board minutes is useful evidence, but the whole fact pattern matters more.

中文答案：較可能屬營業買賣收益。持有期短、以短期融資支持快速轉售、有主動放售行為及商業組織安排，都指向「屬貿易性質的一次性交易」。董事會紀錄的說法有參考價值，但最終仍要整體看事實。

Illustration PT-2 Capital asset disposal

Question. A retailer buys a warehouse for storage, uses it for several years, then sells it after receiving an unsolicited offer. Is the gain automatically taxable because the seller is a business?

中文題目：零售商購入倉庫作儲貨用途，使用數年後因收到買家主動出價而出售。是否因賣方是商業機構，收益便自動須課利得稅？

Answer. No. A business can hold capital assets. If the warehouse was acquired and used as a fixed capital facility rather than trading stock, the gain is more likely capital and outside profits tax, subject to the facts.

中文答案：不是。商業機構也可以持有資本資產。如果倉庫購入及使用目的均屬固定資本設施，而非買賣存貨，出售收益較可能屬資本性質，不屬利得稅課稅範圍；但仍須視乎全部事實。

Illustration PT-3 Source of service income

Question. A Hong Kong company signs contracts in Hong Kong but its staff perform all consultancy fieldwork in Japan. Where should the source analysis focus?

中文題目：香港公司在香港簽約，但員工全部顧問實地工作均在日本進行。判斷利潤來源地時應集中看甚麼？

Answer. Focus on what the taxpayer did to earn the fee and where those profit-producing operations took place. For service income, performance of the services usually carries strong weight; contract signing alone is not always decisive.

中文答案：重點是納稅人做了甚麼來賺取該收入，以及產生利潤的實際操作在何處進行。服務收入通常很重視服務履行地；單靠簽約地點未必具決定性。

Illustration PT-4 Bad debt deduction

Question. A trading debt of HK$90,000 was previously booked as taxable sales income and is later written off as irrecoverable. A separate staff loan of HK$40,000 is also written off. Which write-off is deductible?

中文題目：一筆 HK$90,000 貿易應收款曾計入應課稅銷售收入，後來證實不能收回並撇銷；另有 HK$40,000 員工貸款亦撇銷。哪一項可扣稅？

Answer. The trading debt is deductible because it arose from taxable trading receipts already brought into account. The staff loan is normally not deductible for an ordinary trader because making staff loans is not its money-lending business and the loan principal was not taxable income.

中文答案：貿易壞帳可扣稅，因為它源自已入帳的應課稅營業收入。員工貸款一般不可扣稅，因普通貿易公司並非經營放債業務，而貸款本金亦從未作為應課稅收入入帳。

Question PT-5 Quick MCQ

Question. Which expense is most clearly deductible for profits tax?

中文題目：以下哪項開支最明顯可作利得稅扣除？

A. Private rent of the managing director. B. Capital cost of acquiring a liquor licence. C. Interest on a commercial loan used to buy trading stock, assuming the interest rules are met. D. Cost recovered from an insurer.

Answer. C. The borrowing is for trading stock and can satisfy the production-of-profits test, but interest must still pass the specific interest deduction conditions.

中文答案：C。借款用於購買營業存貨，較能符合「產生應課稅利潤」的要求；但利息仍須通過利息扣除的特定條件。

2. Salaries Tax - Employment Income and Benefits

Question ST-1 Employment vs self-employment

Question. A marketing worker has fixed office hours, uses the company's equipment, reports to a director, and receives a monthly salary plus commission. Salaries tax or profits tax?

中文題目：市場推廣人員有固定辦公時間，使用公司設備，向董事匯報，並收取月薪加佣金。應較可能屬薪俸稅還是利得稅？

Answer. Salaries tax is more likely. Control, integration into the employer's organization, and lack of entrepreneurial risk point to employment rather than an independent profession or business.

中文答案：較可能屬薪俸稅。受僱主控制、融入僱主組織、缺乏自行承擔營商風險，均指向僱傭關係而非獨立專業或業務。

Question ST-2 Contract for services

Question. A consultant serves several clients, rents her own office, hires assistants, bears overheads, and invoices fixed project fees. What tax head is more likely?

中文題目：一名顧問服務多名客戶，自租辦公室、聘請助理、自行承擔營運開支，並按項目收費。較可能屬哪一稅種？

Answer. Profits tax is more likely. She appears to be carrying on a profession or business on her own account rather than holding an employment.

中文答案：較可能屬利得稅。她看似以自己名義經營專業或業務，而非受僱於單一僱主。

Question ST-3 Share option timing

Question. An employee receives an employment-related share option and later exercises it at a discount. When is the benefit normally measured?

中文題目：僱員因受僱關係取得股份期權，其後以折讓價行使。通常何時計算應課稅利益？

Answer. The taxable benefit is generally measured when the option is exercised, released, or assigned, depending on the event, with the gain computed by reference to the relevant market value and exercise price rules.

中文答案：一般在期權被行使、放棄或轉讓時，按相關事件計算應課稅利益，通常會參考市值與行使價等規則計算收益。

3. Property Tax - Rental Income and Corporate Owners

Illustration PrT-1 Tenant-paid expenses

Question. A tenant pays HK$20,000 repair costs that the landlord was obliged to bear under the lease. Is the payment ignored for property tax?

中文題目：租客支付 HK$20,000 修葺費，而根據租約該費用本應由業主承擔。物業稅是否可忽略該款項？

Answer. No. Where the tenant discharges an obligation of the owner, the amount can be treated as consideration for use of the property. The statutory 20% allowance then applies in computing net assessable value.

中文答案：不可忽略。若租客代業主履行責任，該款項可被視為使用物業的代價，然後在計算應評稅淨值時扣除 20% 法定修葺免稅額。

Illustration PrT-2 Simple NAV computation

Question. Annual rent is HK$360,000. Rates of HK$12,000 are paid by the owner. No irrecoverable rent. Compute net assessable value.

中文題目：全年租金 HK$360,000，差餉 HK$12,000 由業主支付，沒有不能追回租金。計算應評稅淨值。

Assessable value before allowance: 360,000 - 12,000 = 348,000
Less statutory repairs allowance: 348,000 x 20% = 69,600
Net assessable value: 278,400

Answer. NAV is HK$278,400.

中文答案：應評稅淨值為 HK$278,400。

Question PrT-3 Corporate property owner

Question. A Hong Kong company lets out an office and the rental income is already included in profits tax. Can it avoid double tax under property tax?

中文題目：香港公司出租辦公室，租金收入已納入利得稅課稅。可否避免再繳物業稅？

Answer. A corporation can usually seek exemption from property tax where the property income is chargeable to profits tax. The rental stream is then dealt with under profits tax rather than being taxed twice.

中文答案：公司如相關物業收入已須繳利得稅，通常可申請豁免物業稅，避免同一租金收入被重複課稅。

4. Personal Assessment - Election and Loss Set-off

Illustration PA-1 Mortgage interest limit

Question. Under personal assessment, an individual has property NAV of HK$60,000 and interest of HK$75,000 on the loan used to buy that income-producing property. How much interest can be deducted against that property income?

中文題目：在個人入息課稅下，某人有物業應評稅淨值 HK$60,000，購買該收租物業的貸款利息為 HK$75,000。可扣除多少利息？

Answer. HK$60,000. The property-loan interest deduction is limited by the net assessable value of the relevant property included in personal assessment.

中文答案：HK$60,000。可扣除的物業貸款利息以納入個人入息課稅的相關物業應評稅淨值為上限。

Illustration PA-2 Business loss limit

Question. Total income after allowable deductions becomes negative because of concessionary deductions and a business loss. How much personal assessment loss can be carried forward?

中文題目：扣除特惠扣除及業務虧損後，總入息變成負數。可結轉的個人入息課稅虧損是多少？

Answer. The carry-forward personal assessment loss is limited to the business loss element. A deficit caused by personal allowances or non-business concessionary deductions is not carried forward as a business loss.

中文答案：可結轉的個人入息課稅虧損以業務虧損部分為限。由個人免稅額或非業務性特惠扣除造成的不足額，不會作為業務虧損結轉。

Question PA-3 Married couple election

Question. A married person wants personal assessment, but the spouse also has income chargeable to tax. Can one spouse elect alone?

中文題目：已婚人士想選擇個人入息課稅，但配偶亦有應課稅收入。一方可否單獨選擇？

Answer. Generally no. Where both spouses have income within the personal assessment framework, joint election is required. This is important when modelling whether personal assessment is beneficial.

中文答案：一般不可以。若夫婦雙方均有屬個人入息課稅框架內的收入，通常需要共同選擇。判斷個人入息課稅是否有利時必須留意這點。

5. Stamp Duty - Instruments, Property, Shares, Relief

Question SD-1 Instrument-based tax

Question. Why is it imprecise to say that stamp duty taxes "transactions"?

中文題目：為何說印花稅是對「交易」課稅並不精確？

Answer. Stamp duty is charged on instruments. A transaction matters because it produces or explains the instrument, but the charge is imposed by reference to the stampable document and the relevant charging head.

中文答案：印花稅是對文書課稅。交易本身重要，是因為它產生或解釋該文書；但真正課稅基礎是可予徵收印花稅的文件及相關課稅項目。

Illustration SD-2 Hong Kong stock transfer

Question. Hong Kong shares are sold for HK$100,000 but market value is HK$120,000. Which amount is used for ad valorem stamp duty?

中文題目：香港股票以 HK$100,000 出售，但市值為 HK$120,000。從價印花稅應以哪個金額計算？

Answer. HK$120,000. For Hong Kong stock transfers, duty is generally computed on the higher of consideration and value. Check the current stock duty rate before filing, as rates have changed over time.

中文答案：HK$120,000。香港股票轉讓一般按代價及價值兩者中較高者計算印花稅。由於股票印花稅率曾有變動，實際申報前應查核現行稅率。

Question SD-3 Associated company relief

Question. ParentCo transfers Hong Kong immovable property to a 100%-owned subsidiary. What relief may be relevant?

中文題目：母公司把香港不動產轉讓予其 100% 擁有的附屬公司。可能涉及哪項印花稅寬免？

Answer. Associated-company relief under SDO s.45 may be relevant if the ownership threshold and continuity conditions are satisfied. The parties must monitor the post-transfer association period because relief can be clawed back if the conditions break.

中文答案：如符合持股比例及持續關聯條件，可能適用《印花稅條例》第 45 條關聯公司寬免。轉讓後仍須監察關聯關係維持期，否則寬免可能被撤回。

6. Cross-border Profits Tax - Withholding and Non-residents

Question CB-1 Non-resident entertainer

Question. A Hong Kong event organizer pays a non-resident performer's company for a Hong Kong performance. Why might Hong Kong tax be withheld even if the performer is paid through a company?

中文題目：香港活動主辦方向非居民表演者的公司支付香港演出費。即使款項經公司支付，為何仍可能需要在香港預扣稅？

Answer. The IRO contains deeming and collection rules for non-resident entertainers and sportspeople. Interposing a company does not necessarily remove the Hong Kong charge where the performance activity is in Hong Kong.

中文答案：《稅務條例》對非居民演藝人員及運動員有視作收入及徵收規則。即使中間有公司收款，只要演出活動在香港進行，未必能避免香港稅務責任。

Illustration CB-2 Deemed profit method

Question. If the law taxes a non-resident entertainer on a deemed profit basis, what are the two moving parts in the computation?

中文題目：若法例以視作利潤方法向非居民表演者課稅，計算時主要有哪兩個變動部分？

Answer. First identify the gross payment that falls within the deeming rule. Then apply the statutory deemed-profit fraction and the applicable tax rate. If the actual-profit method is claimed, only properly connected deductible expenses should be used.

中文答案：第一，確定受視作規則涵蓋的總付款；第二，套用法定視作利潤比例及適用稅率。如改用實際利潤方法，只應扣除與香港演出適當相關的可扣稅開支。
